dishes.title: Tamagoyaki
dishes.summary: A sweet and savoury Japanese omelette built from thin layers of dashi-seasoned egg, each rolled around the last until it forms a neat, sliceable block. It follows the French omelette because it asks for the same control of heat, but over many small layers and with a rhythm you must keep going from the first pour to the last roll.
skills: cooking thin layers in a square pan
rolling and pressing in a mat
equipment: Rectangular tamagoyaki pan, about 5 by 7 inches (13 by 18 cm), or an 8 inch (20 cm) nonstick frying pan
Bamboo sushi mat (makisu) or a clean tea towel
Chopsticks or a thin silicone spatula
Fine mesh sieve and a jug with a pouring lip
Folded kitchen paper for oiling the pan

ingredients.note: at room temperature so they cook evenly
home-made or from instant granules; kombu dashi keeps it vegetarian
the sugar is why it browns so readily, so watch the heat
regular soy works but darkens the egg
a few drops on the daikon

mise: Make or measure the dashi and let it cool to room temperature; hot dashi starts cooking the egg in the bowl.
Stir the sugar, mirin, soy and salt into the dashi until the sugar dissolves completely.

Crack the eggs into a bowl and cut through them with chopsticks in a side to side motion, keeping the chopstick tips on the base of the bowl, for 30 seconds. You want the whites broken up with as few bubbles as possible.
Stir in the seasoned dashi, then pour everything through the sieve into the jug.
Fold a square of kitchen paper into a pad, dip it in the oil and leave it on a saucer by the stove.
Lay the bamboo mat on the board beside the stove, and grate and squeeze the daikon.

timeline.do: Dashi made and cooling; eggs out of the fridge.
Season the dashi, beat and strain the egg, set up the oil pad and mat.
Heat the pan and cook the layers, five or six of them, without stopping.
Roll the finished omelette in the mat and leave it to set.
Unroll, slice and serve warm or at room temperature with daikon.

steps.do: Set the pan over medium heat for 1 minute, then wipe the whole surface, corners included, with the oiled paper pad. Test the heat with a drop of egg from the tip of a chopstick.
steps.look: The test drop sizzles softly at once and sets in about 2 seconds without browning. If it browns instantly the pan is too hot; if it sits wet and silent it is too cool.
steps.mistake: Starting on high heat, which browns the sugar in the egg before a layer can be rolled.
steps.fix: Lift the pan off the heat for 20 seconds, wipe it again with the oil pad and test again. Through the whole cook, move the pan on and off the heat rather than fiddling with the dial.

steps.do: Pour in about a quarter of the egg, roughly 1/4 cup (60 ml), and tilt the pan so it covers the base in a thin even sheet. Pop any large bubbles with the chopstick tip.
steps.look: The egg spreads to every corner and starts to set from the edges within 10 to 15 seconds; the surface stays shiny and slightly wet.
steps.mistake: Pouring too much for the first layer, so it is thick and takes too long to set, and the base browns while the top is raw.
steps.fix: If it is thick, stir it lightly with the chopsticks like a soft scramble for a few seconds; the roll will hide it. Pour less next time.

steps.do: When the egg is about 70 percent set, with the top still glossy, roll it from the far side towards you in folds about 1 1/2 inches (4 cm) wide, using chopsticks or the spatula under the edge.
steps.look: The sheet lifts cleanly and folds over on itself. The surface glues to itself because it is still a little wet.
steps.mistake: Waiting until the layer is fully dry, so it will not stick to itself and the finished block falls apart into separate sheets when sliced.
steps.fix: Roll sooner on the next layer; a slightly damp surface is the glue. A first roll that is a little ragged is normal and gets hidden inside.

steps.do: Push the rolled egg back to the far end of the pan. Wipe the empty part of the pan with the oil pad, and lift the roll to oil under it too.
steps.look: A thin sheen across the whole pan, with no pooled oil.
steps.mistake: Skipping the oiling, so the next layer sticks to the pan and tears when rolled.
steps.fix: If a layer sticks, ease it free with the spatula and accept a small tear; oil thoroughly before every pour from now on.

steps.do: Pour in another quarter of the egg, about 1/4 cup (60 ml). Lift the roll with chopsticks and tilt the pan so the raw egg runs underneath it.
steps.look: The new egg spreads under and behind the roll and begins to set at the edges.
steps.mistake: Forgetting to let egg run under the roll, so the layers do not fuse and the block has a seam that splits.
steps.fix: If you forgot, press the roll down into the new egg while it is still liquid; it will glue as it sets.

steps.do: When this layer is 70 percent set, roll the existing log towards you over it, wrapping the new sheet around the old. Repeat the oil, pour, lift and roll until all the egg is used, usually 4 to 6 layers in total.
steps.look: The log grows thicker and more even with every layer. The outside is pale yellow with at most a few light golden patches.
steps.mistake: Letting the pan creep hotter as you go, so the outer layers brown dark and blister.
steps.fix: Every layer or two, take the pan off the heat for 15 seconds before pouring. A few light gold marks are acceptable; deep brown is not.

steps.do: After the last roll, use the spatula to press the log gently against the side of the pan on all four sides for 5 to 10 seconds each, shaping a neat rectangle.
steps.look: Sharp corners and flat sides, and the log feels springy, not sloppy.
steps.mistake: Pressing too hard, which squeezes liquid out of the centre and tears the outer layer.
steps.fix: Use the flat of the spatula with light pressure; the mat will finish the shaping.

steps.do: Tip the omelette onto the bamboo mat, roll the mat firmly around it and leave it for 5 minutes to set into shape.
steps.look: When unrolled, the surface carries the faint ridged pattern of the mat and the block holds its shape when lifted.
steps.mistake: Slicing straight from the pan, so the layers slide and the slices are uneven.
steps.fix: Give it the full 5 minutes. If you have no mat, wrap it tightly in a tea towel and press it into shape with your hands.

steps.do: Unroll and cut into slices about 3/4 inch (2 cm) thick with a sharp knife, using one long smooth stroke for each slice rather than sawing.
steps.look: Clean slices showing a fine spiral of layers with no gaps or raw egg at the centre.
steps.mistake: Sawing back and forth, which tears the layers.
steps.fix: Wipe the knife with a damp cloth between slices and cut in one pull.

dishes.science: Egg proteins begin to set at around 145°F (63°C) and turn rubbery well above that, so a thin layer in a moderate pan sets in seconds while staying tender. Dashi adds water and glutamates, which dilute the proteins slightly and make the set softer and juicier than a plain omelette. Sugar does two jobs: it raises the temperature at which the proteins bind, keeping the texture custardy, and it browns quickly through caramelisation and the Maillard reaction, which is why heat control matters more here than with an unsweetened egg. Straining removes the chalazae and stringy white, giving an even texture. Each layer fuses to the last because its surface proteins are still partly unset when rolled, so they bond as they finish cooking together.
dishes.plating: Serve three or four slices on a small rectangular plate, cut faces turned up so the spiral shows, slightly overlapping in a line. Place a small neat mound of squeezed grated daikon at one end with a few drops of soy on top. Keep the plate clean and the arrangement sparse; in Japanese service the precision of the slice is the decoration.

pairing.drink: A chilled glass of dry Junmai sake or a dry German Riesling. Both have enough acidity and light sweetness to match the sugar in the egg without overpowering the delicate dashi.
pairing.brennans: C.H. Berres ‘Old Vines’ Riesling 2022: an off-dry Mosel Riesling with bright acidity that echoes the sweet and savoury balance of the egg.

variations: Dashimaki tamago: double the dashi to 6 tbsp (90 ml), leave out the sugar, and cook more gently; it is softer, juicier and harder to roll.
Nori tamagoyaki: lay a sheet of nori over the second layer before rolling for a dark spiral through the slice.
Spring onion and shirasu: scatter finely sliced spring onion and tiny dried fish over the first two layers.
safety: Cook every layer until set; tamagoyaki is served fully cooked, with no runny egg inside.
If holding for a bento or packed lunch, cool it quickly and keep it chilled below 40°F (4°C).

dishes.title: Tortilla Española
dishes.summary: Spain's thick potato and onion omelette, the potatoes poached slowly in olive oil until soft, soaked in beaten egg and cooked into a cake that is flipped whole with a plate. It teaches low heat as a technique in its own right, the confit of potatoes, and the nerve to turn a heavy pan over in one committed movement.
skills: poaching potatoes slowly in olive oil
equipment: 10 inch (25 cm) nonstick or well seasoned frying pan with sloping sides
Large heavy sauté pan or a second wide frying pan for poaching the potatoes
Flat plate or pan lid at least 1 inch (2.5 cm) wider than the frying pan
Colander set over a heatproof bowl to catch the oil
Large mixing bowl and a fork or whisk
Oven gloves or a thick dry cloth

ingredients.note: peeled, quartered lengthways and sliced 1/8 inch (3 mm) thick
ordinary olive oil, not your best extra virgin; it is strained and reused
1/2 tsp (3 g) for the potatoes, 1 tsp (6 g) for the eggs

mise: Peel the potatoes, quarter them lengthways and slice 1/8 inch (3 mm) thick. Do not rinse; the surface starch helps the tortilla hold together.
Halve and thinly slice the onion.
Set the colander over a heatproof bowl next to the stove.
Crack the eggs into the large bowl, add 1 tsp (6 g) salt and beat until uniform but not frothy.
Find the plate or lid for the flip and check it covers the frying pan with room to spare.
Clear a path from the stove to the sink, and have oven gloves to hand.

timeline.do: Slice potatoes and onion; beat the eggs with salt.
Poach the potatoes and onion in oil over medium-low heat, about 20 minutes.
Drain, then fold the hot potatoes into the egg and rest 10 minutes.
Cook the first side, about 4 minutes.
Flip and cook the second side, 2 to 3 minutes.
Rest on the plate; serve warm or at room temperature.

steps.do: Pour the olive oil into the sauté pan and heat over medium heat until a slice of potato dropped in sizzles gently, about 3 minutes, roughly 250°F (120°C) if you have a thermometer. Add the potatoes, onion and 1/2 tsp (3 g) salt, and spread them out.
steps.look: Small, lazy bubbles rise around the potatoes; they should be just covered or nearly covered by oil. No browning.
steps.mistake: Oil so hot the potatoes fry and turn golden and crisp, which gives a dry, chewy tortilla.
steps.fix: Turn the heat down to medium-low at once. If edges have browned, carry on; the next batch will be better.

steps.do: Cook for 15 to 20 minutes over medium-low heat, turning the potatoes gently with the spatula every 3 or 4 minutes so they cook evenly without breaking up completely.
steps.look: The potatoes turn soft and slightly translucent and break when pressed with the spatula. The onion is soft and pale gold at most. A slice crushes easily between your fingers once cooled for a moment.
steps.mistake: Pulling the potatoes while still firm in the centre, so the tortilla is crunchy and raw tasting.
steps.fix: Taste a slice: if there is any resistance, give it 5 more minutes.

steps.do: Tip the potatoes and onion into the colander over the bowl and let them drain for 2 minutes, shaking once. Save the oil.
steps.look: The potatoes glisten but are not swimming. Most of the oil is in the bowl below.
steps.mistake: Not draining, so the egg mixture is greasy and the tortilla weeps oil.
steps.fix: Press lightly with the spatula to release more oil; keep 2 tbsp (30 ml) of the drained oil for the pan.

steps.do: While still hot, add the potatoes to the beaten eggs and fold together, pressing a few potatoes to break them up a little. Cover and leave to rest for 10 minutes.
steps.look: The egg thickens and turns slightly creamy as the heat of the potatoes begins to warm it. The mixture looks loose and porridge-like.
steps.mistake: Skipping the rest, so the egg and potato stay separate and the tortilla falls apart.
steps.fix: Give it the full 10 minutes; this is when starch and egg bind. Taste the egg for salt on a teaspoon after cooking a drop in the pan, and adjust.

steps.do: Heat 2 tbsp (30 ml) of the saved oil in the frying pan over medium-high heat until it shimmers, then pour in the potato and egg mixture all at once. Shake the pan and run the spatula around the edge to shape a rounded rim. After 30 seconds reduce to medium.
steps.look: A steady sizzle at the edges. The base sets and the edges pull in slightly as you run the spatula round them.
steps.mistake: A cold pan, so the egg sticks and the tortilla will not release for the flip.
steps.fix: Shake the pan every 30 seconds; as long as the whole tortilla slides freely, it will turn. If a patch sticks, slide the spatula underneath to free it.

steps.do: Cook for 3 to 4 minutes on medium, shaking the pan often, until the base is golden and the top is set around the outer inch (2.5 cm) but still liquid in the middle.
steps.look: When you shake the pan, the whole tortilla slides as one disc. The edges look set, the centre wobbles.
steps.mistake: Cooking the first side too long on high heat, so the base burns before the inside sets.
steps.fix: Lower the heat; browning should be golden, not dark brown.

steps.do: The flip: take the pan off the heat. Place the plate upside down on top of the pan. Wearing oven gloves, hold the plate firmly with one hand flat on it, grip the handle with the other, and in one quick confident movement, over the sink or the stove, turn the pan upside down so the tortilla lands on the plate.
steps.look: The tortilla drops onto the plate in one piece with the golden side facing up. A little runny egg may escape.
steps.mistake: Hesitating or turning slowly, which lets the tortilla slide out of position and break.
steps.fix: If it breaks, push the pieces back together on the plate; once it goes back in the pan the egg will glue it.

steps.do: Add 1 tsp (5 ml) more oil to the pan, then slide the tortilla back in, uncooked side down. Tuck the edges in with the spatula to round them, and cook 2 to 3 minutes over medium heat.
steps.look: The edges become neat and rounded. Press the centre lightly with a finger: it should feel set but still slightly soft, like a firm cushion.
steps.mistake: Cooking it until hard all the way through, which makes it dry and rubbery.
steps.fix: In Spain the centre is often left just creamy. Cook longer only if you prefer it fully set, and see the safety note.

steps.do: Slide or flip the tortilla onto a clean plate and leave it to rest for at least 5 minutes before cutting into wedges.
steps.look: The tortilla firms a little as it cools, and slices hold their shape with a moist, layered interior.
steps.mistake: Cutting immediately, so the soft centre runs.
steps.fix: Wait; tortilla is often eaten at room temperature, and it slices more cleanly once rested.

dishes.science: Cooking potatoes in oil at around 250°F (120°C), well below frying temperature, is a confit: heat travels in gently and the water inside the potato never boils violently, so the starch swells and softens while the surface stays tender rather than forming a crust. Because oil does not penetrate a potato that is still releasing steam, the slices absorb surprisingly little fat. When the hot potato meets beaten egg, its heat begins to thicken the egg proteins slightly and the surface starch dissolves into them, so after a ten-minute rest the mixture behaves as one batter. In the pan, the egg sets from the hot base upward, which is why a short first side and a gentle second side keep the centre moist.
dishes.plating: Serve on a board or round plate, cut into neat wedges, with one wedge pulled slightly away to show the layered, golden interior. For breakfast or tapas, cut into 1 1/2 inch (4 cm) squares and spear each with a cocktail stick. A small mound of alioli or a few slices of jamón on the side is enough.

pairing.drink: A chilled Manzanilla sherry. It is bone dry and salty, which cuts through the olive oil and egg, and it is what many Spanish bars pour with a pincho de tortilla.
pairing.brennans: La Cigarrera Manzanilla Sanlúcar de Barrameda NV (375 ml): a dry, saline Manzanilla that is the classic Spanish partner for tortilla.

variations: Tortilla sin cebolla: leave out the onion for the plainer style some Spanish cooks insist on.
Tortilla con chorizo: fry 3 oz (85 g) of sliced cured chorizo, drain it, and fold it in with the potatoes.
Tortilla de patatas y pimientos: add one sliced green pepper to the potatoes for the last 10 minutes of poaching.
safety: A creamy centre means the egg is not fully cooked; for anyone pregnant, elderly, very young or with a weak immune system, use pasteurised eggs or cook until the centre is set, 160°F (71°C).
Hot oil: never leave the poaching pan unattended, keep the oil no more than half the depth of the pan and lower potatoes in gently.
Let the reused oil cool completely before straining and storing it, and do not reuse it more than two or three times.

dishes.title: Chilaquiles Verdes
dishes.summary: Fried corn tortilla chips simmered for a minute in a charred tomatillo salsa verde, topped with crema, cheese, onion and a fried egg. It is in the course because it brings three skills together: charring vegetables for depth, frying chips so they stay crisp, and timing the soak to the second so the dish lands between crunch and softness.
equipment: Rimmed baking tray lined with foil
Heavy pot or deep frying pan, at least 4 inches (10 cm) deep
Wire rack set over a tray
12 inch (30 cm) wide frying pan or sauté pan
Nonstick frying pan for the eggs

ingredients.item: Corn tortillas, preferably a day old
ingredients.note: cut into 6 wedges each; slightly dry tortillas fry crisper
husked and rinsed of their sticky coating
use 1 for a milder salsa, or swap for 1 jalapeño
the half cut in thick wedges for charring; the quarter sliced paper thin and rinsed
plus a few sprigs to garnish
one per person, or two for hearty appetites

ingredients.item: Mexican crema or soured cream thinned with a little milk

mise: Cut the tortillas into 6 wedges each and spread them on a tray to dry for 30 minutes if they are fresh.
Husk and rinse the tomatillos; halve any larger than a golf ball.
Set the oven's overhead grill (broiler) to high with a rack about 4 inches (10 cm) below the element.
Slice the garnish onion paper thin and soak it in cold water to soften its bite; drain before serving.
Pick the coriander; crumble the cheese; thin the crema with 1 tbsp (15 ml) milk if it is stiff.
Set up the frying station: pot with oil, thermometer clipped on, wire rack over a tray beside it, spider ready. Keep the area dry and handles turned inwards.

timeline.do: Cut and dry tortillas. Prepare garnishes.
Char the tomatillos, chillies, onion and garlic under the grill, 10 to 12 minutes.
Blend the salsa and simmer it 10 minutes. Meanwhile heat the frying oil.
Fry the chips in batches and drain on the rack.
Fry the eggs. Slice the avocado.
Bring the salsa back to a simmer and toss the chips in it for 60 to 90 seconds.
Plate at once with crema, cheese, onion, avocado and the egg on top.

steps.do: Spread the tomatillos, chillies, onion wedges and unpeeled garlic on the foil-lined tray and slide it under the hot grill. Grill for 5 to 6 minutes, until blackened in patches, then turn everything with tongs and grill another 4 to 5 minutes.
steps.look: Tomatillos blistered and charred in spots, slumped and olive green, leaking juice. Chillies blackened and soft. You smell a sweet, smoky char.
steps.mistake: Pulling them while still bright green and firm, which gives a sharp, raw-tasting salsa.
steps.fix: Leave them until they collapse; a tomatillo that holds its shape is not cooked through. Black patches are flavour, but rescue the garlic if it chars completely.

steps.do: Let everything cool for 5 minutes. Squeeze the garlic from its skin, pull the stems off the chillies, and tip the vegetables with all the juices from the tray into the blender. Add the coriander and 1 tsp (6 g) salt and blend until fairly smooth, about 30 seconds.
steps.look: A speckled, pale olive green purée with flecks of char.
steps.mistake: Blending piping hot vegetables with the lid clamped down; steam pressure can blow the lid off.
steps.fix: Let them cool a few minutes, fill the blender no more than half, and vent the lid with a folded towel over it.

steps.do: Heat 1 tbsp (15 ml) oil in the wide pan over medium-high heat until shimmering. Pour in the salsa all at once (it will spit) and stir. Add the stock and simmer for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring now and then.
steps.look: The salsa hisses loudly, then settles into a simmer. It darkens slightly from bright to deeper green and thickens to the consistency of single cream.
steps.mistake: Skipping the fry and simmer, so the salsa tastes raw and watery and drowns the chips.
steps.fix: If it is too thick, add stock a splash at a time; too thin, simmer a few minutes longer. Taste and add salt; it should be well seasoned and tangy.

steps.do: Meanwhile heat the frying oil to 350°F (175°C) over medium-high heat. Fry the tortilla wedges in 3 or 4 batches, a handful at a time, stirring with the spider, for 2 to 3 minutes per batch.
steps.look: Vigorous bubbling that slows as the chips crisp. They turn golden, and the noise drops from a roar to a gentle fizz when they are done. Lifted out, they feel rigid.
steps.mistake: Overloading the pot, which drops the oil temperature so the chips soak up oil and turn leathery.
steps.fix: Fry smaller batches and let the oil return to 350°F (175°C) on the thermometer between them.

steps.do: Lift each batch onto the wire rack and sprinkle immediately with a pinch of salt.
steps.look: Chips that snap cleanly, with no oily pools beneath them.
steps.mistake: Draining on kitchen paper, where the chips sit in their own oil and steam soft underneath.
steps.fix: Use the rack. If the chips soften before use, crisp them in a 300°F (150°C) oven for 5 minutes.

steps.do: Fry the eggs in a nonstick pan with a little oil over medium heat, basting the whites with the hot oil, for 2 to 3 minutes until the whites are set and the yolks still soft. Slice the avocado.
steps.look: Whites fully set and lacy at the edge, yolks glossy and domed.
steps.mistake: Frying the eggs after the chips are in the sauce, so the chips go soggy while you wait.
steps.fix: Eggs first, held on a warm plate. The chips in salsa wait for nothing.

steps.do: Bring the salsa back to a lively simmer. Tip in all the chips and fold them through with tongs or a spatula for 60 to 90 seconds only, then take the pan off the heat.
steps.look: Every chip coated in green, the edges still crisp and the centres just beginning to soften. You can still hear a faint crackle as you fold.
steps.mistake: Letting the chips sit in the sauce for minutes, which turns them to mush.
steps.fix: Count the seconds out loud. If they softened too much, scatter a handful of fresh chips over the top for crunch.

steps.do: Divide among warm plates straight away. Zigzag the crema over each, scatter the cheese and the drained onion, lay on the avocado and top each plate with a fried egg and a few coriander sprigs.
steps.look: A glossy green mound with white crema lines, white cheese, pale onion rings, green avocado and a golden yolk on top.
steps.mistake: Plating slowly or garnishing in the pan, so the chips keep soaking.
steps.fix: Have every garnish lined up before the chips go in; the whole plate-up should take under 2 minutes.

dishes.science: Charring tomatillos under intense heat drives off water, concentrates their sugars and creates new roasted, smoky compounds through the Maillard reaction and the breakdown of sugars at the surface. Frying the blended salsa briefly in hot oil does the same again: water evaporates quickly at the surface and the flavours deepen and round off, a step Mexican cooks call sazonar. The chips stay crisp because frying at 350°F (175°C) drives nearly all the water out of the tortilla and sets its starch into a rigid, porous structure. When that dry starch meets hot liquid it immediately starts to absorb and soften, so the soak time decides the texture. Tomatillos are high in pectin, which is why the salsa clings rather than running off.
dishes.plating: Use wide, warm, shallow plates. Pile the chilaquiles into a loose mound, not flattened, so some edges stand up crisp. Pipe or spoon the crema in thin parallel zigzags, then scatter cheese and onion so that colour is spread evenly. Fan three avocado slices on one side and crown the top with the egg, yolk centred, then two or three coriander sprigs. Serve refried beans in a separate small bowl so they do not wet the chips.

pairing.drink: A Michelada or a Bloody Mary: the tomato, lime and spice echo the tang of the tomatillo, and it is a classic late breakfast drink.
pairing.brennans: Brennan’s Bloody Mary: savoury, spiced and bright, it meets the sharp green salsa on equal terms at brunch.

variations: Chilaquiles rojos: char 1 lb (450 g) plum tomatoes and 2 rehydrated guajillo chillies instead of tomatillos and serranos.
With chicken: fold 2 cups (280 g) shredded poached chicken into the salsa a minute before the chips.
Divorciados: make half a batch of salsa roja and serve green on one side, red on the other, the egg in the middle.
safety: Deep frying: fill the pot no more than one third full, keep the thermometer in, lower chips in gently, and never add water. Keep a lid nearby to smother a fire; never use water on burning oil.
Use a thermometer and do not let oil go above 375°F (190°C).
For soft-yolked eggs and anyone vulnerable (pregnant, elderly, very young, immune compromised), use pasteurised eggs or cook the yolk until firm.

dishes.title: Croque Madame
dishes.summary: The Parisian café sandwich of ham and Gruyère, coated in a cheese sauce, browned under the overhead grill (broiler) and crowned with a fried egg. It is here because it teaches béchamel, the first of the mother sauces, and its offspring mornay, then puts both to work in a dish where timing and heat from above decide everything.
skills: a béchamel from roux and milk
equipment: Medium heavy saucepan, about 2 quarts (2 litres)
Large heavy frying pan or griddle
Rimmed baking tray lined with baking paper
Nonstick frying pan for the eggs

ingredients.note: 2 tbsp (28 g) for the roux, 2 tbsp (28 g) for toasting
adjust to taste; the ham and cheese are salty
2 oz (55 g) in the sauce, the rest on the sandwiches

ingredients.item: Pain de mie or good white sandwich bread
ingredients.note: slightly stale bread toasts more evenly

ingredients.item: Thinly sliced cooked ham (jambon de Paris)

mise: Warm the milk in a small pan or the microwave until steaming, with the bay leaf if using; do not boil.
Grate all the Gruyère and divide it: 2 oz (55 g) for the sauce, 3 oz (85 g) for the sandwiches.
Line the baking tray with baking paper and set the oven's overhead grill to high, rack about 5 inches (12 cm) below the element.
Lay out the bread slices, ham and mustard for assembly.
Snip the chives.
Soften 2 tbsp (28 g) butter for spreading on the outside of the bread.

timeline.do: Warm the milk, grate the cheese, heat the grill.
Make the roux and béchamel, simmer 8 minutes, finish as mornay.
Assemble and toast the sandwiches in the frying pan.
Spread with mornay and cheese and grill until bubbling and spotted brown.
Fry the eggs.
Egg on each sandwich, chives, serve.

steps.do: Melt 2 tbsp (28 g) butter in the saucepan over medium-low heat. When it foams, add the flour all at once and whisk constantly for 2 minutes.
steps.look: A smooth paste that bubbles gently and smells of biscuits, still pale like sand. This is a white roux.
steps.mistake: Letting the roux brown, which gives a nutty, darker sauce with less thickening power.
steps.fix: Keep the heat low. If it has turned beyond light straw colour, start again; it costs only a minute.

steps.do: Take the pan off the heat and remove the bay leaf from the milk. Pour in about a third of the warm milk while whisking hard, then return the pan to medium heat and add the rest of the milk in two more additions, whisking until smooth each time.
steps.look: The mixture seizes into a thick paste with the first milk, then loosens to a smooth, lump-free sauce as more milk goes in.
steps.mistake: Dumping cold milk into a hot roux all at once and not whisking, which makes lumps.
steps.fix: Whisk vigorously into the corners. If lumps remain, push the sauce through a sieve with the back of a ladle.

steps.do: Bring the sauce to a gentle simmer, whisking, and cook for 6 to 8 minutes, stirring the bottom and corners with a spatula every minute or so.
steps.look: The sauce thickens until it coats the back of a spoon and a finger drawn through it leaves a clean line. The raw flour taste is gone.
steps.mistake: Stopping as soon as it thickens, so the sauce tastes of raw flour and pasty starch.
steps.fix: Keep simmering gently for the full time; taste a little and you will notice the change from floury to smooth and milky.

steps.do: Off the heat, stir in 2 oz (55 g) of the Gruyère, a few gratings of nutmeg, 1/2 tsp (3 g) salt and a pinch of white pepper. Stir until the cheese melts. You now have a mornay sauce.
steps.look: A thick, glossy, pale gold sauce that falls slowly from the spoon in ribbons.
steps.mistake: Adding the cheese over high heat or boiling it afterwards, which makes it stringy and greasy.
steps.fix: Always add cheese off the heat. If it splits, whisk in 1 tbsp (15 ml) warm milk until smooth again.

steps.do: Assemble: spread 4 slices of bread with mustard on one side. Lay ham on top, then divide half of the remaining Gruyère, about 1 1/2 oz (40 g), between the four (the other half is for the topping), then close with the other bread. Butter the outsides lightly.
steps.look: Four neat sandwiches, ham and cheese reaching the edges but not hanging over.
steps.mistake: Overfilling, so the sandwich slides apart and heats unevenly.
steps.fix: One even layer of ham, folded to fit, is enough.

steps.do: Toast the sandwiches in the large frying pan over medium heat for 2 to 3 minutes per side, pressing gently with the fish slice, until golden on both sides.
steps.look: Even golden brown faces and the cheese inside starting to melt at the edges.
steps.mistake: High heat, which burns the bread before the cheese melts.
steps.fix: Lower the heat; the grill will finish heating the centre.

steps.do: Move the sandwiches to the lined tray. Spread a thick layer of mornay over the top of each, right to the edges, about 3 tbsp (45 ml) each, then scatter the remaining Gruyère over. Slide under the grill for 3 to 5 minutes.
steps.look: The sauce puffs and bubbles and the top browns in deep golden and toasty brown spots. You smell browned cheese.
steps.mistake: Walking away from the grill; it goes from golden to burnt in under a minute.
steps.fix: Stand and watch, turning the tray once for even colour. If one corner darkens fast, move it away from the hot spot.

steps.do: While the sandwiches grill, fry the eggs in a little butter in the nonstick pan over medium-low heat for 3 minutes, until the whites are completely set and the yolks still soft. Season with a pinch of salt.
steps.look: Tender, fully set whites with no browned, crispy edges, and bright yolks.
steps.mistake: Frying the eggs hot and fast, which gives tough, frilly whites that look untidy on the sandwich.
steps.fix: Lower the heat and cover the pan for the last minute to set the top of the white.

steps.do: Lift each sandwich onto a warm plate, slide an egg on top with the fish slice and finish with chives and a twist of pepper.
steps.look: A golden, bubbling crust with a neat egg sitting in the centre.
steps.mistake: Leaving the finished sandwiches waiting while the eggs cook, so the sauce sets and the bread steams soft.
steps.fix: Time the eggs so both finish together; that is the station skill.

dishes.science: A roux works because flour starch granules are first coated in fat, which keeps them apart so they do not clump when liquid arrives. As the milk heats to a simmer, the granules absorb water and swell, then burst and release long starch molecules that tangle together and thicken the sauce. That process completes near boiling, which is why béchamel must simmer for several minutes before the raw taste and grainy texture disappear. Cheese is an emulsion of fat, protein and water; heated too hard, its proteins tighten and squeeze out fat, giving strings and grease. The starch in béchamel coats the cheese proteins and stops that, which is why mornay can be grilled hard. Under the grill, milk sugars and proteins brown quickly through the Maillard reaction.
dishes.plating: Serve each croque on a warm plain white plate, slightly off centre, cut corner to corner only if you want to show the layers. A small handful of dressed frisée or watercress with a sharp vinaigrette sits beside it to cut the richness. Snip chives over the egg only, and wipe any drips of sauce from the plate rim.

pairing.drink: A dry Crémant or Champagne. The bubbles and acidity scrub the palate after the rich sauce, and toasty bottle aged notes match the browned cheese.
pairing.brennans: Eggs Hussarde: Brennan's own brunch classic that also builds on ham and a classic sauce, a good dish to compare when describing richness to guests.

variations: Croque monsieur: the same sandwich without the egg.
Croque provençal: add a slice of ripe tomato under the cheese.
Croque norvégienne: replace the ham with smoked salmon and finish with dill.
safety: The grill element and tray are extremely hot; use oven gloves and pull the tray out on its rack rather than reaching in.
For anyone vulnerable, use pasteurised eggs if the yolk is served runny, or cook it until firm.

dishes.title: Galette Complète (Breton Buckwheat Crêpe)
dishes.summary: A thin, lacy buckwheat crêpe from Brittany, filled with ham, Gruyère and an egg and folded into a square so the yolk peeks out of a window. It takes the crêpe lesson onto buckwheat, a flour with no gluten that handles differently and needs a long rest and a confident spread.
skills: folding around ham, Gruyère and egg
equipment: 11 to 12 inch (28 to 30 cm) crêpe pan, flat cast iron or carbon steel, or a large nonstick frying pan
Crêpe spreader (rozell) or the back of a ladle
Ladle that holds about 1/2 cup (120 ml)
Long thin palette knife or offset spatula
Folded kitchen paper and a small dish of melted butter
Baking tray and a low oven for holding

ingredients.note: pure buckwheat, sometimes sold as sarrasin or blé noir

ingredients.item: Coarse grey sea salt or fine salt

ingredients.note: optional but makes the batter easier for a first attempt
for the pan and to brush the finished galettes

mise: At least 2 hours ahead, or the night before, make the batter so it can rest.
Grate the cheese and lay out the ham slices, folded in half.
Crack each filling egg into its own small cup so you can slide it in cleanly.
Melt the butter and fold a kitchen paper pad for wiping the pan.
Heat the oven to 200°F (95°C) with a baking tray inside for holding finished galettes.

timeline.do: Make the batter and leave it to rest in the fridge.
Stir the batter and adjust its thickness. Heat the pan and the holding oven.
Cook a test galette, then fill and fold each one, about 4 minutes each.
Brush with butter and serve.

steps.do: Whisk the buckwheat flour and salt in the bowl. Make a well, add the batter egg if using and about half the water, and whisk from the centre outwards to a thick smooth paste. Beat this paste hard for 2 minutes, then whisk in the rest of the water to make a batter.
steps.look: A smooth, grey-brown batter the thickness of single cream, with no lumps. It smells earthy and slightly nutty.
steps.mistake: Adding all the water at once, which leaves stubborn lumps of flour.
steps.fix: Whisk lumps against the side of the bowl or pass the batter through a sieve.

steps.do: Cover and refrigerate for at least 2 hours, ideally overnight.
steps.look: After resting, the batter has thickened slightly and may have a few bubbles on the surface.
steps.mistake: Cooking it straight away; unrested buckwheat batter tears and is gritty.
steps.fix: If short of time, rest it for at least 1 hour at room temperature. Before cooking, stir and add water 1 tbsp (15 ml) at a time until it runs off a spoon like single cream.

steps.do: Heat the pan over medium-high heat for 3 minutes. Wipe it with the butter-dipped paper pad. Pour about 1/2 cup (120 ml) batter into the centre and immediately spread it outwards in a spiral with the spreader, or tilt and swirl the pan, to cover the base in one thin layer.
steps.look: The batter sizzles on contact and sets almost instantly into a thin sheet full of tiny holes. It should be about 1/16 inch (2 mm) thick.
steps.mistake: A pan that is not hot enough, so the batter slides around and the galette is pale and limp.
steps.fix: Use the first galette as a test and expect to discard or eat it. Adjust the heat and the batter thickness from what it tells you.

steps.do: Cook for 1 to 2 minutes, without moving it, until the edges lift and brown and the top looks dry. Run the palette knife round the edge and flip it over.
steps.look: The underside is a deep lacy brown and the edges are crisp and pulling away from the pan.
steps.mistake: Trying to flip too early, so it tears.
steps.fix: Wait until the edge lifts by itself; buckwheat has no gluten to hold it together until it is set.

steps.do: Turn the heat to medium. Brush the top with a little melted butter, scatter a quarter of the cheese in the middle, lay a slice of ham on it, then make a small well in the cheese and slide in an egg. Spread the white a little with the back of a spoon so it cooks evenly, keeping the yolk whole.
steps.look: The white starts to turn opaque from the edges in, and the cheese begins to melt.
steps.mistake: Leaving the white thick around the yolk, so the yolk overcooks before the white sets.
steps.fix: Spread the white thinly; you can cover the pan with a lid for 30 seconds to help the top set.

steps.do: When the white is set but the yolk still soft, about 2 to 3 minutes, fold in four sides of the galette with the palette knife to make a square, leaving the yolk visible in the middle.
steps.look: A neat square with crisp brown edges framing the cheese, ham and a glossy yolk.
steps.mistake: Folding before the white has set, so it runs out as a slimy layer.
steps.fix: Give it 30 seconds more with the lid on, then fold.

steps.do: Slide onto a warm plate or the holding tray in the oven, brush the edges with a little more butter and grind black pepper over the yolk. Wipe the pan with butter and repeat with the remaining batter and fillings.
steps.look: Glossy, crisp edges, and the pan ready and evenly greased for the next one.
steps.mistake: Not re-greasing, so each galette sticks more than the last.
steps.fix: Wipe the pan with the butter pad before every galette.

dishes.science: Buckwheat is not wheat and contains no gluten, so its batter has no stretchy network to hold it together. Its structure instead comes from starch and protein that set with heat, and from some soluble fibres that make the batter slightly viscous. Resting the batter lets the flour hydrate fully, so the starch swells evenly and the galette holds together instead of tearing, and it softens the gritty texture of the bran. A very hot pan is essential: the thin layer of batter sets the instant it lands, and the rapid evaporation of water creates the tiny holes that give a galette its lacy look. Butter on the surface browns and crisps the edges, giving the nutty, toasty flavour.
dishes.plating: Serve each galette on a large warm flat plate, folded side up, so the square frames the yolk like a window. Brush the edges with a final touch of butter so they shine. A small side salad of dressed lamb's lettuce and a bowl of dry cider complete the Breton picture.

pairing.drink: A dry Breton or Normandy cider, served in a bowl in the Breton way. Its tart apple acidity and light bubbles cut the butter and cheese.
pairing.brennans: Pierre Sparr Brut Rosé Crémant d’Alsace NV: a fresh, fruity sparkling wine that does for the butter and cheese what cider does in Brittany.

variations: Galette forestière: sautéed mushrooms and crème fraîche instead of ham.
Galette saucisse: a grilled Breton sausage rolled in a galette, eaten in the hand.
Galette with goat's cheese, honey and walnuts for a sweeter savoury version.
safety: Galettes are traditionally served with a soft yolk; for anyone vulnerable, use pasteurised eggs or cook until the yolk is set.
Keep the batter refrigerated while resting if it contains egg, and use it within 24 hours.

dishes.title: Kedgeree
dishes.summary: Smoked haddock poached in milk, flaked through basmati rice cooked in that smoky milk with curry spices, onion and butter, finished with jammy eggs, herbs and lemon. It introduces poaching fish gently below the boil, and shows how one cooking liquid can carry flavour through a whole dish.
equipment: Wide shallow pan or deep frying pan with a lid, for poaching
Medium heavy saucepan with a tight lid, for the rice
Large wide sauté pan or casserole, for finishing
Small saucepan for the eggs, and a bowl of iced water
Fine sieve and a measuring jug
Fish slice and a fork for flaking

ingredients.note: undyed is pale cream, not yellow; skin on is fine
rinsed until the water runs clear

ingredients.item: Flat-leaf parsley and coriander leaves, chopped

ingredients.note: half juiced, half cut in wedges
taste first; the fish is salty

mise: Rinse the rice in a sieve under cold water, rubbing with your fingers, until the water runs clear, about 1 minute. Leave it to drain.
Slice the onion; chop the herbs; crush the cardamom; cut the lemon.
Fill a small pan with water and bring it to the boil for the eggs; set a bowl of iced water beside it.
Lay the haddock skin side down in the wide pan.
Measure the spices into a small dish so they go in together.

timeline.do: Rinse rice, slice onion, water on for eggs.
Poach the haddock in milk, 6 to 8 minutes; strain and keep the milk.
Cook the rice in the poaching milk and water, 12 minutes plus 10 minutes resting.
Boil eggs 7 minutes, ice, peel. Soften the onion in butter, 12 to 15 minutes.
Bloom spices, fold in rice and flaked fish.
Eggs, herbs and lemon on top; serve warm.

steps.do: Pour the milk over the haddock with the bay leaves and add enough water just to cover the fish. Set over medium heat and bring to a bare simmer, then reduce to low, cover and poach for 6 to 8 minutes depending on thickness.
steps.look: Small bubbles at the edge of the pan only, never a rolling boil. The flesh turns from translucent to opaque and flakes when pressed at the thickest part.
steps.mistake: Boiling the milk, which toughens the fish, breaks it into shreds and can make the milk catch.
steps.fix: Pull the pan off the heat as soon as you see bubbles break the surface; the fish will finish cooking in the hot milk.

steps.do: Lift the fish onto a plate with the fish slice. Strain the poaching liquid into the jug and measure out 2 cups (480 ml) for the rice, topping up with water if there is less; keep any extra to loosen the finished dish. When the fish is cool enough to handle, peel off the skin and break the flesh into large flakes, checking carefully for pin bones.
steps.look: Pale, moist, large flakes. No bones. The liquid in the jug is smoky, salty and pale.
steps.mistake: Flaking the fish finely, so it vanishes into the rice.
steps.fix: Break it into pieces about the size of a thumbnail; it will break up further when folded.

steps.do: Put the rice in the saucepan with the cardamom and the 2 cups (480 ml) of poaching liquid. Bring to the boil, stir once, then cover tightly, turn the heat to its lowest and cook for 12 minutes. Turn off the heat and leave covered for 10 minutes.
steps.look: When you lift the lid, small steam holes dot the surface and the liquid is absorbed. The grains are separate and tender with no hard core.
steps.mistake: Lifting the lid and stirring during cooking, which breaks the grains and lets steam escape.
steps.fix: If the rice is still firm after resting, sprinkle 2 tbsp (30 ml) hot water over, cover and rest 5 minutes more.

steps.do: Lower the eggs into the boiling water with a spoon and boil for exactly 7 minutes, then move them to the iced water for 3 minutes. Peel under cold running water.
steps.look: When halved, the whites are set and the yolks are jammy, deep orange and soft set in the middle.
steps.mistake: Boiling them for 10 minutes or more, which gives chalky yolks with a grey ring.
steps.fix: Use a timer and ice them immediately. Room temperature eggs need only 6 1/2 minutes.

steps.do: Melt 3 tbsp (42 g) butter in the wide pan over medium-low heat. Add the onion with a pinch of salt and cook gently for 12 to 15 minutes, stirring now and then.
steps.look: The onion becomes soft, sweet and pale golden, collapsing in the pan. It smells sweet, not sharp.
steps.mistake: Rushing on high heat, so the onion browns at the edges and stays crunchy.
steps.fix: Lower the heat and add a splash of water if it begins to catch.

steps.do: Add the curry powder and turmeric to the onion and stir for 30 to 60 seconds until fragrant.
steps.look: The butter turns golden yellow and the spices smell toasty and warm, not raw and dusty.
steps.mistake: Burning the spices, which makes them bitter.
steps.fix: If they smell acrid or turn dark, start the onion again. Keep the heat medium-low.

steps.do: Tip in the rice and fold it through the spiced onion with a spatula, lifting from underneath until every grain is stained yellow. Add the flaked fish, the remaining butter, the cream if using and half the herbs, and fold very gently for 1 to 2 minutes until hot through. Squeeze in the lemon juice, taste and season.
steps.look: Golden, separate grains with large flakes of fish still whole. It smells of smoke, butter and spice.
steps.mistake: Stirring hard, which mashes the rice and breaks the fish into threads.
steps.fix: Use a lifting and folding motion, turning the pan, not a stirring one.

steps.do: Halve or quarter the eggs and arrange them on top, then scatter over the remaining herbs and serve with lemon wedges.
steps.look: Orange yolks glistening on golden rice, flecked with green.
steps.mistake: Folding the eggs in, so the yolks smear through the rice.
steps.fix: Eggs go on at the end and stay on top.

dishes.science: Smoked fish is lightly salted and cured, and its proteins tighten quickly above about 140°F (60°C), squeezing out moisture. Poaching below the boil keeps the outside of the fillet from overcooking before the centre is done, so the flakes stay large and moist. Milk works well because its fat and proteins absorb smoky, fat soluble flavour compounds released from the fish; cooking the rice in that liquid carries the smoke into every grain. Rinsing basmati removes loose surface starch, so the grains stay separate instead of gluing together. Curry spices are fat soluble too, which is why they are cooked briefly in butter: the hot fat releases and spreads their aromatic oils before the rice arrives.
dishes.plating: Serve family style from a warm wide dish or in shallow bowls. Mound the rice loosely, not pressed, then nestle the egg halves into the surface cut side up, spaced evenly. Scatter herbs over the eggs and the rice, add a lemon wedge at the side and a little extra black pepper on the yolks.

pairing.drink: A dry Riesling or a Grüner Veltliner. Their bright acidity cuts the butter and smoke, and a little spice in the wine suits the curry.
pairing.brennans: Loimer ‘Lois’ Grüner Veltliner 2022: crisp and peppery, it handles smoke, spice and egg together.

variations: Salmon kedgeree: hot-smoked salmon flaked through at the end instead of poached haddock.
Lentil kedgeree: add 1/2 cup (100 g) red lentils to the rice with an extra 1/2 cup (120 ml) liquid for a nod to khichdi.
Spiced up: add a slit green chilli and 1 tsp (2 g) cumin seeds to the butter with the onion.
safety: Cook the fish until opaque and flaking, 145°F (63°C) at the thickest point.
Cooked rice must not sit warm for long. Cool leftovers within an hour, refrigerate, and reheat only once until steaming hot, 165°F (74°C).
Jammy eggs are partly cooked; for anyone vulnerable, use pasteurised eggs or boil for 10 minutes.

dishes.title: Ackee and Saltfish
dishes.summary: Jamaica's national dish of desalted salt cod sautéed with onion, peppers, tomato, thyme and Scotch bonnet, then gently folded with buttery ackee. It teaches how to work with preserved food, by soaking and tasting salt cod until it is right, and how to fold a fragile ingredient without breaking it.
skills: folding in ackee without breaking it
equipment: Large bowl for soaking, and cling film
Medium saucepan for boiling the fish
12 inch (30 cm) frying pan or sauté pan
Chef's knife and board, and disposable gloves for the Scotch bonnet

ingredients.note: the thicker the piece, the longer the soak
sliced, whites and greens kept apart
seeded and minced for heat, or added whole for perfume only

mise: The night before, rinse the salt cod under cold running water, put it in a large bowl, cover with plenty of cold water and refrigerate for 12 hours, changing the water at least twice.
Drain the ackee very gently in a colander; do not stir or rinse hard. Leave it to sit.
Wearing gloves, seed and mince the Scotch bonnet; wash the board and knife straight after and do not touch your eyes.
Slice the onion, pepper and spring onions; dice the tomato; strip the thyme; mince the garlic.

timeline.do: Rinse the salt cod and put it to soak in the fridge, changing the water twice.
Boil the soaked cod 15 minutes; taste for salt; flake.
Prep vegetables; drain the ackee.
Sauté aromatics, add fish, then fold in ackee.
Serve with fried dumplings, boiled green bananas or hard dough bread.

steps.do: Drain the soaked cod, put it in the saucepan, cover with fresh cold water and bring to a boil over high heat. Simmer for 15 minutes, then drain. Taste a small flake.
steps.look: The fish turns opaque white and flakes when pressed. It should taste pleasantly salty, like well seasoned food, not harsh like brine.
steps.mistake: Skipping the taste, so an under-soaked fish makes the dish inedibly salty.
steps.fix: If still too salty, cover with fresh water and boil for another 10 minutes, then taste again. Repeat until right.

steps.do: When cool enough to touch, flake the fish with a fork or your fingers into bite sized pieces, removing any skin, bones and dark membranes.
steps.look: Clean white flakes about 1/2 inch (1 cm) across.
steps.mistake: Shredding it into fine threads, which turns stringy.
steps.fix: Keep the flakes chunky; they break a little more in the pan.

steps.do: Heat the oil in the frying pan over medium heat. Add the onion and the white parts of the spring onions and cook for 4 to 5 minutes, stirring, until soft and translucent. Add the garlic, thyme and Scotch bonnet and cook 1 minute more.
steps.look: Soft, glossy onion and a powerful, fruity, peppery smell from the Scotch bonnet.
steps.mistake: Letting the garlic brown, which turns bitter.
steps.fix: Lower the heat before adding garlic, and keep it moving.

steps.do: Add the bell pepper and tomato and cook for 3 minutes, until the pepper is just tender and the tomato starts to break down.
steps.look: The tomato juices loosen the pan into a light sauce; the pepper is still bright.
steps.mistake: Cooking the peppers to mush.
steps.fix: Pull them while they still have a little bite.

steps.do: Add the flaked saltfish, the butter if using and the black pepper. Stir for 2 to 3 minutes to heat through and soak up the flavours.
steps.look: The fish is coated in the tomato and onion and steaming hot.
steps.mistake: Adding salt; the fish carries all the salt the dish needs.
steps.fix: Taste before seasoning with anything other than pepper.

steps.do: Reduce the heat to low. Tip the drained ackee over the top. Using a spatula, fold the ackee in with just two or three gentle lifts from the bottom of the pan. Cover and leave for 2 to 3 minutes to warm through.
steps.look: Plump, buttery yellow ackee pieces, mostly whole, nestled among the fish and peppers. It looks like softly scrambled egg.
steps.mistake: Stirring vigorously, which turns the ackee into yellow paste.
steps.fix: Stop folding as soon as it is mixed. If it has broken, serve it anyway: the flavour is the same, but fold less next time.

steps.do: Scatter the green spring onion over the top and serve straight from the pan.
steps.look: Bright yellow, red and green, glossy and steaming.
steps.mistake: Leaving it on the heat, which dries and breaks the ackee further.
steps.fix: Take it off the heat as soon as the ackee is hot.

dishes.science: Salt cod is preserved by salting and drying, which draws water out of the fish and makes it inhospitable to bacteria. Soaking reverses that by osmosis: fresh water moves back into the flesh while salt moves out into the surrounding water, and changing the water keeps that gradient steep so desalting continues. Boiling then finishes the job and cooks the fish. Ackee is a fruit whose cream coloured arils are rich in fat, which is why they taste buttery and soften into a texture like scrambled egg. Their cell walls are delicate, especially after canning, so heat and stirring break them apart easily. Unripe ackee contains hypoglycin, a toxin, which is why only commercially prepared canned ackee or properly ripened fruit is used.
dishes.plating: Serve on a warm plate in a loose mound, with two or three fried dumplings or boiled green banana halves leaning against it, and a slice of avocado if you like. Finish with a little fresh thyme and the green spring onion, so the yellow of the ackee shows through.

pairing.drink: A rum punch or a fresh ginger beer cocktail. The spice of ginger and the sweetness of rum suit Scotch bonnet heat and salty fish.

variations: Callaloo and saltfish: swap the ackee for 8 oz (225 g) of steamed callaloo or spinach.
With bacon: render 2 rashers of diced bacon at the start and cook the onion in the fat.
Saltfish fritters: mix the flaked cooked fish into a light flour batter with spring onion and Scotch bonnet and shallow fry spoonfuls.
safety: Use only canned ackee or fruit that has opened naturally on the tree; unripe or improperly prepared ackee contains hypoglycin, which is toxic. Never use the seeds or the pink membrane.
Soak salt cod in the fridge, not on the counter.
Wear gloves when cutting Scotch bonnet and wash hands, board and knife straight away.

dishes.title: Country Ham with Redeye Gravy
dishes.summary: Slices of salty dry-cured country ham fried in cast iron, the pan then deglazed with black coffee to make a thin, sharp gravy for spooning over ham, grits and biscuits. It is the most basic pan sauce there is: brown bits on the pan, a liquid to lift them, and a quick reduction.
equipment: Shallow dish for soaking the ham (optional)
Small saucepan for grits, with a whisk
Warm plates and a low oven

ingredients.note: bone-in centre slices if possible; check if the label says to cook before eating
only if the ham is very lean
to serve; cooked in 4 cups (960 ml) water and milk with butter
to serve, home-made from the Commis course

mise: If the ham is very salty, soak the slices in water or milk for 30 minutes, then pat dry.
With scissors, snip through the fat around the edge of each slice every 1 inch (2.5 cm) so it does not curl in the pan.
Brew the coffee strong and keep it hot.
Start the grits 40 minutes before serving and keep them warm.
Warm the plates in a 200°F (95°C) oven.

timeline.do: Soak the ham if salty. Start the grits.
Brew coffee; snip the ham fat; heat the skillet.
Fry the ham in two batches, 2 to 3 minutes a side.
Deglaze with coffee, reduce 2 minutes.
Spoon gravy over ham, grits and split biscuits.

steps.do: Heat the skillet over medium heat for 3 minutes. Lay two ham slices in the pan, fat edge touching the hot iron. Add the butter only if the ham has very little fat of its own.
steps.look: A steady sizzle as soon as the ham touches. The fat at the edges starts to turn clear and run.
steps.mistake: A pan that is too hot, which scorches the sugars in the cure before the ham heats through.
steps.fix: Medium is right. If it smokes, lift the pan off the heat for a minute.

steps.do: Fry for 2 to 3 minutes a side, pressing the slices flat with tongs, until browned at the edges and hot throughout. Move to a warm plate in the oven and fry the remaining slices.
steps.look: Edges browned and lightly crisp, the lean deep rosy red, fat translucent and golden. A brown crust (the fond) builds on the pan surface. The kitchen smells smoky and porky.
steps.mistake: Cooking too long, which makes country ham hard, dry and even saltier.
steps.fix: Country ham is lean and cured; it needs only to heat through and brown. Pull it as soon as both sides are coloured.

steps.do: Pour off all but about 1 tbsp (15 ml) of fat from the pan, keeping the brown bits. Return the pan to medium-high heat for 30 seconds.
steps.look: The fond on the bottom is deep brown, not black.
steps.mistake: Pouring away the browned bits with the fat.
steps.fix: Tilt the pan and spoon the fat off from one side; the fond stays stuck to the iron.

steps.do: Stand back and pour the hot coffee into the pan all at once. Add the sugar if using. Scrape the bottom firmly with the wooden spatula to lift every brown bit.
steps.look: A loud hiss and a cloud of steam; the coffee turns a rich, reddish brown as the fond dissolves into it.
steps.mistake: Leaning over the pan, and being caught by the burst of steam.
steps.fix: Hold the pan at arm's length and pour away from you.

steps.do: Add the water and simmer for 2 minutes, stirring, until reduced by about a third. Taste it.
steps.look: A thin, glossy, dark gravy with drops of ham fat floating on top that gather into a circle in the middle, the red eye.
steps.mistake: Expecting it to thicken like a flour gravy; redeye is meant to be thin.
steps.fix: If it tastes too strong or salty, add another splash of water; too weak, reduce a minute longer.

steps.do: Plate the ham beside a spoon of grits and a split biscuit, and spoon the hot gravy over all three.
steps.look: Shiny ham, gravy pooling into the grits and soaking into the biscuit.
steps.mistake: Letting the gravy cool; the fat sets and it turns greasy.
steps.fix: Serve straight from the skillet while it is bubbling.

dishes.science: Country ham is dry cured with salt, often sugar, then aged for months. Salt draws out water and concentrates flavour, and slow enzyme activity during ageing breaks proteins into savoury amino acids, which is why it tastes intense and needs very little cooking. Frying it creates fond: proteins and sugars from the ham stick to the hot iron and brown through the Maillard reaction. Those browned compounds dissolve readily in liquid, so a splash of hot coffee lifts them in seconds. Coffee works because its bitterness and acidity balance the salt and sweetness of the ham. Redeye gravy has no flour or starch, so it stays thin, and the rendered fat floats as a separate layer rather than emulsifying.
dishes.plating: Serve on a warm plate: a slice of ham laid across the centre, a spoon of grits in a neat pool to one side, and a split biscuit leaning on the grits. Spoon the gravy over the ham and let some run into the grits so the red eye of fat shows on top.

pairing.drink: Strong coffee with chicory, or for a late brunch a Brandy Milk Punch, whose cold cream and nutmeg soothe the salt.
pairing.brennans: Buttermilk Biscuit: Brennan's own biscuit is the natural partner for soaking up a thin, salty gravy like redeye.

variations: Without sugar: leave out the brown sugar for the sharper, more bitter gravy many Southern cooks prefer.
City ham: use a thick slice of cooked wet-cured ham, which is milder and needs only to brown.
With eggs: fry two eggs in the ham fat before deglazing and serve them alongside.
safety: Many dry-cured country hams are sold uncooked; if the label says cook before eating, fry until the meat reaches 145°F (63°C).
Hot coffee hitting a hot pan throws up scalding steam; pour away from you.

dishes.title: Full English Breakfast
dishes.summary: Sausages, back bacon, black pudding, grilled tomatoes, buttery mushrooms, beans, fried bread or toast and eggs, all hot and on one plate at the same moment. It is the first real lesson in running a station, because the cooking is easy and the timing is everything.
skills: running several pans and the overhead grill (broiler) at once
equipment: Large heavy frying pan, 12 inch (30 cm)
Second frying pan for mushrooms and eggs, 10 inch (25 cm) nonstick
Rimmed baking tray with a rack, for the overhead grill
Ovenproof dish for holding, and a low oven

ingredients.item: Good pork sausages (Cumberland, Lincolnshire or similar)

ingredients.note: wiped and halved or thickly sliced

ingredients.item: Bread for toast or fried bread
Fine salt, black pepper, fresh thyme

mise: Put the plates and an ovenproof holding dish beside the oven; they go in to warm once the grill has done the tomatoes, because one oven cannot be the grill and a low oven at once.
Set the overhead grill to medium-high, rack 4 inches (10 cm) below.
Halve the tomatoes, season the cut sides and add a little thyme and a drop of oil.
Wipe and slice the mushrooms; peel the black pudding; open the beans into the saucepan.
Lay everything out in cooking order on a tray: sausages, tomatoes, bacon, black pudding, mushrooms, beans, bread, eggs.
Make a running order on paper with times; this is how a line cook works.

timeline.do: Overhead grill on. Prep everything into order.
Sausages into the big pan over medium-low heat; turn every 3 to 4 minutes, about 20 to 25 minutes in all.
Tomatoes under the grill, about 10 to 12 minutes; then grill off, oven to 200°F (95°C), door open 2 minutes, and the plates, holding dish and tomatoes in.
Mushrooms in butter in the second pan, 8 to 10 minutes, then to the holding dish.
Bacon beside the sausages, 2 to 3 minutes a side. Black pudding into the bacon fat, 2 minutes a side. Hold.
Beans on low heat. Sausages checked at 160°F (71°C) and into the holding dish.
Fry the eggs in the second pan. Toast the bread.
Plate everything at once on hot plates.

steps.do: Put the oil in the large pan over medium-low heat, add the sausages and cook slowly for 20 to 25 minutes, turning them every 3 to 4 minutes with tongs so they colour evenly.
steps.look: A gentle, steady sizzle, never violent spitting. Skins turn glossy and evenly golden brown all over, with no burst splits.
steps.mistake: High heat, which splits the skins and leaves the outside burnt while the centre stays raw.
steps.fix: Lower the heat; patience is the technique. If the skins split, keep going, they are still fine to eat.

steps.do: As soon as the sausages are in, put the tomato halves cut side up on the rack under the grill and cook for 10 to 12 minutes. Move them to the holding dish, switch the grill off, set the oven to 200°F (95°C) and leave the door open for 2 minutes so the heat falls, then put the plates and the holding dish in to keep warm.
steps.look: The cut surface softens, sizzles and takes light brown spots at the edges; the tomatoes slump but hold their shape.
steps.mistake: Putting them too close to the element, so they char on top and stay cold inside.
steps.fix: Lower the rack a notch and give them longer.

steps.do: Melt the butter in the second pan over medium-high heat. Add the mushrooms in one layer with a pinch of salt and leave them for 2 minutes before stirring. Cook for 8 to 10 minutes in total, then move them to the warm holding dish. Wipe the pan.
steps.look: First they release water and go quiet, then the water evaporates, the sizzle returns and they brown deeply at the edges and smell nutty.
steps.mistake: Crowding the pan or stirring constantly, so they stew grey in their liquid.
steps.fix: Keep the heat up and wait for the water to go; the browning only starts once the pan is dry again.

steps.do: Push the sausages to one side and lay the bacon in the large pan. Cook 2 to 3 minutes a side over medium heat. Move the bacon to the holding dish, then fry the black pudding slices in the bacon fat for 2 minutes a side.
steps.look: Bacon fat turns translucent and golden with crisp edges; the lean is pink-brown, not grey. Black pudding develops a crisp, dark crust and smells spiced.
steps.mistake: Overcooking the black pudding, which dries out and crumbles.
steps.fix: It is already cooked; you are only crisping and heating it. Two minutes a side is plenty.

steps.do: Check the sausages with the probe thermometer in the thickest one: they are done at 160°F (71°C). Move them to the holding dish. Warm the beans over low heat, stirring now and then.
steps.look: Juices run clear and the inside is no longer pink. Beans steaming gently, not boiling.
steps.mistake: Boiling the beans hard so the sauce catches and the beans burst.
steps.fix: Low heat; take them off when they steam.

steps.do: Fry the eggs in the wiped second pan with a spoonful of fat from the sausage pan over medium heat, spooning the hot fat over the whites, for 2 to 3 minutes. Meanwhile toast the bread, or fry it in the remaining fat in the large pan for 1 minute a side.
steps.look: Whites set and opaque, yolks glossy. Toast golden and hot, or fried bread crisp and golden through.
steps.mistake: Cooking the eggs first and holding them, which overcooks the yolks and toughens the whites.
steps.fix: Eggs and toast are always last. Everything else holds; they do not.

steps.do: Take the warm plates out and plate everything in under a minute: sausages, bacon, black pudding, tomato and mushrooms around the edge, beans contained to one side, egg on top or at the front, toast on a side plate.
steps.look: Every item hot, glossy and distinct; no puddles of bean sauce under the bacon.
steps.mistake: Letting beans flood the plate and soak the toast.
steps.fix: Spoon the beans into a neat pile or a small ramekin.

dishes.science: A sausage is a fatty, salted mince in a casing, and cooking it gently lets the fat melt and baste the meat from inside while the proteins set slowly, so the centre reaches a safe 160°F (71°C) before the casing bursts from steam pressure. Bacon fat renders as it heats, and that fat then becomes the cooking medium for the next item, carrying flavour from pan to pan. Mushrooms are about 90 percent water; they must give it up before the surface can rise above 212°F (100°C) and brown through the Maillard reaction. Holding food in a low oven works for items with fat and structure, like sausages and bacon, but eggs and toast lose moisture fast, which is why they are cooked last.
dishes.plating: Use a large, very hot oval or round plate. Work round it like a clock: sausages and bacon crossed at the back, black pudding beside them, tomato and mushrooms on the right, beans contained in a neat pile at the left or in a small ramekin, and the egg at the front where the eye lands. Toast on a side plate so it stays crisp, butter on the table.

pairing.drink: A pot of strong English breakfast tea, or for a late brunch a Bloody Mary, which handles the salt and fat.
pairing.brennans: Thick-Cut Bacon: Brennan's own breakfast side, useful for comparing how a thicker rasher renders and crisps against back bacon.

variations: Full Scottish: add tattie scones and Lorne sausage.
Full Irish: add white pudding and soda bread.
Vegetarian full: grilled halloumi, vegetarian sausages and wilted spinach with garlic.
safety: Pork sausages must reach 160°F (71°C) in the centre; use a probe rather than guessing by colour.
Keep held food above 140°F (60°C) and serve within 30 minutes.
For anyone vulnerable, cook the egg yolks until firm or use pasteurised eggs.

dishes.title: Grillades and Grits
dishes.summary: Thin medallions of beef browned hard, then braised in a dark roux gravy with the trinity, tomatoes and stock until tender, served over slow-cooked creamy grits. The New Orleans brunch classic is a true braise, the first in the course, and it brings together pounding, browning, a roux and the patience of low heat.
equipment: Heavy 5 to 6 quart (5 to 6 litre) Dutch oven or cast iron casserole with lid
Meat mallet or a small heavy pan, and cling film
Heavy saucepan for grits, and a whisk

ingredients.item: Beef top round or bottom round steak
ingredients.note: or veal round; trimmed of sinew
or salt, black pepper, paprika, cayenne and garlic powder

ingredients.item: Milk and water for the grits

mise: Cut the beef into palm-size pieces about 3 inches (7.5 cm) across. Lay them between sheets of cling film and pound to an even 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick.
Season the meat on both sides with the Creole seasoning. Put the dredging flour in the shallow dish.
Dice the onion, pepper and celery the same size so they cook evenly, and keep them together in one bowl: this is the trinity. Mince the garlic separately.
Open the tomatoes, measure the stock and warm it in a pan.
Set the wire rack over a tray beside the stove for the browned meat.

timeline.do: Pound, cut and season the beef; dice the trinity.
Dredge and brown the beef in batches, about 10 minutes in all.
Make the roux to the colour of peanut butter, 8 to 10 minutes; add trinity, garlic, tomatoes, stock.
Meat back in; braise covered on low, 75 to 90 minutes.
Start the grits; stir every 5 minutes for 45 to 50 minutes.
Finish grits with butter and cheese; check the gravy seasoning.
Grits in bowls, grillades and gravy over, spring onion and parsley.

steps.do: Heat 3 tbsp (45 ml) oil in the Dutch oven over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Dredge a few pieces of beef in flour, shake off the excess, and lay them in the pan with space between. Brown for 1 1/2 to 2 minutes a side, then move to the rack. Repeat in batches, adding a little oil if needed.
steps.look: A loud sizzle as each piece goes in. A deep brown crust forms; the meat releases easily from the pan when it is ready to turn. A dark fond builds on the bottom of the pot.
steps.mistake: Crowding the pot, which drops the heat so the meat steams grey and the flour coating turns gummy.
steps.fix: Brown in three or four batches; let the oil reheat between them. If fond is turning black, lower the heat slightly.

steps.do: Lower the heat to medium. Add the remaining oil to the pot (you want about 1/4 cup (60 ml) of fat in total) and whisk in the roux flour. Stir constantly with the flat spatula, scraping the whole bottom, for 8 to 10 minutes.
steps.look: The roux goes from pale to blond to the colour of peanut butter, a medium brown, and smells nutty and toasty. The fond dissolves into it.
steps.mistake: Turning up the heat or walking away, so the roux scorches with black specks and a bitter, burnt smell.
steps.fix: If you see black flecks or smell burning, the roux cannot be saved; wipe the pot and start the roux again. Never taste hot roux; it sticks to skin and burns badly.

steps.do: Add the trinity all at once and stir; it will hiss and steam. Cook for 5 to 6 minutes, stirring, until the vegetables soften. Add the garlic for the last minute.
steps.look: The vegetables slump and turn glossy, coated in roux; the roux darkens a shade further as their moisture stops it from burning.
steps.mistake: Adding the vegetables slowly, giving the roux time to burn in the meantime.
steps.fix: Have the trinity bowl in your hand before the roux reaches its colour.

steps.do: Stir in the crushed tomatoes and cook for 2 minutes, then gradually pour in the warm stock, stirring to keep it smooth. Add the bay, thyme, Worcestershire and hot sauce, and bring to a simmer.
steps.look: A smooth, russet brown gravy that coats the back of a spoon lightly.
steps.mistake: Adding cold stock in one go, which can make the roux lumpy.
steps.fix: Warm stock, added in three parts, stirring each time until smooth.

steps.do: Return the browned beef and any juices from the tray to the pot, pushing the pieces under the gravy. Cover, reduce the heat to low and braise for 75 to 90 minutes, stirring gently every 20 minutes so nothing catches.
steps.look: A lazy bubble every few seconds, not a boil. The gravy darkens and thickens and the meat becomes tender enough to cut with the side of a fork.
steps.mistake: Boiling the braise, which tightens the meat and makes it tough and stringy.
steps.fix: Turn the heat to the lowest setting or move the pot into a 300°F (150°C) oven. If the gravy gets too thick, add a splash of stock or water.

steps.do: About an hour before serving, bring the milk, water and 1 tsp (6 g) salt to a simmer in the saucepan. Whisk in the grits in a slow stream, whisking until smooth. Reduce to the lowest heat, cover and cook for 45 to 50 minutes, whisking every 5 minutes and scraping the bottom.
steps.look: The grits thicken within 5 minutes, then slowly turn creamy and soft, losing all grittiness. The surface bubbles slowly like lava.
steps.mistake: Not stirring, so the grits stick and scorch on the bottom, or cooking too hot, so they spit.
steps.fix: Lowest heat and regular whisking. Add hot water a splash at a time if they become too thick to whisk.

steps.do: Finish the grits off the heat with the butter and cheese, stirring until melted. Taste and season. Taste the gravy too, fish out the bay and thyme stems, and adjust the salt, hot sauce and Worcestershire.
steps.look: Grits silky and loose enough to settle into a pool on the plate. Gravy glossy, deep russet and well seasoned, the beef tender.
steps.mistake: Seasoning the gravy at the start and finding it too salty after reduction.
steps.fix: Season at the end. If it is too salty, add a splash of unsalted stock or water.

steps.do: Spoon the grits into warm shallow bowls, lay two or three grillades on top, ladle gravy generously over everything and finish with spring onions and parsley.
steps.look: White grits pooled under dark, glossy gravy, green flecks on top.
steps.mistake: Serving the grits too stiff, so they sit in a lump.
steps.fix: Loosen them with a splash of hot milk just before serving.

dishes.science: Round steak is lean and full of connective tissue. Pounding it thin breaks up muscle fibres and shortens the distance heat has to travel. Browning the floured meat creates flavour through the Maillard reaction and leaves fond in the pot that later dissolves into the gravy. The roux thickens because starch granules swell in liquid, but the longer a roux browns, the more its starch breaks down, so a darker roux gives more flavour and less thickening. During braising at a gentle simmer, collagen in the meat slowly converts into gelatin, which makes the meat tender and gives the gravy body. Boiling would instead tighten the muscle proteins and squeeze out moisture.
dishes.plating: Use warm, wide, shallow bowls. Pool the grits in the centre and shake the bowl so they settle flat. Overlap two or three grillades on top, ladle gravy over the meat so it runs onto the grits, and scatter spring onions and parsley in a band across the middle. Wipe the rim before serving.

pairing.drink: A Brandy Milk Punch or a Bloody Mary, the two classic New Orleans brunch drinks; one soothes, the other matches the spice.
pairing.brennans: Cheddar Grits: Brennan's own side, the same base this dish sits on, worth tasting to judge how creamy and loose grits should be.

variations: Veal grillades: use veal round for a more delicate, traditional version and reduce the braise to 60 minutes.
Pork grillades: use pounded pork shoulder steaks and braise for 90 minutes.
Creamier grits: replace half the water with single cream.
safety: Hot roux sticks to skin and burns badly; stir with a long-handled spoon, keep children away and never touch or taste it hot.
Hot grits spit; keep the lid partly on and stir with a long whisk.
Cool leftovers quickly and reheat until steaming, 165°F (74°C).
