dishes.title: Pan con Chicharrón
dishes.summary: Lima's weekend breakfast sandwich: pork belly simmered in seasoned water until the water cooks away and the meat fries golden in its own fat, layered in a crusty roll with fried sweet potato and a sharp salsa criolla. It teaches rendering from start to finish, and how to judge a pan by its sound.
skills: simmering pork belly until the water cooks off and it fries in its own fat
equipment: 12 inch (30 cm) heavy, wide, deep sauté pan or cast iron casserole
Medium frying pan for the sweet potato

ingredients.note: enough to come just level with the meat

ingredients.item: Crusty white rolls (pan francés or small baguette rolls)

ingredients.note: seeded and sliced thin; a seeded jalapeño works

mise: Cut the pork belly into even cubes so they all finish together.
Slice the red onion paper thin, soak it in salted cold water for 10 minutes, then drain and squeeze dry; this softens its bite.
Slice the sweet potato into even rounds.
Juice the limes; slice the ají; chop the coriander.
Set the wire rack over a tray beside the stove and fit the splatter guard nearby.

timeline.do: Cube the pork and start the simmer.
Soak the onion; slice sweet potato and ají.
Water gone: the pork starts frying in its fat. Turn as each side colours.
Pork onto the rack. Fry the sweet potato in some of the rendered fat.
Dress the salsa criolla. Warm the rolls.
Build the sandwiches and serve hot.

steps.do: Put the pork, salt, garlic, cumin and pepper in the wide pan and pour in water to come just level with the top of the meat. Bring to a boil over high heat, then reduce to a steady medium simmer, uncovered.
steps.look: Bubbles across the whole surface. Grey foam rises at first.
steps.mistake: Covering the pan, which stops the water evaporating so the pork never gets to fry.
steps.fix: Leave it uncovered. Skim off the first grey foam with a spoon if you like a cleaner flavour.

steps.do: Simmer for 35 to 45 minutes, stirring every 10 minutes, as the water reduces.
steps.look: The water level drops steadily, turning cloudy and fatty. The pork turns pale and the fat becomes translucent at the edges.
steps.mistake: Boiling hard on high heat, so the water goes too quickly before the collagen in the pork has softened.
steps.fix: If the water runs out early, add 1/2 cup (120 ml) more and keep simmering until a skewer slips easily into the meat.

steps.do: Listen. When the water has gone, the sound changes from soft bubbling to a sharp crackle. Turn the heat to medium, fit the splatter guard and stop stirring. Let the cubes fry in their own rendered fat.
steps.look: A clear layer of fat about 1/4 inch (6 mm) deep in the pan. The crackle is loud and steady; you can smell roasting pork.
steps.mistake: Continuing to stir, which stops a crust forming.
steps.fix: Leave each side for 3 to 4 minutes before turning; the pieces will release when browned.

steps.do: Turn the cubes with tongs as each face turns deep amber, frying for 12 to 15 minutes in total until browned all over and the skin is blistered and glassy.
steps.look: Deep golden brown meat, skin puffed and crackly. Two pieces knocked together sound hollow and crisp.
steps.mistake: Pulling them while the skin is still pale and chewy.
steps.fix: Give them a few more minutes, turning; keep the heat at medium so the meat does not burn while the skin crisps.

steps.do: Lift the chicharrón onto the wire rack. Pour off all but 3 tbsp (45 ml) of fat into a heatproof bowl to cool.
steps.look: The pieces stay crisp on the rack; fat drips through.
steps.mistake: Draining on paper towel, where the bottoms steam and go soft.
steps.fix: Use the rack, and keep the pieces apart.

steps.do: Heat the 3 tbsp (45 ml) fat in the frying pan over medium heat. Fry the sweet potato slices in one layer for 4 to 5 minutes a side, in batches if needed.
steps.look: Edges caramelised and dark gold, centres soft when pierced with a knife tip.
steps.mistake: Heat too high, so the sugary sweet potato burns outside and stays hard inside.
steps.fix: Lower the heat to medium-low and cover the pan for a minute to steam the centres through.

steps.do: Make the salsa criolla: toss the drained onion with the lime juice, ají, coriander, olive oil and a good pinch of salt. Leave for 5 minutes.
steps.look: The onion turns bright pink and softens slightly, glistening with lime.
steps.mistake: Making it hours ahead, so the onion goes limp and watery.
steps.fix: Dress it no more than 15 minutes before serving.

steps.do: Warm the rolls in a 350°F (175°C) oven for 3 minutes, split them, and build: two or three slices of sweet potato, then chicharrón sliced thick, then a generous pile of salsa criolla.
steps.look: Crisp golden pork and bright pink onion spilling slightly from a crusty roll.
steps.mistake: Cold, soft rolls that collapse under the juicy filling.
steps.fix: Warm them briefly; the crust is what holds the sandwich together.

dishes.science: Pork belly is layered fat and muscle held together by tough collagen. Dropped straight into hot fat, the outside proteins tighten and the collagen has no time to soften, so the meat is crisp outside but rubbery inside. Simmering in water first holds the meat at no more than 212°F (100°C), the boiling point of water, while collagen slowly melts into gelatin and the fat begins to render out. As long as any water remains, the pan cannot get hot enough to brown or burn anything. Once the water has evaporated, the rendered fat takes over and its temperature climbs well past boiling, so the surface dries, browns through the Maillard reaction and the skin puffs as trapped moisture turns to steam.
dishes.plating: Serve each sandwich on a board or plate, cut on the diagonal and slightly apart so the layers show: orange sweet potato, golden pork, pink onion. Add a small pot of extra salsa criolla or ají sauce on the side.

pairing.drink: A Peruvian chicha morada or a pisco sour later in the day; lime and pisco cut through the pork fat.

variations: Chicharrón de pollo: use bone-in chicken thighs cut in pieces, simmered and fried the same way.
Pan con chicharrón with ají amarillo sauce: blend 2 tbsp (30 g) ají amarillo paste with mayonnaise and lime to spread in the roll.
Breakfast plate: serve the chicharrón and sweet potato without bread, with fried eggs and salsa criolla.
safety: Rendering fat spits violently, especially as the last water evaporates; use a splatter guard, long tongs and keep your face back.
Pork is safe at 145°F (63°C) with a 3 minute rest; chicharrón is cooked far beyond this.
Let the reserved fat cool completely before moving or storing it.

dishes.title: Tiroler Gröstl
dishes.summary: The Tyrolean hash of cooked potatoes crisped in a wide pan with onion, smoked bacon or leftover roast, caraway and marjoram, topped with a fried egg. It shows how to crisp a cooked potato properly and how to make a second meal from a roast.
skills: parboiled potatoes crisped in a hot pan
equipment: 12 inch (30 cm) cast iron or heavy carbon steel frying pan
Saucepan for boiling potatoes (if not using leftovers)
Second pan for frying the eggs
Mortar and pestle or rolling pin for the caraway

ingredients.note: boiled in their skins and chilled, ideally the day before

ingredients.item: Smoked bacon (speck) or leftover roast pork or beef
Lard, clarified butter or neutral oil
ingredients.note: plus more if the bacon is lean
to finish, and for the eggs

mise: If you have no cooked potatoes, boil them whole in their skins in salted water for 20 to 25 minutes until a knife slips in, drain, and let them steam dry and cool completely, at least 30 minutes.
Peel the cold potatoes (or leave the skins on) and slice 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick.
Cube the bacon or roast; slice the onion.
Crush the caraway lightly; snip the chives.

timeline.do: Boil and cool potatoes if not already cooked.
Slice potatoes, cube bacon, slice onion.
Render bacon, then fry potatoes undisturbed, 12 to 15 minutes.
Onion in until bronze; bacon back with caraway and marjoram.
Fry the eggs.
Eggs on top, chives, serve from the pan.

steps.do: Put the bacon in the cold cast iron pan, set over medium heat and cook for 6 to 8 minutes, stirring occasionally. Lift out with a slotted spoon, leaving the fat. If using leftover roast, brown it in 1 tbsp (15 ml) lard for 3 minutes and lift out.
steps.look: The bacon fat turns clear and runs into the pan; the edges of the bacon brown and crisp.
steps.mistake: Starting in a hot pan, so the bacon browns outside before its fat has rendered.
steps.fix: Starting cold lets the fat melt out slowly; if the pan smokes, lower the heat.

steps.do: Add the lard to the bacon fat so you have about 3 tbsp (45 ml) in the pan, and raise the heat to medium-high. When it shimmers, add the potato slices in a single layer. Season with salt and leave them alone for 5 to 6 minutes.
steps.look: A steady, lively sizzle. When you lift the edge of one slice, the underside is a deep golden crust.
steps.mistake: Stirring or flipping constantly, so the potatoes break up and never form a crust.
steps.fix: Resist; every flip you skip is more crust. If they stick, wait: a crust releases on its own.

steps.do: Turn the potatoes in sections with the flat spatula, scraping under the crust, and fry another 5 to 6 minutes without stirring. Repeat once more if needed.
steps.look: Most slices golden brown and crisp on two sides, some broken edges extra crunchy.
steps.mistake: Too many potatoes in the pan, so they steam instead of fry.
steps.fix: Use a bigger pan or cook in two batches, keeping the first warm in the oven.

steps.do: Push the potatoes to the side and add the onion to the cleared space with a little more fat if the pan looks dry. Cook for 5 to 6 minutes, stirring the onion only, until soft and bronzed, then mix it through the potatoes.
steps.look: Onion soft, sweet and bronze, its edges browned.
steps.mistake: Adding the onion at the start, so it burns before the potatoes crisp.
steps.fix: Onion always goes in after the potatoes have their crust.

steps.do: Return the bacon or roast to the pan with the caraway and marjoram and toss for 2 minutes until everything is hot. Add the butter, taste and season with salt and plenty of pepper.
steps.look: Glossy, crisp, well browned hash, the caraway smelling warm and slightly aniseed.
steps.mistake: Burning the caraway, which turns it bitter.
steps.fix: Add the spices at the end over medium heat and keep the hash moving.

steps.do: In the second pan, fry the eggs in a little butter over medium heat for 2 to 3 minutes, until the whites are set and the yolks still runny.
steps.look: Set whites with lightly crisp edges and glossy yolks.
steps.mistake: Cooking the eggs early so they go cold and rubbery.
steps.fix: Start the eggs only once the hash is finished and resting off the heat.

steps.do: Slide the eggs onto the hash, scatter with chives and serve in the pan at the table.
steps.look: Golden potatoes, dark bacon and bright yolks.
steps.mistake: Covering the hash with a lid to keep it warm, which steams away the crisp.
steps.fix: Serve straight away uncovered.

dishes.science: Potatoes cooked a day ahead and chilled crisp far better than freshly boiled ones. As cooked starch cools, its molecules re-associate into tighter crystalline regions, a process called retrogradation, which firms the potato so slices hold their shape in the pan. The surface has also dried in the fridge, and a drier surface reaches browning temperature faster, because water must evaporate before the temperature can rise above 212°F (100°C). Cast iron holds heat well, so the pan does not cool when the potatoes go in. Leaving them undisturbed keeps the surface in constant contact with hot fat, so the Maillard reaction can build a deep crust. Caraway seeds carry aromatic oils that are released by gentle crushing and warm fat.
dishes.plating: Serve the Gröstl in its pan on a board at the table, eggs in the centre, or plate it in a loose mound on warm plates with an egg on each, yolk up, and chives scattered over. A spoon of crunchy sauerkraut or a small green salad on the side is traditional in the Tyrol.

pairing.drink: A crisp Grüner Veltliner or a cold Austrian lager; both cut the fat and suit the caraway.
pairing.brennans: Bründlmayer ‘Terrassen’ Grüner Veltliner 2023 (375 ml): an Austrian Grüner whose white pepper and lift suit an Alpine hash.

variations: Beef Gröstl: use leftover roast beef or boiled beef (Tafelspitz), sliced thin.
Vegetarian Gröstl: replace bacon with sautéed mushrooms and add a handful of grated mountain cheese at the end.
Kasnocken style: melt slices of mountain cheese over the hash under the overhead grill (broiler) before the eggs.
safety: Leftover roast should have been chilled within two hours of cooking and used within three to four days; heat it until steaming hot, 165°F (74°C).
Cool boiled potatoes uncovered and then refrigerate; do not leave them out overnight.
For anyone vulnerable, cook the yolks until firm or use pasteurised eggs.

dishes.title: Boxty
dishes.summary: An Irish potato pancake made from half grated raw potato and half mashed potato, bound with flour and buttermilk and fried golden in butter. It teaches why water is the enemy of a crisp edge, and how combining raw and cooked starch gives crunch and tenderness in one bite.
equipment: Clean thin tea towel or muslin for squeezing
Two bowls, one for the potato liquid
Saucepan for the mash, and a masher or ricer
Large heavy frying pan or flat griddle, 12 inch (30 cm)
Baking tray with a rack and a low oven for holding

ingredients.item: Floury potatoes (Russet or Maris Piper), for the mash
ingredients.note: peeled and cut in even chunks
for frying, plus more to serve

ingredients.item: Smoked salmon and crème fraîche, or bacon and eggs

mise: Boil the mash potatoes in salted water for 15 to 18 minutes until soft, drain and let steam dry for 3 minutes, then mash or rice until smooth and leave to cool a little.
Grate the raw potatoes on the fine side of the box grater into a bowl.
Line a second bowl with the tea towel ready for squeezing.
Mix the flour, baking powder and salt.
Heat the oven to 200°F (95°C) with a rack over a tray for holding.

timeline.do: Boil the potatoes for the mash.
Mash; grate and squeeze the raw potato; let the starch settle.
Mix the batter.
Fry the boxty in batches, about 8 minutes per batch.
Serve hot with your toppings.

steps.do: Tip the grated raw potato into the towel, gather it up and twist hard over the bowl to squeeze out as much liquid as possible. Set the dry potato aside.
steps.look: A surprising amount of cloudy, pinkish liquid in the bowl, and a dry, fluffy pile of grated potato in the towel.
steps.mistake: A half-hearted squeeze, leaving the potato wet, which makes the boxty soggy and grey.
steps.fix: Squeeze in two or three goes, re-twisting the towel each time, until only drips come out.

steps.do: Leave the liquid for 5 minutes, then carefully pour off and discard the watery liquid, keeping the thick white starch that has settled at the bottom.
steps.look: A firm white paste on the bottom of the bowl.
steps.mistake: Pouring the starch away with the water.
steps.fix: Tilt the bowl slowly; the starch stays put as a solid layer.

steps.do: Add the squeezed raw potato, the mash and the flour mixture to the starch and mix with a fork. Add the buttermilk a little at a time, stirring, until you have a thick batter that drops reluctantly from a spoon.
steps.look: A thick, speckled batter, like a stiff porridge. It holds its shape briefly when spooned.
steps.mistake: Adding all the buttermilk at once, so the batter is runny and the pancakes spread flat.
steps.fix: If too thin, add flour 1 tbsp (8 g) at a time. If too stiff to drop, add buttermilk 1 tbsp (15 ml) at a time.

steps.do: Melt 1 tbsp (14 g) butter in the frying pan over medium heat until it foams. Drop in heaped spoonfuls of batter, about 1/4 cup (60 ml) each, and flatten into rounds about 1/2 inch (1 cm) thick and 3 to 4 inches (8 to 10 cm) across. Leave space between them.
steps.look: The butter sizzles round the edges. The batter holds its shape when flattened.
steps.mistake: A pan that is too hot, so the butter burns black before the inside cooks.
steps.fix: Medium heat and foaming, not smoking, butter. Wipe out burnt butter between batches.

steps.do: Fry for 4 minutes without moving them, then flip and fry 4 minutes more.
steps.look: Deep golden brown faces with a lacy, crisp edge where the raw potato has fried. The centre springs back when pressed.
steps.mistake: Flipping too early, so they break and the crust tears away.
steps.fix: Wait until the edges look set and golden. If the centre is still raw after 8 minutes, lower the heat and give it 2 more minutes per side.

steps.do: Hold the cooked boxty on the rack in the low oven while you fry the rest, adding fresh butter for each batch.
steps.look: They stay crisp on the rack.
steps.mistake: Stacking them on a plate, where they steam and soften.
steps.fix: Keep them in one layer on the rack.

steps.do: Serve two or three per person with smoked salmon, a spoon of crème fraîche and chives, or with bacon and fried eggs.
steps.look: Golden, crisp pancakes with a soft, tender centre.
steps.mistake: Letting them sit too long before serving.
steps.fix: Serve within 15 minutes of frying.

dishes.science: Raw potato is about 80 percent water, and water is the enemy of crispness because nothing can brown until it has evaporated. Squeezing removes much of that water, so the shreds fry quickly into a lacy, crisp edge. The liquid squeezed out also carries potato starch, which settles to the bottom of the bowl. Adding that starch back helps bind the pancake without extra flour. Cooked mashed potato contributes swollen, gelatinised starch that stays soft and creamy, keeping the centre tender. Buttermilk is acidic, so it reacts with the baking powder to make carbon dioxide bubbles, lightening the batter. The milk solids in the butter brown as the boxty fries, adding a nutty flavour.
dishes.plating: Stack three boxty slightly overlapping on a warm plate. For smoked salmon, drape a ribbon of salmon over the top, add a neat quenelle of crème fraîche and a scatter of chives. For a cooked breakfast, set two rashers of bacon crossed beside the stack and the egg on top.

pairing.drink: With smoked salmon, a glass of dry sparkling wine; with bacon and eggs, a strong cup of tea or an Irish coffee for a lazy weekend brunch.
pairing.brennans: Brennan’s Irish Coffee: whiskey, coffee and cream with an Irish potato pancake makes a fitting pairing for a weekend brunch.

variations: Boxty dumplings: shape the mixture into a firm dough with extra flour, boil, slice and fry.
Boxty bread: press the mixture into a round, score in quarters and bake on a griddle.
Spring onion boxty: fold 4 sliced spring onions into the batter.
safety: Grated raw potato turns grey quickly; grate just before squeezing and cooking, not hours ahead.
Hot butter can spit if the batter is wet; lower spoonfuls in gently.

dishes.title: Akara (Black-Eyed Bean Fritters)
dishes.summary: Light, crisp fritters made from skinned black-eyed beans blended with onion and pepper, whipped until airy and deep fried. They are the first deep frying in the course, and they teach that a batter can rise with nothing but beaten air when its consistency is exactly right.
skills: deep frying at a steady temperature safely
equipment: Large bowl for soaking and skinning
Large mixing bowl and a sturdy wooden spoon or electric whisk
Heavy pot at least 4 inches (10 cm) deep, or a deep fryer

ingredients.note: seeded for less heat; or 1 red bell pepper plus 1 Scotch bonnet
or another neutral oil with a high smoke point

mise: Soak the beans in plenty of warm water for at least 2 hours.
Skin the beans (step 1), which takes about 20 minutes.
Chop the onion and seed the chillies, wearing gloves.

Set up the frying station: pot no more than one third full of oil, thermometer clipped on, rack over a tray to one side, spider in hand, and a lid within reach. Keep water and wet hands away from the oil.

timeline.do: Put the beans to soak in warm water.
Skin the beans by rubbing and floating off the skins.
Blend to a thick paste. Start heating the oil.
Whip the paste until it floats in water; salt it.
Fry in batches of 6 to 8, about 4 to 5 minutes each.
Serve hot.

steps.do: Drain the soaked beans, cover with fresh water and rub handfuls hard between your palms. The skins will loosen. Swirl the water, let the skins float to the top and pour them off. Repeat, adding fresh water each time, until almost all the beans are white with no skins and no black eyes left.
steps.look: Clean, ivory beans split into halves. The water you pour off is full of floating skins.
steps.mistake: Leaving lots of skin on, which makes the akara coarse, grey and heavy.
steps.fix: Keep rubbing and floating; it takes several rounds. A few stray skins are fine.

steps.do: Put the skinned beans, onion and chillies in the blender with 3 tbsp (45 ml) water and blend, stopping to scrape down the sides, until you have a smooth, very thick paste. Add more water only 1 tbsp (15 ml) at a time if the blades will not turn.
steps.look: A thick, smooth, pale paste that holds a ridge when dragged with a spoon.
steps.mistake: Adding too much water, so the paste is runny and spreads flat in the oil.
steps.fix: If it is too loose, there is no easy rescue; let it sit and drain in a fine sieve for 10 minutes, then whip longer. Next time use less water.

steps.do: Heat the oil over medium heat to 350°F (175°C).
steps.look: The thermometer reads 350°F (175°C). A drop of paste sizzles at once and floats to the surface.
steps.mistake: Frying in oil that is too cool, so the akara soak up oil and turn heavy.
steps.fix: Wait for the thermometer; adjust the heat to hold it between 340 and 360°F (170 and 180°C).

steps.do: Tip the paste into the mixing bowl and beat it hard with the wooden spoon, in a circular lifting motion, for 5 to 8 minutes (or 3 to 4 minutes with an electric whisk). Test by dropping a tiny spoonful into a glass of cold water.
steps.look: The paste lightens in colour and becomes fluffy and increased in volume. The test spoonful floats.
steps.mistake: Stopping before it floats, so the akara are dense.
steps.fix: Keep beating and test again every minute.

steps.do: Now stir in the salt gently, just until mixed.
steps.look: The paste stays light and fluffy.
steps.mistake: Adding salt before whipping, which slackens the paste and knocks out the air.
steps.fix: Salt always last. If the paste collapses, beat for another minute.

steps.do: Scoop a heaped tablespoon of paste and push it off with a second spoon close to the oil surface, letting it slide in gently. Add 6 to 8 fritters, spaced apart, and fry for 2 to 3 minutes until the undersides are deep golden, then turn them with the spider.
steps.look: The fritters sink, then rise and puff, with vigorous bubbling. The underside turns deep golden brown.
steps.mistake: Dropping from a height, which splashes hot oil, or overcrowding, which drops the oil temperature.
steps.fix: Lower the spoon close to the oil. Fry in batches and let the oil come back to 350°F (175°C) between them.

steps.do: Fry the second side for 2 minutes until evenly golden brown, then lift onto the rack to drain standing on their sides.
steps.look: Round, golden fritters that feel light. Broken open, the inside is fluffy and cooked through, not wet.
steps.mistake: Pulling them too soon, so they are pale and doughy inside.
steps.fix: Break one open to check the first batch, and adjust the time.

steps.do: Serve hot, as they are or with pap (ogi), custard, bread or a pepper sauce.
steps.look: Crisp shells that crackle when bitten.
steps.mistake: Letting them sit in a pile, where they steam soft.
steps.fix: Keep them on the rack in a 200°F (95°C) oven if holding.

dishes.science: Akara has no baking powder or yeast. Its rise comes entirely from air beaten into the bean paste. Beans are rich in protein and starch, and when blended with very little water, the proteins can form a stable foam that traps air, much as egg white does. The float test tells you the paste is less dense than water, meaning enough air is held in it. Salt early would draw water out of the paste and loosen it, letting the foam collapse. In hot oil at 350°F (175°C), the trapped air and the water in the paste expand as steam, puffing the fritter, while the surface dries and browns into a crisp shell. Skins are removed because they are fibrous and do not foam.
dishes.plating: Pile the akara on a warm plate lined with a folded cloth napkin or banana leaf, in a loose pyramid. Serve a small bowl of hot pepper sauce and a bowl of warm pap or custard alongside, or split some open into soft bread as a sandwich.

pairing.drink: A chilled Chapman, the Nigerian fruit punch of citrus soda, grenadine and bitters, or a hot cup of black tea.

variations: Acarajé: the Brazilian version, split and filled with vatapá and dried shrimp.
Akara with shrimp: fold 1/4 cup (30 g) chopped dried shrimp into the paste after whipping.
Koose: the Ghanaian name for the same fritters, often with more pepper.
safety: Deep frying: fill the pot no more than one third full, use a thermometer and never leave it unattended.
Never add water to hot oil and never put water on an oil fire; turn off the heat and cover with a lid.
Keep the pan handle turned inwards and children and pets away from the stove.
Let the oil cool completely before straining or moving it.

dishes.title: Nasi Lemak
dishes.summary: Malaysia's national breakfast of coconut rice scented with pandan, served with a dark, sweet and fiery sambal, crisp fried anchovies and peanuts, a boiled egg and cucumber. It asks for four separate components and a sambal cooked slowly until the oil separates, a skill that every curry paste after it relies on.
equipment: Heavy saucepan with tight lid, or a rice cooker
Blender or a mortar and pestle
Heavy frying pan for the sambal
Small saucepan for eggs and a bowl of iced water
Spider or slotted spoon, and a wire rack

ingredients.note: rinsed until the water runs clear
seeded and soaked in hot water 20 minutes
toasted in a dry pan until fragrant
soaked in 1/4 cup (60 ml) warm water and strained
1/2 cup (120 ml) for the sambal, the rest for frying
sliced into rings, for the sambal

mise: Soak the dried chillies in hot water for 20 minutes; snip them first and shake out the seeds for a milder sambal.
Rinse the rice in three or four changes of water until clear; drain.
Toast the belacan in a dry pan for 1 to 2 minutes, pressing it flat, until it smells strongly and turns crumbly. Open a window.
Soak and strain the tamarind; grate the palm sugar.
Rinse the anchovies quickly and dry them thoroughly on a towel; wet anchovies spit in hot oil.
Knot the pandan leaves; slice the ginger, cucumber and red onion.

timeline.do: Soak chillies. Rinse rice. Toast belacan.
Blend the sambal paste; start frying it slowly, 20 to 25 minutes.
Start the coconut rice, 15 minutes plus 10 minutes resting.
Boil the eggs 9 minutes; ice and peel.
Fry the peanuts, then the anchovies, and drain.
Finish the sambal with tamarind, sugar, onion and some anchovies.
Mound the rice and arrange everything around it.

steps.do: Drain the chillies and blend them with the shallots, garlic and belacan, adding 2 to 3 tbsp (30 to 45 ml) water, to a smooth red paste.
steps.look: A smooth, bright red paste with no visible pieces of shallot.
steps.mistake: Leaving the paste coarse, so it fries unevenly and tastes raw in places.
steps.fix: Blend longer, scraping down; add water a spoon at a time if it will not move.

steps.do: Heat 1/2 cup (120 ml) oil in the heavy frying pan over medium heat. Add the paste (it will spit) and fry, stirring often and scraping the base, for 20 to 25 minutes, turning the heat lower as it darkens.
steps.look: First it bubbles wetly and smells sharp and raw. Then it reduces, darkens from bright red to deep brick red and smells sweet and roasted, and the oil separates out and pools red around the edges.
steps.mistake: Stopping too soon, when the paste is still bright red and wet, so the sambal tastes raw and harsh.
steps.fix: Keep going until the oil splits from the paste. If it catches, add a tablespoon of water, scrape, and lower the heat.

steps.do: Meanwhile put the rice, coconut milk, water, salt, pandan and ginger in the saucepan. Stir once and bring to the boil over medium-high heat. Reduce to the lowest heat, cover tightly and cook 15 minutes. Turn off the heat and leave covered for 10 minutes.
steps.look: The liquid is absorbed, steam holes dot the surface, the grains are glossy, separate and smell of pandan.
steps.mistake: Boiling hard with the lid off, so the coconut milk scorches on the bottom.
steps.fix: Lowest heat once boiling. If the bottom catches a little, do not scrape it into the rice; serve from the top.

steps.do: Boil the eggs in simmering water for 9 minutes, then cool in iced water for 3 minutes and peel. Halve them just before serving.
steps.look: Firm whites and just set, deep yellow yolks.
steps.mistake: Overcooking, so the yolks turn grey.
steps.fix: Use a timer and ice them straight away.

steps.do: Heat the remaining oil in the wok to 325°F (160°C). Fry the peanuts for 4 to 5 minutes, stirring, until they crackle and darken slightly, then lift onto the rack. Fry the dry anchovies for 2 to 3 minutes until golden and crisp, then lift out.
steps.look: Peanuts deep golden under their skins and smelling toasty; anchovies glassy and golden, crisp when cooled.
steps.mistake: Frying in oil that is too hot, so the peanuts burn inside before the outside colours, or frying wet anchovies, which spit violently.
steps.fix: Hold the temperature near 325°F (160°C). Pull them slightly early: both darken and crisp more as they cool.

steps.do: Finish the sambal: stir in the strained tamarind water, palm sugar and a pinch of salt, add the sliced red onion and simmer for 5 minutes. Stir in a small handful of the fried anchovies. Taste.
steps.look: A glossy, dark, jammy sambal with soft onion rings. It should taste sweet first, then sour, then hot, with a deep savoury base.
steps.mistake: An unbalanced sambal, too sharp or too sweet.
steps.fix: Adjust with a little more sugar for sweetness, tamarind for sourness, salt for depth; taste after each addition.

steps.do: Fluff the rice with a fork, removing the pandan and ginger. Pack a cup or small bowl with rice, turn it out onto a plate or banana leaf, and arrange the sambal, a pile of anchovies and peanuts, half an egg and cucumber coins around it.
steps.look: A neat dome of glossy white rice surrounded by red, brown, white and green.
steps.mistake: Pouring the sambal over the rice, which hides it and soaks the grains.
steps.fix: Keep each component separate so each person can mix as they eat.

dishes.science: Cooking a paste of chillies and shallots in oil until it splits is a slow reduction. First the water in the paste boils off, which is why it bubbles and spits. Once the water is gone, the temperature rises, and sugars and amino acids in the shallots and chillies brown through the Maillard reaction and caramelisation, turning harsh, raw flavours sweet and deep. The oil separating out is the sign that little water is left. Chilli colour and heat compounds dissolve in fat, which is why the oil turns red. In the rice, coconut fat coats the starch granules, keeping the grains separate and glossy, while pandan releases a fragrant compound that gives its distinctive aroma.
dishes.plating: Line a plate with a square of banana leaf, briefly passed over a flame to make it pliable and glossy. Turn out a dome of rice in the centre. Set the sambal in a neat spoonful at one side, a small heap of peanuts and anchovies at another, two halves of egg cut side up and fanned cucumber coins, so each component has its own space around the rice.

pairing.drink: Teh tarik, the frothy pulled milk tea that is served with nasi lemak across Malaysia, or an off-dry Riesling to cool the chilli.
pairing.brennans: C.H. Berres ‘Old Vines’ Riesling 2022: its touch of sweetness and acidity cool the sambal and lift the coconut rice.

variations: Nasi lemak ayam goreng: add turmeric-marinated fried chicken thighs.
Sambal sotong: simmer cleaned squid rings in the finished sambal for 2 minutes.
Vegetarian: leave out the belacan and anchovies and add fried tempeh.
safety: Hot oil: use a thermometer, dry the anchovies thoroughly and lower ingredients in gently; never leave the wok unattended.
Cooked rice should not sit warm for hours; serve within two hours, or chill quickly and reheat until steaming.
Sambal paste spits as it fries; stand back and use a splatter guard.

dishes.title: Chechebsa
dishes.summary: A griddled flatbread torn into pieces and tossed in niter kibbeh, Ethiopia's spiced clarified butter, with berbere, then served with honey and fresh cheese. It introduces clarifying butter, a skill every later sauce uses, and the care needed to bloom a chilli blend that scorches in seconds.
skills: clarifying spiced butter for niter kibbeh
equipment: Small heavy saucepan for the niter kibbeh
Fine sieve lined with muslin or a coffee filter
Heavy 10 to 12 inch (25 to 30 cm) frying pan, cast iron or nonstick
Wooden spoon and a flat spatula

ingredients.item: Unsalted butter, for the niter kibbeh
ingredients.note: makes more than you need; it keeps for weeks

ingredients.item: Shallot or red onion, finely chopped
Spices for the butter: fenugreek seeds, cumin seeds, cardamom seeds, dried oregano or besobela, ground turmeric
ingredients.note: add 1 small cinnamon stick and 2 cloves if you like
or barley flour for the highland version

ingredients.item: Ayib (fresh Ethiopian cheese) or ricotta or cottage cheese

mise: Make the niter kibbeh first; it needs 30 to 40 minutes and can be made days ahead.
Chop the shallot, crush the garlic, grate the ginger and measure the spices for the butter.
Line the sieve with muslin and set it over the jar.
Measure the flour, salt and water for the bread.
Have the honey and cheese ready in small bowls.

timeline.do: Make the niter kibbeh: melt, simmer with aromatics 30 to 40 minutes, strain.
Make the dough and rest it, covered, 15 minutes.
Roll and cook two flatbreads on a dry pan, about 4 minutes each.
Tear the hot bread into small pieces.
Bloom berbere in niter kibbeh, toss the bread.
Serve with honey and cold ayib.

steps.do: Melt the butter in the small saucepan over low heat. When it is liquid and starting to foam, add the shallot, garlic, ginger and spices. Keep it at a very gentle simmer, just a few bubbles, for 30 to 40 minutes, without stirring.
steps.look: White foam rises then thins; the milk solids sink and turn light golden brown on the bottom. The butter on top becomes clear and golden and smells nutty and deeply spiced.
steps.mistake: Heat too high, so the milk solids burn black and the butter tastes bitter.
steps.fix: Keep it on the lowest heat. If the solids darken beyond toffee brown, strain immediately.

steps.do: Pour the butter slowly through the lined sieve into the jar, leaving the browned solids behind. Let it cool slightly.
steps.look: A clear, golden liquid butter, fragrant with spice, with no cloudy milk solids.
steps.mistake: Pouring the solids through, which makes the butter cloudy and short-lived.
steps.fix: Strain again through fresh muslin if cloudy. Kept in the fridge it lasts a month.

steps.do: Mix the flour and salt in the bowl. Pour in the warm water in a stream, stirring, then knead for 4 to 5 minutes until the dough is smooth and no longer sticks to the bowl. Cover and rest for 15 minutes.
steps.look: A soft, smooth dough that springs back slowly when pressed.
steps.mistake: A dough that is too wet, which sticks and steams on the pan rather than drying.
steps.fix: Knead in flour 1 tbsp (8 g) at a time until it stops sticking.

steps.do: Divide the dough in two and roll each into a round about 1/8 inch (3 mm) thick. Heat the dry pan over medium heat and cook each round for about 2 minutes per side, without any fat.
steps.look: The surface dulls and blisters, and the underside shows brown freckles. The bread is cooked through and slightly dry.
steps.mistake: Oiling the pan, which keeps the bread moist so it turns pasty when tossed in butter later.
steps.fix: Cook it dry; you want a slightly firm bread that absorbs the butter.

steps.do: While still hot, tear the bread into small pieces about the size of your thumbnail. Use a cloth to protect your fingers.
steps.look: Soft, irregular pieces with torn, fluffy edges.
steps.mistake: Letting the bread cool first, so it cracks and crumbles instead of tearing.
steps.fix: Work fast while hot; if it cools, warm it in the dry pan for 30 seconds.

steps.do: Wipe the pan, put it on the lowest heat and add 6 tbsp (80 g) niter kibbeh. When melted and just warm, stir in the berbere and cook for about 40 seconds.
steps.look: The butter turns brick red and the berbere darkens by one shade, smelling toasted rather than raw and dusty.
steps.mistake: Adding berbere to hot butter on high heat, so it scorches black and bitter in seconds.
steps.fix: If it smells acrid or turns dark brown, start again with fresh butter: burnt berbere cannot be rescued.

steps.do: Add the torn bread at once and fold it through the spiced butter for 1 to 2 minutes, until every piece is coated and glossy.
steps.look: Each piece shiny and red-orange, warm through.
steps.mistake: Leaving the bread in too long over heat, so the butter fries the pieces hard.
steps.fix: Toss just until coated and hot, then plate.

steps.do: Pile onto warm plates, make a hollow in the top, drizzle honey over and serve with a spoonful of cold ayib.
steps.look: A glossy red mound with a ribbon of honey and a white spoon of cheese.
steps.mistake: Mixing the cheese in, which melts and loses the cool contrast.
steps.fix: Keep the cheese cold and on the side.

dishes.science: Clarifying butter removes its water and milk solids. Butter is about 80 percent fat, 15 percent water and the rest proteins and sugars. Gentle heat boils off the water and lets the milk solids sink and brown, adding nutty flavour, while the spices infuse the fat. Once strained, the clear fat no longer spoils as quickly and can be heated without burning. Berbere is mostly ground chilli, which is rich in sugars, so it scorches fast. Warm fat dissolves its colour and capsaicin, spreading heat and flavour through the dish, but only below about 300°F (150°C); hotter fat burns the sugars. The bread is cooked dry so its surface sets and can absorb the butter without collapsing into paste.
dishes.plating: Mound the chechebsa in the centre of a warm plate or traditional woven basket, keeping it loose rather than packed. Drizzle honey in a thin spiral over the top, and place a neat quenelle of ayib on one side. A cup of Ethiopian coffee or spiced tea alongside completes the plate.

pairing.drink: Ethiopian coffee, strong and black, or a sweet spiced tea; for later in the day, an off-dry Gewürztraminer that stands up to berbere.

variations: Fit-fit: use leftover injera instead of fresh flatbread.
Barley chechebsa: use barley flour for a nuttier, denser bread.
Milder version: halve the berbere and add a pinch of cinnamon to the butter.
safety: Clarified butter is very hot when strained; let it cool for a few minutes and pour slowly away from you.
Store niter kibbeh in a clean jar in the fridge and use a clean spoon each time.

dishes.title: Cachapas con Queso de Mano
dishes.summary: Thick, sweet pancakes of blended fresh corn cooked on a buttered pan and folded around soft, milky fresh cheese. They teach how fresh corn, with its sugar, water and lack of gluten, behaves entirely differently from masa or wheat batter.
skills: blending fresh corn to a batter
equipment: Sharp knife and a large bowl or a tube pan for cutting corn off the cob
Heavy 10 to 12 inch (25 to 30 cm) frying pan, griddle or comal
Ladle that holds about 2/3 cup (150 ml)
Wide thin fish slice or spatula

ingredients.note: from about 6 ears; frozen and thawed, well drained, works
depends on how sweet the corn is

ingredients.item: Queso de mano, or fresh mozzarella, or another soft fresh curd cheese

mise: Stand each corn cob upright in a large bowl and slice down close to the cob to remove the kernels; then scrape the cob with the back of the knife to collect the milky pulp.
Slice the cheese thickly and let it come to room temperature.
Heat the oven to 200°F (95°C) for holding.
Measure the masarepa and a little extra in case the batter needs thickening.

timeline.do: Cut the corn from the cobs. Slice the cheese.
Blend the batter coarse; stir in masarepa; rest 10 minutes.
Cook the cachapas one or two at a time, about 8 minutes each.
Fill with cheese, fold and serve with butter.

steps.do: Put the corn, egg, milk, sugar and salt in the blender. Pulse in short bursts, 10 to 15 times, stopping while the mixture is still coarse and speckled with pieces of kernel.
steps.look: A thick, pale yellow batter, like porridge with visible flecks of corn skin and kernel.
steps.mistake: Blending to a smooth purée, which loses the texture and makes the pancake gluey.
steps.fix: If over-blended, stir in a handful of whole kernels for texture, and add a little more masarepa.

steps.do: Pour into a bowl, stir in the masarepa and rest the batter for 10 minutes. Check the thickness.
steps.look: A spoonful mounds briefly before slowly settling, like a thick pancake batter.
steps.mistake: A batter that runs like single cream, which will spread thin and tear.
steps.fix: Add masarepa 1 tbsp (10 g) at a time, waiting 2 minutes after each for it to absorb.

steps.do: Melt 1 tbsp (14 g) butter in the pan over medium-low heat. Ladle in about 2/3 cup (150 ml) of batter and spread it with the back of the ladle into a round about 6 inches (15 cm) across and 3/8 inch (8 to 10 mm) thick.
steps.look: A gentle sizzle at the edges. The batter holds its round.
steps.mistake: Medium-high heat, which burns the sugary base before the thick middle sets.
steps.fix: Keep the heat medium-low; the cachapa cooks slowly and evenly.

steps.do: Cook without moving for 4 to 5 minutes, until the surface has turned from glossy to matte and bubbles appear, and the edges lift without tearing.
steps.look: Matte top, set rim, and a deep golden underside when you peek.
steps.mistake: Flipping by the clock rather than the surface, so the cachapa tears into scrambled batter.
steps.fix: Wait for the matte surface. If it tears, push it back together in the pan; it will set.

steps.do: Slide the spatula fully underneath and flip in one smooth movement. Cook 3 minutes more.
steps.look: Both sides golden with darker caramelised spots. The cachapa feels firm and springy when pressed.
steps.mistake: A half-hearted flip that folds the pancake on itself.
steps.fix: Use a wide spatula, get it right under, and turn with commitment.

steps.do: Lay slices of cheese over half the cachapa, fold the other half over and press for a moment with the spatula. Move to the oven while you cook the rest, adding butter to the pan each time.
steps.look: Cheese softening and just beginning to melt at the edges.
steps.mistake: Leaving it in the hot pan with the cheese for minutes, so the cheese melts out and burns.
steps.fix: The residual heat is enough; fold, press and move it off.

steps.do: Serve hot with a knob of butter melting on top.
steps.look: A golden half-moon, cheese peeping out, butter pooling.
steps.mistake: Holding them too long, so they turn leathery.
steps.fix: Serve within 15 minutes of cooking.

dishes.science: Fresh corn kernels are full of water, sugar and a soft, starchy pulp, but contain no gluten. When blended, the starch disperses through the liquid; heat makes it swell and set into a soft structure, which is the only thing holding the cachapa together. Because heat travels up from the pan, the base sets and caramelises long before the top, so you flip only when the surface has dried and turned matte, meaning the starch above has set. The masarepa is precooked corn flour, which absorbs extra water and adds body. The sugar in fresh corn browns quickly through caramelisation, which is why medium-low heat is essential: high heat burns the base before the thick centre cooks.
dishes.plating: Serve one folded cachapa per plate, the fold facing the diner so the cheese is visible. Place a knob of butter on top to melt down the sides. A small bowl of nata or soured cream and a few slices of fried ham alongside make it a full Venezuelan breakfast.

pairing.drink: A papelón con limón, the Venezuelan drink of raw cane sugar and lime, or a café con leche.

variations: Cachapa with ham: add a slice of ham with the cheese.
Cachapa con chicharrón: fill with crisp pork crackling and cheese.
Sweeter cachapa: add 1 tbsp (12 g) more sugar and serve with a drizzle of condensed milk.
safety: Cut corn kernels away from your body, holding the cob steady inside a large bowl.
Batter with raw egg should be cooked within the hour or kept in the fridge.

dishes.title: Cong You Bing (Scallion Pancakes)
dishes.summary: Flaky, chewy flatbreads made from a hot water dough rolled with oil and scallions, coiled, rolled again and pan fried until crisp. They are a first, simple lesson in lamination, building layers by separating sheets of dough with fat.
skills: rolling, oiling, coiling and rolling again for layers
equipment: Mixing bowl and chopsticks or a spoon
Small bowl for the oil paste
10 inch (25 cm) heavy frying pan, cast iron or nonstick
Cling film or a damp tea towel

ingredients.note: green and white parts, sliced thin and patted dry

ingredients.item: Soy sauce and black or rice vinegar, for dipping
ingredients.note: add chilli oil if you like

mise: Slice the spring onions thinly and dry them well on a towel; wet onions make the layers stick and the dough tear.
Make the oil paste: stir the 3 tbsp (45 ml) oil, 2 tbsp (16 g) flour and sesame oil together in a small bowl until smooth.
Boil the kettle and measure the water.
Mix the dipping sauce.

timeline.do: Make the hot water dough; rest 30 minutes covered.
Roll, paint, scatter, coil and rest the coils 15 minutes.
Roll out each coil and fry, about 6 to 8 minutes each.
Scrunch, cut into wedges and serve with dipping sauce.

steps.do: Put the flour in the bowl and pour in the just-boiled water in a stream, stirring with chopsticks until it forms shaggy clumps. When cool enough to handle, knead in the bowl for 5 minutes until smooth.
steps.look: A soft, smooth dough that feels slightly tacky but does not stick to your hands.
steps.mistake: Burning your hands by kneading too early.
steps.fix: Stir with chopsticks first and wait 2 or 3 minutes before kneading. If the dough is sticky, dust with a little flour.

steps.do: Cover with cling film and rest for 30 minutes at room temperature.
steps.look: After resting, the dough is relaxed and stretches without springing back.
steps.mistake: Skipping the rest, so the dough fights back and tears when rolled thin.
steps.fix: If the dough springs back while rolling, cover it and rest 10 minutes more.

steps.do: Divide into 4 pieces. On a lightly oiled surface, roll one piece into a thin rectangle about 10 by 8 inches (25 by 20 cm), as thin as you can without tearing.
steps.look: You can almost see the work surface through the dough.
steps.mistake: Rolling on a heavily floured surface, which dries the dough and stops layers sealing.
steps.fix: Use a light film of oil instead of flour.

steps.do: Brush the sheet thinly with the oil paste, sprinkle with a pinch of salt and a quarter of the spring onions.
steps.look: An even, thin, glossy coating with spring onion scattered all over.
steps.mistake: Too much paste, which oozes out and makes the pancake greasy.
steps.fix: Brush thinly; you need just enough to separate the layers.

steps.do: Starting from a long side, roll the sheet up tightly into a long rope like a cigar. Then coil the rope into a spiral like a snail shell and tuck the end underneath. Repeat with the other pieces. Cover and rest 15 minutes.
steps.look: Four neat snails, slightly oily.
steps.mistake: Rolling loosely, which leaves air pockets that burst.
steps.fix: Roll tightly and press gently as you go.

steps.do: Press each coil flat with your palm, then roll it gently into a round about 7 inches (18 cm) across and 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick.
steps.look: Spring onion showing faintly through the dough; a few may poke through.
steps.mistake: Pressing too hard, which squashes the layers together.
steps.fix: Roll gently from the centre outwards, turning the pancake as you go.

steps.do: Heat 1 tbsp (15 ml) frying oil in the pan over medium heat. Fry one pancake for 3 to 4 minutes per side, pressing with the spatula and rotating it in the pan every 30 seconds.
steps.look: A crackling sizzle; both sides deep golden and crisp, the edges flaking.
steps.mistake: High heat, which burns the outside while the inner layers stay doughy.
steps.fix: Medium heat, and keep rotating for even colour.

steps.do: Remove to a board and, while hot, scrunch it from the sides towards the middle with your hands or two spatulas to break open the layers. Cut into wedges and serve with the dipping sauce.
steps.look: Layers visibly separate and fluff up, shattering at the edges.
steps.mistake: Cutting it flat without scrunching, so the layers stay pressed together.
steps.fix: Push the sides in firmly; it is a classic street stall move.

dishes.science: Pouring boiling water onto flour changes how the dough behaves. The heat partly cooks the starch so it absorbs more water, and it weakens the gluten-forming proteins, so the dough is soft, pliable and less elastic. That lets it be rolled very thin without springing back, which is essential for many layers. Lamination is the second half: when a thin sheet is brushed with oil paste and rolled and coiled, each layer of dough is separated from the next by a film of fat. In the hot pan, the water in each layer turns to steam and pushes the layers apart, while the fat fries them crisp. Flour in the oil paste stops the fat soaking straight into the dough.
dishes.plating: Cut each pancake into six wedges and stack them slightly fanned on a warm plate or bamboo board, layered edges facing out. Serve the dipping sauce in a small dish to one side, with a few fresh rings of spring onion on top.

pairing.drink: Hot soy milk, the classic Chinese breakfast drink, or a cold lager with the dipping sauce later in the day.

variations: Egg scallion pancake: when the pancake is nearly done, pour a beaten egg into the pan and press the pancake on top so it sticks.
Sesame: sprinkle toasted sesame seeds on the layers with the spring onion.
Chilli: add a pinch of chilli flakes and Sichuan pepper to the oil paste.
safety: Take care when mixing boiling water into flour; use chopsticks and let the dough cool before kneading.
Hot oil can spit as spring onions hit it; lay the pancake away from you into the pan.

dishes.title: Aloo Paratha
dishes.summary: Whole wheat flatbreads stuffed with a spiced potato filling, rolled thin without tearing and cooked on a tawa with ghee until crisp in patches. It teaches dough strength, why a filling must be dry and cold, and how to roll a stuffed dough evenly.
equipment: Rolling pin, ideally a thin Indian belan
Tawa or heavy flat frying pan, 10 to 12 inch (25 to 30 cm)
Flat spatula and a folded clean cloth for pressing
Small dry frying pan for roasting cumin

ingredients.note: boiled in their skins and cooled completely

ingredients.item: Cumin seeds, dry roasted and coarsely ground
Deghi mirch or mild Kashmiri chilli powder
Plain yoghurt, pickle and butter to serve

mise: Boil the potatoes whole in their skins for 20 to 25 minutes until tender, drain and let them cool completely, at least 45 minutes; the day before is best.
Dry roast the cumin seeds in a small pan for 1 minute until fragrant, then grind coarsely.
Mince the ginger and chillies; chop the coriander; crush the ajwain.
Melt the ghee for cooking and keep it in a small bowl with a spoon by the tawa.

timeline.do: Boil potatoes; cool completely.
Make the dough; rest 30 minutes covered.
Grate potatoes and mix the filling, salt last.
Stuff, roll and cook parathas one at a time, about 5 minutes each.
Serve hot with yoghurt, pickle and butter.

steps.do: Mix the atta and salt in the bowl, rub in 1 tbsp (15 g) ghee, then add the water gradually, mixing with your hand. Knead for 6 minutes on the counter.
steps.look: A soft, smooth dough that takes a fingertip with little resistance and springs back slowly. It should be softer than a bread dough.
steps.mistake: A stiff dough, which cracks when you try to seal the filling inside.
steps.fix: Wet your hand and knead in more water a teaspoon at a time until soft.

steps.do: Cover and rest for 30 minutes.
steps.look: The dough relaxes and becomes silky.
steps.mistake: Rolling straight away, so the dough tears.
steps.fix: Give it the full rest; gluten relaxes and the bran softens.

steps.do: Peel the cold potatoes and grate them on the coarse side of the box grater into a wide bowl. Add the ginger, chillies, ajwain, amchur, roasted cumin, chilli powder and coriander and toss with your fingertips so the threads stay loose. Add the salt only now.
steps.look: A dry, loose, fluffy filling, speckled with green and red, with no lumps.
steps.mistake: Mashing warm potatoes, which makes a wet, gluey filling that bursts through the dough.
steps.fix: If the filling is wet, spread it on a tray for 10 minutes to dry, or mix in 1 tbsp (8 g) of atta.

steps.do: Divide the dough into 8 balls and the filling into 8 equal portions. Flatten a ball into a cup about 4 inches (10 cm) across, thicker in the middle. Place a portion of filling, about the same weight as the dough, in the cup.
steps.look: A small cup of dough holding a rounded heap of filling.
steps.mistake: Too much filling, which tears through when rolled.
steps.fix: Start with a little less filling until your sealing improves.

steps.do: Pull the edges of the dough up over the filling, pleating as you go, and pinch them together at the top. Pinch off any excess knot of dough and press the ball flat, seam side down, in a little flour.
steps.look: A sealed, flat disc with no filling showing.
steps.mistake: A thick knot of dough at the seal, which stays raw and heavy.
steps.fix: Pinch off the extra dough at the top before flattening.

steps.do: Roll the disc gently from the centre outwards, turning it a quarter turn after every few strokes and dusting with flour as needed, to a round about 7 inches (18 cm) across.
steps.look: An even round where you can faintly see the filling through the dough.
steps.mistake: Pressing hard at the edges, which thins them so the filling bursts out.
steps.fix: Light, even pressure from the centre out. If a small tear appears, patch it with a pinch of dough and dust with flour.

steps.do: Heat the tawa over medium heat. Lay the paratha on it dry and cook for 1 minute, until small bubbles appear and the underside has light brown spots. Flip and cook 1 minute more.
steps.look: Faint brown freckles on both sides and the dough no longer looks raw.
steps.mistake: A tawa that is too hot, which scorches the outside before the inside cooks.
steps.fix: Lower the heat; parathas cook through slowly.

steps.do: Spread 1 tsp (5 g) ghee over the top, flip and spread ghee on the other side. Press the edges and centre with the folded cloth, turning every 30 seconds, until puffed in places and golden with crisp patches, about 2 minutes more.
steps.look: Golden brown patches all over, crisp edges, and the paratha puffing as steam builds inside.
steps.mistake: Too much ghee, so it fries greasy rather than crisp.
steps.fix: Use a little ghee and press; the pressure gives the crisp patches.

steps.do: Serve each paratha hot as it comes off the tawa, with a spoon of yoghurt, pickle and a knob of butter on top.
steps.look: Butter melting into a golden, crisp paratha.
steps.mistake: Stacking them while hot, which makes them soggy.
steps.fix: Stack them wrapped in a clean cloth if you must hold them, and serve within 10 minutes.

dishes.science: Atta is whole wheat flour ground fine, with bran and germ included. The bran cuts gluten strands, so the dough needs a full rest to hydrate and become extensible enough to roll without tearing. The filling must be dry and cold because steam is the enemy of a sealed paratha. Boiling potatoes whole in their skins limits how much water they absorb. Grating rather than mashing keeps the starch cells intact; mashing bursts them, releasing sticky starch that turns into wet glue. Salt draws water out of the potato by osmosis, so it goes in only at the last moment. On the tawa, the dry first cook sets the dough; ghee then fries the surface crisp while steam inside puffs the layers.
dishes.plating: Serve one paratha whole on a warm plate, or cut into quarters and stacked, with a knob of butter melting on top. Arrange a small bowl of yoghurt and a smaller one of mango or lime pickle beside it.

pairing.drink: A glass of sweet or salted lassi, or a hot masala chai.

variations: Gobi paratha: replace the potato with finely grated, salted and squeezed cauliflower.
Paneer paratha: crumbled paneer with green chilli and coriander.
Onion paratha: add finely chopped red onion to the potato filling, squeezed dry first.
safety: Cool boiled potatoes quickly and refrigerate if preparing ahead; use within two days.
The tawa stays very hot long after cooking; handle it with a cloth.

dishes.title: Karjalanpiirakka (Karelian Pies)
dishes.summary: Little open pies of paper-thin rye crust crimped around creamy rice porridge, baked in a very hot oven, brushed with butter and topped with egg butter. They teach how to roll a dough with almost no gluten very thin and crimp it by hand.
equipment: Thin rolling pin, ideally a narrow Finnish pin or a dowel
Two baking trays lined with baking paper
Small saucepan for melted butter and milk

ingredients.note: makes the dough easier to roll

ingredients.item: Unsalted butter and milk for brushing
Soft unsalted butter for egg butter

mise: Make the rice porridge first: it needs about 40 minutes and must cool before filling.
Heat the oven to its highest setting, ideally 525 to 550°F (275 to 290°C), with a rack in the upper third.
Line two trays with baking paper.
Hard boil the eggs for 10 minutes, cool in iced water and peel.
Warm the brushing butter and milk together in a small pan.

timeline.do: Make the rice porridge, 40 minutes; spread to cool.
Heat the oven to maximum. Boil eggs for egg butter.
Make the rye dough; roll into a log and cut 16 pieces.
Roll each piece paper thin, fill and crimp.
Bake in batches 10 to 15 minutes; brush with butter milk; cover to soften.
Serve warm with egg butter.

steps.do: Bring the water to the boil in the heavy saucepan, add the rice and simmer for 10 minutes until the water is absorbed. Add the milk and salt and bring back to a simmer, then cook on low heat for 30 to 35 minutes, stirring every few minutes, until thick. Stir in the butter and spread on a plate to cool.
steps.look: A thick, creamy porridge in which the rice is soft and a spoon leaves a trail that slowly fills in.
steps.mistake: Not stirring, so the milk catches and burns on the bottom.
steps.fix: Stir often and scrape the base; if it catches, transfer the unburnt porridge to a clean pan without scraping.

steps.do: Mix the rye flour, plain flour and salt in a bowl, add the cold water and work it together with your hand into a firm, smooth dough, about 2 minutes. It does not need long kneading.
steps.look: A firm, slightly sticky, dark grey-brown dough that holds together.
steps.mistake: Expecting it to stretch like wheat dough; rye has little gluten.
steps.fix: If it crumbles, add water 1 tsp (5 ml) at a time; if sticky, add a little rye flour.

steps.do: Roll the dough into a log and cut into 16 equal pieces. Keep them covered. Dust the counter with rye flour and roll one piece into a very thin oval about 6 inches (15 cm) long and 4 inches (10 cm) wide, turning it often.
steps.look: A dough sheet thin enough that you can almost see the counter through it, about 1/16 inch (1 to 2 mm).
steps.mistake: Rolling too thick, which gives a tough, chewy crust.
steps.fix: Keep rolling, dusting with rye flour; a thin pin gives more control.

steps.do: Spread about 2 tbsp (30 g) of cooled porridge along the middle of the oval, leaving a border of 3/4 inch (2 cm).
steps.look: A neat strip of rice in the centre.
steps.mistake: Too much filling, which spills over during baking.
steps.fix: Keep the filling a thin layer about 3/8 inch (1 cm) thick.

steps.do: Fold the border in over the edge of the filling all round, then pinch and crimp it with your thumb and forefinger along both long sides, making little pleats close together, leaving the rice visible in the middle.
steps.look: A boat shape with a pleated rim and an open centre of rice.
steps.mistake: Pressing the pleats too loosely, so they unfold in the oven.
steps.fix: Pinch firmly, each pleat overlapping the last.

steps.do: Place the pies on the lined trays. Bake on the upper rack in the very hot oven for 10 to 15 minutes.
steps.look: The crimped edges turn brown and crisp, the rice filling develops golden brown spots.
steps.mistake: A cool oven, which dries the crust slowly and makes it hard and leathery.
steps.fix: Give the oven a full 30 minutes to heat to maximum before baking.

steps.do: As soon as they come out, brush each pie all over with the warm butter and milk. Stack them on a plate and cover with a clean cloth for 10 minutes.
steps.look: The crust softens slightly and turns glossy.
steps.mistake: Leaving them unbrushed, so the crust is brittle.
steps.fix: Brush generously and cover; the steam softens them perfectly.

steps.do: Make the egg butter: chop the boiled eggs finely, then mix with the very soft butter and a pinch of salt with a fork until spreadable.
steps.look: A creamy, yellow and white flecked spread.
steps.mistake: Using cold butter, which will not mix smoothly.
steps.fix: Let the butter soften at room temperature or beat it alone first.

steps.do: Serve the pies warm with a generous spoonful of egg butter on top of each.
steps.look: Glossy pies with a pale mound of egg butter in the centre of the rice.
steps.mistake: Spreading egg butter on hot pies, so it melts away.
steps.fix: Let the pies cool slightly first.

dishes.science: Rye flour contains proteins that form very little gluten, plus gums called pentosans that absorb lots of water and make the dough sticky. That is why rye dough does not stretch like wheat dough: there is no elastic network, so it must be rolled rather than pulled, and it tears if handled roughly. A little wheat flour adds just enough gluten to make rolling easier. The pies bake in an extremely hot oven so the thin crust crisps and browns in minutes before it can dry out and harden. Brushing with butter and milk straight after baking, then covering them, lets steam soften the crust. Rice porridge is thick because swollen rice starch leaks into the milk.
dishes.plating: Arrange three or four pies on a wooden board or plate, pleated edges neat, each topped with a quenelle of egg butter. A cup of strong coffee beside them is the Finnish way.

pairing.drink: Strong filter coffee, as served in Finland, or a glass of cold buttermilk.

variations: Potato filling: use smooth mashed potato with butter instead of rice porridge.
Carrot and rice: mix grated cooked carrot into the porridge.
Barley filling: use pearl barley porridge, the older traditional version.
safety: A very hot oven at 525 to 550°F (275 to 290°C) gives severe burns; use long oven gloves and pull trays out carefully.
Cool rice porridge quickly and refrigerate if not using within an hour.

dishes.title: Banitsa
dishes.summary: Bulgaria's breakfast pie of filo sheets rolled around a filling of eggs, yoghurt and crumbled sirene cheese, coiled in a tin and baked deep bronze. It is the first work with filo, the thinnest dough a cook handles, and teaches how to keep it from drying and tearing.
skills: layering with egg, yoghurt and sirene
equipment: 9 to 10 inch (23 to 25 cm) round metal baking tin or ovenproof frying pan
Two mixing bowls and a whisk
Small saucepan or bowl for the butter and oil
Clean damp tea towel and cling film

ingredients.note: thawed overnight in the fridge if frozen

ingredients.item: Sirene (Bulgarian brined white cheese) or feta
Bulgarian or plain whole milk yoghurt

ingredients.note: no salt; the cheese is salty

mise: Thaw frozen filo overnight in the fridge, then leave it in its packet at room temperature for 1 hour before opening; cold filo cracks.
Heat the oven to 375°F (190°C) with a rack in the middle.
Mix the melted butter and oil in a small bowl; brush the tin with some of it.
Crumble the cheese by hand into pieces the size of peas.
Clear a large dry work surface. Have the damp tea towel and cling film ready to cover the filo.

timeline.do: Filo out of the fridge to come to room temperature.
Oven on. Make the filling; oil the tin.
Roll the filo ropes and coil them into the tin.
Into the oven for 40 to 45 minutes; check from 35 minutes.
Out of the oven; rest 10 minutes under a cloth.
Cut into wedges and serve warm.

steps.do: Whisk the eggs, yoghurt and bicarbonate of soda in a bowl for 1 minute until the mixture foams and lifts. Fold in the crumbled cheese and a good grind of black pepper.
steps.look: A thick, slightly foamy, lumpy mixture with visible pieces of white cheese.
steps.mistake: Mashing the cheese to a paste, which melts into the custard and sets rubbery.
steps.fix: Crumble by hand into pea-sized rubble, then fold, not beat.

steps.do: Unroll the filo and immediately cover the stack with cling film and then the damp tea towel. Work with one sheet at a time, keeping the rest covered.
steps.look: Soft, pliable sheets that drape without cracking.
steps.mistake: Leaving the stack uncovered while you work, so the edges dry and crack within minutes.
steps.fix: If a sheet tears, patch it with a piece from another sheet; once rolled, tears disappear.

steps.do: Lay one sheet on the counter, long side towards you, and brush it lightly all over with the butter and oil. Spoon a line of filling, about 3 tbsp (45 g), along the long edge nearest you.
steps.look: A thin glossy sheen over the sheet, with a ribbon of filling along one edge.
steps.mistake: Soaking the filo in fat, which makes the pie greasy.
steps.fix: Brush lightly; dabbing is enough on the middle.

steps.do: Roll the sheet loosely away from you around the filling into a rope, like a loose cigar, without squeezing.
steps.look: A loose, even rope with filling inside along its length.
steps.mistake: Rolling tightly, which compresses the layers and makes the inside stodgy.
steps.fix: Leave the roll loose so steam can escape and the layers crisp.

steps.do: Coil the first rope in the centre of the tin, then wrap each following rope around it in a spiral, leaving a gap the width of a finger between the turns.
steps.look: A loose spiral filling the tin from the centre outwards, with small gaps between coils.
steps.mistake: Packing the coils edge to edge, so the middle stews while the rim burns.
steps.fix: Leave gaps; the pie puffs and fills them as it bakes.

steps.do: Brush the top with the remaining butter and oil and pour any leftover filling into the gaps. Bake for 40 to 45 minutes.
steps.look: The banitsa puffs, turns deep bronze and blisters on top. When tapped, it sounds hollow, and a skewer pushed into the centre comes out without wet custard.
steps.mistake: Taking it out when only pale gold, so the inside is underdone and soggy.
steps.fix: Bake on; cover loosely with foil if the top is browning too fast before the centre is set.

steps.do: Rest the banitsa in the tin under a clean cloth for 10 minutes, then cut into wedges.
steps.look: Flaky, crisp top layers with a soft, cheesy custard inside.
steps.mistake: Cutting it straight from the oven, so the filling runs and the filo shatters everywhere.
steps.fix: Let it rest; the cloth softens the top slightly the Bulgarian way and makes it easier to cut.

dishes.science: Filo is an unleavened dough rolled so thin that it has almost no moisture to spare, which is why it dries and cracks within minutes in the air. Covering it keeps the surface humid. Brushing each sheet with fat separates the layers so that, in the oven, water in the dough turns to steam and the fat fries each layer crisp. Bicarbonate of soda is an alkali; it reacts with the lactic acid in the yoghurt to release carbon dioxide, which lightens the custard and helps hold the coils apart so steam can escape. Sirene is a brined cheese whose proteins are set by acid and salt, so it softens but does not melt into strings, keeping the filling distinct.
dishes.plating: Cut into neat wedges with a sharp serrated knife and serve on a plate with the spiral visible. Traditionally it is eaten warm with a glass of ayran or boza. A spoon of extra yoghurt on the side is welcome.

pairing.drink: A glass of ayran (salted yoghurt drink), or a crisp dry white such as an Assyrtiko, whose acidity cuts through cheese and butter.
pairing.brennans: Gaia ‘Wild Ferment’ Assyrtiko Santorini 2023: a mineral, saline Greek white that matches salty brined cheese and flaky pastry.

variations: Spinach banitsa: add 8 oz (225 g) wilted, squeezed spinach to the filling.
Pumpkin banitsa (tikvenik): a sweet version with grated pumpkin, walnuts, sugar and cinnamon.
Layered banitsa: stack sheets flat in a tray with filling between every two, then pour a little sparkling water over before baking.
safety: Bake until the egg filling is fully set; a skewer should come out clean of liquid egg.
Use oven gloves; the tin and the oil in it are very hot.

dishes.title: Bánh Bao (Vietnamese Steamed Pork Buns)
dishes.summary: Soft, snowy steamed buns filled with seasoned pork, wood ear mushroom, onion and a piece of egg, pleated closed and steamed until puffed. This is the first yeast dough in the course cooked by steam rather than the oven, and it teaches how to pleat a bun and keep its surface smooth.
skills: a pork, egg and wood ear filling
equipment: Large mixing bowl or stand mixer with dough hook
Bamboo or metal steamer with a lid, set over a wok or wide pot
Squares of baking paper, 4 inch (10 cm)
Clean tea towel to wrap the steamer lid

ingredients.note: low protein flour gives the whitest, softest bun
hard boiled and peeled; large eggs quartered

mise: Soak the wood ear in hot water for 20 minutes, trim off any hard knobs and chop finely.
Boil the eggs: large eggs 10 minutes, quail eggs 3 minutes. Cool in iced water, peel and quarter large eggs.
Chop the onion and garlic finely.
Cut 8 squares of baking paper.
Warm the milk to about 100°F (38°C), comfortably warm to a fingertip.

timeline.do: Make the dough; knead 10 minutes; first rise 60 to 75 minutes.
Mix and chill the filling; boil eggs.
Divide the dough, roll wrappers, fill and pleat.
Second rise, 20 to 30 minutes. Bring the steamer water to the boil.
Steam 12 to 15 minutes; rest 3 to 5 minutes before lifting the lid.
Serve hot.

steps.do: Mix the flour, yeast, sugar, baking powder and salt in the bowl. Add the warm milk and oil and stir into a shaggy dough, then knead by hand for 10 minutes (or 6 to 7 minutes on low in a mixer).
steps.look: A very smooth, soft, slightly tacky dough that springs back slowly when pressed.
steps.mistake: Under-kneading, which gives buns with a rough, pitted surface.
steps.fix: Keep kneading until the surface looks satiny. A smooth dough gives a smooth bun.

steps.do: Cover the bowl and leave in a warm place for 60 to 75 minutes.
steps.look: The dough roughly doubles in size and a finger pressed in leaves a dent that slowly fills back.
steps.mistake: Letting it overproof until it collapses and smells strongly of alcohol.
steps.fix: If overproofed, knock it back, knead 1 minute and let it rise again for 20 minutes.

steps.do: While it rises, mix the pork, wood ear, onion, garlic, fish sauce, oyster sauce, sugar and pepper in a bowl, stirring hard in one direction for 1 minute until sticky. Chill until needed.
steps.look: A sticky, cohesive filling that holds together in a ball.
steps.mistake: A loose filling that falls apart and leaks juice during pleating.
steps.fix: Stir longer; the salt in the sauces makes the proteins sticky. Chill so it firms up.

steps.do: Knock back the dough, knead briefly and roll into a log. Cut into 8 equal pieces, about 2 3/4 oz (75 g) each. Roll each piece into a ball, then into a round about 4 1/2 inches (11 cm) across, thicker in the middle and thinner at the edges.
steps.look: Even rounds with a slightly thicker centre that will sit under the filling.
steps.mistake: Rolling evenly thin, so the bottom tears and the top pleats are bulky.
steps.fix: Roll the edges only, turning the round, so the centre stays thicker.

steps.do: Place a heaped tablespoon of filling, about 1 1/2 oz (40 g), in the centre, press a piece of egg and a slice of sausage into it. Holding the round in one hand, pleat the edge with the other, folding and pinching small pleats all the way round, rotating the bun, then twist the top to seal.
steps.look: A round bun with a neat spiral of pleats meeting at the top.
steps.mistake: Getting filling on the edges, which stops the pleats sealing.
steps.fix: Wipe the edges clean with a dry finger; keep the filling in the centre.

steps.do: Set each bun on a square of baking paper in the steamer basket, 2 inches (5 cm) apart. Cover and let rise for 20 to 30 minutes until slightly puffed. Meanwhile bring water in the wok to the boil.
steps.look: The buns look puffy and feel light and airy.
steps.mistake: Placing the buns too close, so they stick together as they expand.
steps.fix: Steam in two batches if needed.

steps.do: Wrap the steamer lid in a tea towel to catch drips. Set the basket over the boiling water, cover and steam over medium-high heat for 12 to 15 minutes.
steps.look: The buns puff up, turn smooth, white and glossy, and spring back when touched.
steps.mistake: Condensation dripping onto the buns, which leaves wet spots and wrinkles.
steps.fix: The tea towel round the lid stops this; keep it from touching the flame.

steps.do: Turn off the heat and leave the lid on for 3 to 5 minutes before opening it slowly. Check the filling of one bun with the thermometer.
steps.look: Smooth, puffed buns; the filling reads at least 160°F (71°C).
steps.mistake: Lifting the lid immediately, which makes the buns deflate and wrinkle from the sudden temperature change.
steps.fix: Always rest the buns with the lid on before opening.

dishes.science: Yeast feeds on sugar in the dough and releases carbon dioxide, which gluten traps in tiny bubbles, making the dough rise. Baking powder adds a second burst of gas in the steamer for an extra soft, open crumb. Steaming cooks at about 212°F (100°C), much cooler than an oven, so the surface never browns and stays white and soft. The moist heat sets the outside gently while gases expand inside. A sudden blast of cold air when the lid is lifted makes the gases in the bun contract faster than the set structure can hold, so the surface wrinkles; resting the buns lets the temperature drop gradually. Low protein flour forms less gluten, which keeps the buns tender rather than chewy.
dishes.plating: Serve the buns on their baking paper squares in the bamboo steamer basket at the table, or on a plate with one bun torn open to show the filling and egg. A small dish of chilli sauce on the side.

pairing.drink: Hot jasmine tea or a Vietnamese iced coffee with condensed milk.

variations: Chicken bánh bao: replace the pork with minced chicken thigh.
Vegetarian: replace the pork with crumbled firm tofu, shiitake and glass noodles, seasoned with soy.
Bánh bao chay: plain buns without filling, served with braised pork belly.
safety: The pork filling must reach 160°F (71°C) in the centre.
Steam is hotter than it looks; open the lid away from your face and lift baskets with oven gloves.
Keep the steamer topped up with boiling water so it never boils dry.
