dishes.title: Thịt Kho Trứng (Caramel Pork and Eggs)
dishes.summary: Pork belly braised slowly in a dark caramel, fish sauce and coconut water until meltingly soft, with hard boiled eggs simmered alongside until they turn amber, served with rice and pickled greens. It extends caramel cooking to a long, slow braise and teaches you to take sugar to a dark, bitter sweet colour without burning it.
skills: braising pork belly in coconut water
equipment: Heavy pot or clay pot with a lid, 4 quart (4 litres)
Small heavy saucepan for the caramel
Ladle and a fine spoon for skimming

ingredients.note: plus 3 tbsp (45 ml) to stop it
fresh or from a carton, unsweetened

ingredients.item: Pickled mustard greens or quick pickled bean sprouts

mise: Cut the pork into even cubes, each with skin, fat and meat.
Blanch the pork: cover with cold water, bring to a boil, boil 3 minutes, then drain and rinse off the scum. This keeps the braise clear.
Boil the eggs: lower into simmering water for 9 minutes, chill in iced water, peel carefully.
Chop shallots and garlic.
Measure the fish sauce and coconut water; set the extra water beside the caramel pan.

timeline.do: Cut and blanch the pork; boil and peel the eggs.
Make the caramel to a dark mahogany; stop it with water.
Pork into the caramel with shallot and garlic; add fish sauce and coconut water.
Simmer covered, skimming, 1 hour.
Add the eggs; simmer uncovered 30 to 40 minutes.
Rice, pickles and serve.

steps.do: Put the sugar and 3 tbsp (45 ml) water in the small heavy saucepan over medium heat. Swirl, do not stir, until the sugar dissolves and bubbles. Keep cooking, swirling, 6 to 10 minutes as it colours.
steps.look: Clear syrup, then pale gold, then amber, then a dark mahogany like strong tea, with a smell that is bitter sweet and smoky but not acrid; small wisps of smoke.
steps.mistake: Stirring with a spoon, which makes the sugar crystallise into a grainy mass.
steps.fix: Swirl the pan only. If crystals form, add 2 tbsp (30 ml) water and heat gently until they dissolve, then carry on.

steps.do: When it is dark mahogany, take it off the heat and, standing back, pour in the remaining 3 tbsp (45 ml) water. It will spit and steam. Swirl until smooth.
steps.look: A violent hiss, then a dark, pourable caramel sauce.
steps.mistake: Going past mahogany to black, which tastes burnt.
steps.fix: If it smells harshly burnt or is black, discard and start again; it will ruin the braise.

steps.do: Put the blanched pork into the big pot over medium high heat, pour over the caramel and add the shallots and garlic. Stir for 3 to 4 minutes so the pork is coated and lightly browned.
steps.look: Glossy, dark brown pork; a sweet savoury smell.
steps.mistake: Letting the caramel stick and burn on the pot.
steps.fix: Keep stirring; add a splash of coconut water if it catches.

steps.do: Add the fish sauce, coconut water, pepper and chillies, and enough water to just cover the pork. Bring to a boil, then lower to a gentle simmer. Skim off any foam. Cover and cook 1 hour, skimming the fat occasionally.
steps.look: A clear, amber braising liquid with a gentle bubble.
steps.mistake: Boiling hard, which makes the liquid cloudy and the pork stringy.
steps.fix: Lowest simmer, lid slightly ajar.

steps.do: Add the peeled eggs, pushing them into the liquid. Simmer uncovered for 30 to 40 minutes, turning the eggs now and then, until the pork is very tender and the liquid has reduced by about half.
steps.look: The eggs turn evenly amber brown; the pork skin is soft and wobbly; a skewer slides through the meat with no resistance.
steps.mistake: Eggs with pale patches where they floated above the liquid.
steps.fix: Turn them every 10 minutes so every side sits in the braise.

steps.do: Skim off excess fat from the surface. Taste the sauce; it should be savoury, slightly sweet and peppery. Adjust with a little fish sauce or sugar. Garnish with spring onion.
steps.look: A glossy, dark amber sauce, the pork shining.
steps.mistake: A sauce that is too salty from over reduction.
steps.fix: Add a splash of water or coconut water to dilute.

dishes.science: Caramelisation breaks sugar molecules apart under heat into hundreds of new compounds: as the colour deepens, sweetness falls and bitter, roasted flavours rise. Vietnamese cooks take it dark because the caramel is seasoning and colour, not sweetness. Water stops the cooking instantly by cooling the sugar, though it spits because the sugar is far above boiling point. Pork belly is layered with fat and collagen; long, gentle simmering melts collagen into gelatine, which makes the meat soft and the sauce silky. Coconut water adds natural sugars and a gentle fruity sweetness without the fat of coconut milk. The egg whites absorb the coloured braise because their porous protein gel takes in liquid and pigment over time.
dishes.plating: Use a deep bowl or the clay pot itself. Halve two eggs lengthways to show the yolk and lay them cut side up among the pork cubes, skin side up. Spoon the glossy sauce over and add spring onion and a slice of chilli. Serve with plain jasmine rice and a small dish of pickled mustard greens, whose sourness balances the richness.

pairing.drink: An off dry Vouvray or a cold lager. A little sweetness meets the caramel, and acidity cuts the fat.
pairing.brennans: Domaine Huet ‘Clos du Bourg’ Vouvray Demi-Sec 2015: a Loire Chenin Blanc from the Brennan's list whose honeyed sweetness and acidity suit a caramel braise.

variations: Cá kho tộ: braise thick catfish or salmon steaks in the same caramel and fish sauce in a clay pot for 25 minutes.
Use quail eggs for a more delicate version; boil them 3 minutes and add for the last 20 minutes.
Pressure cooker: braise the pork 25 minutes on high, then add the eggs and reduce uncovered.
safety: Hot caramel causes severe burns. Use a heavy pan, keep children away, stand back when adding water, and never touch or taste it.
Pork is cooked well past 145°F (63°C) in this braise.
Cool leftovers quickly and refrigerate within 2 hours; the braise keeps 3 days and tastes better the next day.

dishes.title: Massaman Curry with Beef
dishes.summary: Beef chuck braised slowly in coconut milk with a massaman paste pounded by hand from dried chillies, aromatics and toasted dry spices, finished with potatoes, onions and roasted peanuts and balanced with tamarind, palm sugar and fish sauce. It takes the green curry lesson slow and deep: a paste made in a mortar, fried in cracked coconut cream, then a long braise.
skills: pounding a paste with dry spices
equipment: Large granite mortar and pestle (or a small food processor)
Small dry frying pan for toasting spices

ingredients.note: do not shake; you need the thick cream on top
peeled and cut into 1 1/2 inch (4 cm) chunks
deseeded, soaked in hot water 15 minutes
tender lower part only, thinly sliced

ingredients.item: Paste: green cardamom pods (seeds only), cloves, white peppercorns

mise: Soak the chillies; cut them into small pieces once soft and squeeze dry.
Toast the shallots and garlic for the paste in a dry pan until charred in spots, then the lemongrass and galangal briefly. Cool.
Toast the coriander, cumin, cardamom seeds, cloves and peppercorns in the dry pan over medium heat for 2 minutes until fragrant, cool and grind fine in the mortar first.
Wrap the shrimp paste in foil and toast it in the dry pan 1 minute each side.
Cut the beef; peel and cut the potatoes; peel the small onions.
Open the coconut milk and spoon off the thick cream from the top into a bowl.

timeline.do: Toast and pound the paste, 30 to 40 minutes.
Crack the coconut cream and fry the paste.
Beef in, then coconut milk and whole spices; braise 1 1/2 to 2 hours.
Potatoes and onions in; 30 minutes more.
Season with tamarind, palm sugar and fish sauce; peanuts in.

steps.do: Pound the paste: with the ground spices and salt in the mortar, add the chillies and pound until broken down. Add lemongrass and galangal and pound until fibrous and fine. Add shallots and garlic, then the shrimp paste, pounding each until absorbed, until you have a smooth, thick, deep red paste.
steps.look: No visible pieces of lemongrass or chilli skin; a paste that smears smooth between finger and thumb and smells intensely fragrant.
steps.mistake: Adding everything at once, which leaves stringy lumps of lemongrass.
steps.fix: Go from the hardest and driest ingredients to the wettest, and pound with a firm, dropping motion, scraping down often.

steps.do: Heat 1 cup (240 ml) of the thick coconut cream in the casserole over medium heat, stirring, until it boils, thickens and the oil separates (it cracks), about 5 to 8 minutes. Add 5 to 6 tbsp (80 to 90 g) of the paste and fry, stirring constantly, for 5 to 8 minutes.
steps.look: The cream bubbles thick, then splits to a curd with clear oil around the edges; the paste darkens and smells nutty and toasted, with red oil pooling.
steps.mistake: Frying the paste in cream that has not cracked, so it boils instead of fries and tastes raw.
steps.fix: Keep cooking the cream until the oil clearly separates. If your coconut milk will not crack, add 1 tbsp (15 ml) oil.

steps.do: Add the beef and stir to coat it in the paste, cooking 3 to 4 minutes. Add the rest of the coconut milk, the cinnamon, star anise and bay, and enough water to just cover the beef. Bring to a simmer.
steps.look: A red orange curry with drops of red oil on the surface.
steps.mistake: A rolling boil, which toughens the beef and can split the coconut milk grainy.
steps.fix: Lower to a gentle simmer, with a bubble breaking every second or two.

steps.do: Simmer partly covered for 1 1/2 to 2 hours, stirring occasionally and adding water if the beef is exposed, until the beef is tender.
steps.look: The beef yields easily to a spoon; the sauce has reduced and thickened.
steps.mistake: Adding potatoes at the start so they fall apart into mush.
steps.fix: Potatoes go in only when the beef is nearly tender.

steps.do: Add the potatoes and onions and simmer 25 to 30 minutes until the potatoes are tender but whole.
steps.look: A knife slides into the potatoes; the onions are soft and translucent.
steps.mistake: Stirring hard and breaking the potatoes.
steps.fix: Stir gently from the bottom.

steps.do: Season: add the tamarind, palm sugar and fish sauce, then taste. Adjust until sweet, salty and sour are all present and in balance, with sweetness leading slightly. Stir in the peanuts. Remove the cinnamon and star anise.
steps.look: A glossy, thick, reddish brown curry that tastes rich, sweet, tangy and gently spiced, never sharp.
steps.mistake: Seasoning early and then reducing, which makes it too salty.
steps.fix: Always balance at the end. If it is too sweet, add tamarind; too salty, add palm sugar and a splash of water.

dishes.science: Pounding crushes the aromatics' cells, releasing their oils and juices and binding them into a paste; a blender chops rather than crushes, so a pounded paste tastes rounder. Toasting dry spices drives off moisture and develops new aromatic compounds. Cracking coconut cream means boiling off water until the fat separates from the proteins; frying the paste in that clear fat extracts fat soluble flavours and colour and gently browns the paste. Beef chuck is rich in collagen, which converts to gelatine over long, moist, gentle heat, making the meat tender. The final balance of tamarind (sour), palm sugar (sweet) and fish sauce (salty) adjusts how each taste is perceived, since sugar softens sourness and salt boosts sweetness.
dishes.plating: Ladle into a warm, deep bowl so that the beef, potatoes and onions show above the sauce, with red oil glistening on top. Scatter a few whole peanuts and a few fried shallots over, and a single sprig of coriander. Serve jasmine rice in a separate bowl, and a quick cucumber relish of cucumber, shallot and chilli in vinegar alongside.

pairing.drink: A rich Alsace Pinot Gris or an aromatic white with a hint of sweetness. Its body matches coconut and its fruit meets the warm spices.
pairing.brennans: Albert Boxler Pinot Gris 2020: an Alsace Pinot Gris from the Brennan's list with the richness for coconut and spice.

variations: Massaman with chicken: use 2 lb (900 g) bone in chicken thighs and braise 40 minutes before adding potatoes.
Lamb shank massaman: braise 4 lamb shanks for 2 1/2 hours.
Shortcut: use 1/3 cup (85 g) good quality bought massaman paste, fried in cracked coconut cream in the same way.
safety: Wear gloves when handling chillies; do not touch eyes.
Contains peanuts, fish and shellfish (shrimp paste); tell guests.
Cool leftovers quickly and refrigerate within 2 hours.

dishes.title: Cochinita Pibil
dishes.summary: Pork shoulder marinated in achiote paste and sour orange juice, wrapped in banana leaves and sealed under foil, then slow cooked in the oven until it collapses into its own juices, served with pickled red onion and habanero. It is the Yucatecan pit roast adapted for a home oven, and it teaches marinating with acid and how a tight seal turns an oven into a steamer.
equipment: Deep ovenproof dish or casserole, about 9 by 13 inch (23 by 33 cm)
Mixing bowl and whisk, or a blender
Tongs or a gas flame or dry pan for wilting the leaves
Glass jar for the pickled onions

ingredients.item: Boneless pork shoulder (butt), fat left on

ingredients.note: or 1/2 cup (120 ml) orange juice, 1/4 cup (60 ml) grapefruit juice and 1/4 cup (60 ml) lime juice
charred in a dry pan, peeled
frozen leaves from Latin or Asian grocers; thawed
1 in the pickle, 1 for a salsa

mise: Blend the achiote paste with the sour orange juice, charred garlic, oregano, cumin and salt until smooth and no gritty specks remain.
Toss the pork in the marinade, cover and refrigerate 6 to 12 hours.
Make the pickled onions: pour boiling water over the sliced onions, drain after 10 seconds, then pack into the jar with the lime juice, a pinch of salt and a sliced habanero. Leave at least 1 hour.
Thaw the banana leaves and wipe them clean with a damp cloth; cut away the thick central rib.
Heat the oven to 300°F (150°C).

timeline.do: Marinate the pork 6 to 12 hours. Make the pickled onions.
Wilt the banana leaves; build and seal the parcel.
Into the oven at 300°F (150°C); do not open for 4 hours.
Check tenderness; warm tortillas.
Shred in the juices and serve.

steps.do: Wilt the banana leaves: pass each piece over a gas flame or press it in a hot dry pan for a few seconds a side.
steps.look: The leaf turns from dull olive to bright, glossy green and goes soft and pliable; it smells faintly of tea.
steps.mistake: Using unwilted leaves, which crack along the ribs and leak.
steps.fix: Wilt every piece until it is floppy; patch any split with an extra piece.

steps.do: Line the dish with the leaves, crossing them so they overhang well on all sides. Pile in the pork and every bit of the marinade, dot the lard over the top, then fold the leaves over to enclose the pork completely.
steps.look: A tight green parcel with no meat showing.
steps.mistake: Leaving gaps, so the juices evaporate and the meat dries.
steps.fix: Lay an extra piece of leaf over any gap.

steps.do: Cover the whole dish with a double layer of foil and crimp it hard all round the rim to seal. Put the lid on top if the dish has one.
steps.look: A tight drum of foil with no openings.
steps.mistake: A loose foil cover that lets steam escape, so the pork roasts dry instead of steaming.
steps.fix: Crimp tightly and press the foil down against the outside of the dish.

steps.do: Cook at 300°F (150°C) for 4 hours without opening.
steps.look: After a while, a rich smell of achiote and citrus fills the kitchen.
steps.mistake: Peeking, which lets out the steam.
steps.fix: Trust the time. The seal is the method.

steps.do: Open the parcel carefully, away from you. Test a chunk by pressing it with a spoon from the side.
steps.look: The pork collapses and shreds with no effort, sitting in a pool of orange red juice topped with red fat.
steps.mistake: Pork that resists, which means it needs more time.
steps.fix: Reseal and cook 30 to 45 minutes more.

steps.do: Shred the pork in the dish with two forks, mixing it thoroughly with all the juices. Taste and add salt or a squeeze of sour orange if needed.
steps.look: Moist, glossy, brick red threads of pork, well coated, never dry.
steps.mistake: Lifting the pork out and draining it, which leaves it dry and stringy.
steps.fix: Keep it in its juices until the moment you serve.

steps.do: Make a quick habanero salsa: finely chop the second habanero (wear gloves), mix with a pinch of salt and 3 tbsp (45 ml) lime juice.
steps.look: A thin, fiery, bright orange salsa.
steps.mistake: Touching your eyes after handling habanero.
steps.fix: Wear gloves, or wash hands with soap twice and keep them away from your face.

dishes.science: Achiote seeds hold bixin, an orange red pigment soluble in fat, which is why the dish turns the lard and juices deep red. Sour orange brings acid, which with salt seasons and slightly firms the outside of the meat over several hours; it penetrates only a little way, so the chunks are cut fairly small. The tightly sealed parcel matters more than the leaf. Trapped steam holds the meat in moist heat near the boiling point of water, so the collagen in pork shoulder slowly converts to gelatine without the surface drying out, the same principle as the original pit, or pib. Banana leaves add a gentle grassy aroma and a natural moisture seal. Onions are pickled because acid softens their sharpness and balances the rich pork.
dishes.plating: Serve on a warm platter or in a shallow clay dish with the juices: a mound of shredded pork, a tangle of bright pink pickled onions on top, and the habanero salsa on the side. For tacos, lay two warm corn tortillas on the plate, fill each with pork and juice, then pickled onion, and finish with a few drops of salsa.

pairing.drink: A cold Mexican lager with a squeeze of lime, or a paloma. Bubbles and citrus refresh against fat and habanero.

variations: Slow cooker: seal the parcel in foil, set in the slow cooker on low for 8 hours.
Pollo pibil: use bone in chicken thighs and cook 1 1/2 hours.
Panuchos: fry small tortillas stuffed with black beans and top with the pork and onions.
safety: Wear gloves when handling habanero.
Open the hot foil parcel away from your face; trapped steam burns.
Pork is cooked far past 145°F (63°C); cool leftovers within 2 hours.

dishes.title: Irish Stew
dishes.summary: Lamb neck on the bone layered in a heavy pot with sliced potatoes, onions and carrots, barely covered with water and simmered gently under a lid until the bottom potatoes melt into a thick broth and the whole ones on top steam tender. It is a braise with no flour and no browning that thickens itself with potato, and teaches patience, skimming and seasoning late.
equipment: Heavy casserole with a lid, 5 quart (5 litres)
Ladle and a wide spoon for skimming
Mandoline or sharp knife for slicing potatoes

ingredients.item: Lamb neck chops or neck fillet on the bone (or shoulder)

ingredients.note: peeled and sliced 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick

mise: Trim any very large pieces of hard fat from the lamb, but leave most of it.
Peel and slice the floury potatoes; peel the small waxy ones and keep them in cold water.
Slice the onions, cut the carrots.
Strip a few thyme leaves; keep the sprigs.

timeline.do: Prep vegetables and lamb.
Layer the pot; add water; bring to a simmer.
Cover and simmer gently 2 hours, skimming.
Season; stir gently so the broken potato thickens the broth.
Butter and parsley; serve.

steps.do: Lay half the sliced potatoes over the base of the casserole, then half the onions and carrots, then all the lamb. Season each layer with a little salt and pepper and tuck in the thyme and bay. Add the remaining onions, carrots and sliced potatoes, then set the whole potatoes on top.
steps.look: Neat layers with the whole potatoes crowning the pot.
steps.mistake: Putting the whole potatoes at the bottom, where they turn to mush and the sliced ones do not thicken the broth.
steps.fix: Sliced at the bottom to dissolve; whole on top to steam.

steps.do: Pour in the water or stock until it comes about two thirds of the way up the ingredients; the whole potatoes should sit above the liquid. Bring slowly to a simmer over medium heat.
steps.look: The liquid reaches a gentle bubble at the edges after 10 minutes.
steps.mistake: Covering everything with water, which makes a thin soup.
steps.fix: Pour some out; the potatoes on top cook in steam.

steps.do: Skim off the grey foam that rises with a wide spoon. Cover with the lid, lower the heat so the surface barely trembles, and cook 2 hours. Skim the fat once or twice. Do not stir.
steps.look: A clear, gently bubbling broth; after an hour the bottom potato slices begin to break down.
steps.mistake: A rolling boil, which makes the lamb tough and the broth cloudy and greasy.
steps.fix: Lowest heat, or cook it in a 300°F (150°C) oven.

steps.do: After 2 hours, check that the lamb is very tender and pulls from the bone. Stir very gently once or twice around the edge so the broken potato slices thicken the broth.
steps.look: A milky, lightly thickened broth, the whole potatoes intact and tender.
steps.mistake: Stirring vigorously, which breaks up the whole potatoes too.
steps.fix: Stir round the edge with a spoon, not through the middle.

steps.do: Taste and season with salt and pepper now; the broth has reduced and concentrated. Remove the thyme stalks and bay leaves.
steps.look: A broth that tastes sweet of onion and rich of lamb.
steps.mistake: Salting heavily at the start, so it ends up too salty.
steps.fix: Season lightly early, and properly at the end.

steps.do: Dot the butter over the stew, scatter with parsley and serve in deep, warm bowls.
steps.look: Gleaming beads of butter on the broth and bright green parsley.
steps.mistake: Serving in flat plates, so the broth runs everywhere.
steps.fix: Deep bowls, with a spoon as well as a fork.

dishes.science: The sliced floury potatoes are high in starch and break down into the liquid during the long simmer; their swollen starch granules thicken the broth without any flour. Waxy potatoes have less starch and firmer cells, so they hold their shape on top, steaming in the vapour trapped under the lid. Lamb neck is a working muscle with lots of collagen; slow, gentle, moist heat below a boil converts that collagen to gelatine, which makes the meat tender and gives the broth body. The bones add more gelatine and flavour. A rolling boil tightens the muscle proteins and squeezes out moisture, and churns fat into the broth so it turns cloudy and greasy.
dishes.plating: Use warm, deep bowls. Ladle in broth and lamb first, then set two whole potatoes on top and spoon a little more broth over. Finish with butter and a generous scatter of parsley. Serve with brown soda bread and salted butter.

pairing.drink: A stout or a dry Irish red ale. Roasted malt and gentle bitterness stand up to lamb without overpowering it.

variations: Brown stew: brown the lamb in batches first and add 1 tbsp (16 g) tomato purée and a splash of stout for a richer, darker stew.
Add pearl barley: 1/4 cup (50 g) rinsed barley with the water for a thicker, more rustic stew.
Mutton stew: use mutton neck and cook 3 hours.
safety: Cool leftovers quickly in a wide container and refrigerate within 2 hours; reheat until steaming hot throughout.

dishes.title: Shepherd's Pie
dishes.summary: Minced lamb browned hard and braised with vegetables, tomato purée, Worcestershire sauce and stock into a thick, glossy filling, topped with buttery mashed potato piped or forked into ridges and baked until crisp and golden. It is classic British home cooking and a lesson in reducing a filling until it will hold under a crust.
skills: a braised lamb mince with stock
equipment: Large heavy frying pan or sauté pan
Piping bag with a large star nozzle (optional) or a fork
Baking dish about 8 by 10 inch (20 by 25 cm), 2 1/2 inch (6 cm) deep

ingredients.note: peeled and cut into even chunks

mise: Finely dice the onion, carrots and celery, all to the same small size; chop the garlic.
Peel and cut the potatoes into even 2 inch (5 cm) chunks so they cook at the same rate.
Measure stock, Worcestershire and flour.
Warm the milk with the butter.
Heat the oven to 400°F (200°C).

timeline.do: Prep vegetables and potatoes.
Brown the lamb; soften the vegetables; build and simmer the filling 30 minutes.
Potatoes on to boil, 20 minutes; mash.
Cool the filling slightly; top with mash.
Bake 25 to 30 minutes.
Rest 10 minutes; serve.

steps.do: Heat the oil in the frying pan over high heat. Add the lamb, spread it out and leave it 3 minutes to brown before breaking it up. Cook until well browned and crisp in places, 8 to 10 minutes. Tip into a bowl, leaving the fat.
steps.look: Brown, crusty bits of lamb and a dark fond on the pan; loud sizzle.
steps.mistake: Grey, steamed mince from a crowded, cool pan.
steps.fix: Brown in two batches if needed, and do not stir too soon.

steps.do: Pour off all but 1 tbsp (15 ml) of the fat. Lower to medium, add onion, carrot and celery with a pinch of salt and cook 8 minutes until soft. Add garlic for 1 minute, then tomato purée and flour, and stir 2 minutes.
steps.look: Soft vegetables coated in a brick red paste, smelling sweet.
steps.mistake: Leaving all the lamb fat in, which makes a greasy filling.
steps.fix: Pour it off; lamb releases plenty.

steps.do: Return the lamb, add the stock, Worcestershire and thyme, and scrape the base. Simmer gently for 25 to 30 minutes, stirring now and then, until thick. Stir in the peas and season well.
steps.look: A thick, glossy filling; a spoon dragged through leaves a clear trail that does not flood.
steps.mistake: A runny filling, which makes the mash sink and the pie soupy.
steps.fix: Keep reducing. The mash cannot fix a wet filling.

steps.do: Meanwhile put the potatoes in cold, salted water, bring to a boil and simmer 15 to 20 minutes until a knife slides in with no resistance. Drain well and leave in the colander 3 minutes to steam dry.
steps.look: Potatoes fluffy at the edges, dry and floury looking.
steps.mistake: Waterlogged potatoes, which make a sloppy mash.
steps.fix: Steam them dry, or return them to the hot pan over low heat for a minute.

steps.do: Press the potatoes through the ricer back into the pan, or mash them. Beat in the warm milk and butter, then the egg yolk. Season.
steps.look: A smooth, firm mash that holds its shape on a spoon.
steps.mistake: Using a food processor or overbeating, which makes the mash gluey.
steps.fix: Use a ricer or masher, and stop as soon as it is smooth.

steps.do: Spread the filling in the dish and let it cool for 10 minutes. Pipe the mash over in rows of rosettes, or spoon it on from the edges inwards and rough it up with a fork into ridges. Sprinkle with cheese if using.
steps.look: An even layer of mash sealed to the edges, with ridges and peaks.
steps.mistake: Spooning hot mash into the middle of a hot filling so it sinks.
steps.fix: Start at the edges to seal, then fill in the centre gently.

steps.do: Set the dish on the tray and bake at 400°F (200°C) for 25 to 30 minutes.
steps.look: The ridges turn crisp and deep golden, and the filling bubbles up at the edges.
steps.mistake: A pale top.
steps.fix: Finish under the overhead grill (broiler) for 2 to 3 minutes, watching closely.

steps.do: Rest for 10 minutes before serving.
steps.look: The filling settles and does not run when spooned.
steps.mistake: Serving straight from the oven, very runny and very hot.
steps.fix: Wait 10 minutes.

dishes.science: Browning the lamb hard creates Maillard flavour compounds and leaves a fond on the pan that dissolves into the stock for depth. Tomato purée and Worcestershire sauce add glutamates and acids that deepen the savoury taste. Reducing the filling concentrates flavour and thickens it, aided by the flour, so it is firm enough to support the mash. Floury potatoes have large, loosely held starch cells that separate easily into fluffy mash; overworking bursts those cells and releases free starch, making mash gluey. The egg yolk adds richness and helps the topping brown. Ridges increase the surface exposed to dry oven heat, so they crisp and brown while the valleys stay soft.
dishes.plating: Spoon a generous square onto a warm plate, keeping the crust intact on top. Serve with buttered green beans or peas and a small jug of extra gravy. The crisp, brown ridges should face the guest.

pairing.drink: A Bordeaux style red, Merlot led, with soft tannin and dark fruit for lamb.
pairing.brennans: Moulin d’Issan Bordeaux Supérieur 2021: a supple, Merlot based Bordeaux from the Brennan's list, a natural match for lamb.

variations: Cottage pie: the same dish made with minced beef.
Sweet potato top: replace half the potatoes with sweet potato.
Individual pies: bake in four small dishes for 20 minutes.
safety: Cook minced lamb until no pink remains; minced meat should reach 160°F (71°C).
Cool leftovers within 2 hours; reheat until piping hot in the centre.

dishes.title: Jamaican Oxtail Stew
dishes.summary: Oxtail seasoned overnight with allspice, thyme, garlic, ginger and scotch bonnet, seared in sugar browned in oil, then braised for hours until the meat falls from the bone, finished with butter beans and small dumplings. It teaches browning sugar for colour, searing collagen rich meat and the long braise that turns it into a sauce that coats the lips.
skills: braising until it falls off the bone
equipment: Heavy Dutch oven, 5 quart (5 litres), with a lid
Wide spoon or fat separator for skimming
Small bowl for the dumpling dough

ingredients.note: left whole so it gives flavour without bursting
with a pinch of salt and about 1/3 cup (80 ml) water

mise: The night before, toss the oxtail with salt, pepper, ground allspice, garlic, ginger, thyme, spring onions and soy sauce; cover and refrigerate.
Next day, lift the oxtail out of the seasoning and pat it dry, scraping the aromatics back into the bowl to keep.
Chop the onion and slice the carrot.
Warm the stock; drain the butter beans.
Mix the dumpling dough just before you need it.

timeline.do: Season the oxtail; refrigerate.
Brown the sugar; sear the oxtail in batches.
Aromatics, stock, scotch bonnet; braise covered 3 to 3 1/2 hours.
Skim fat; check tenderness.
Butter beans and spinners in; uncover and reduce.
Serve over rice and peas.

steps.do: Heat the oil in the Dutch oven over medium heat. Sprinkle in the brown sugar and leave it, swirling the pot gently, until it melts, bubbles and turns very dark brown, almost black at the edges, and begins to smoke slightly, 2 to 4 minutes.
steps.look: The sugar foams and turns from amber to deep mahogany, with a few wisps of smoke; it smells of dark caramel.
steps.mistake: Pulling it while light brown, which gives sweetness rather than colour.
steps.fix: Wait for dark mahogany. If it goes truly black and acrid, wipe the pot and start again.

steps.do: Immediately add the first batch of oxtail, one layer only, standing back from the spatter. Sear 3 to 4 minutes a side until coated in a dark, glossy crust. Move to a plate and repeat in batches.
steps.look: Deep brown, almost lacquered pieces; a strong sizzle.
steps.mistake: Overcrowding, so the oxtail stews and never browns.
steps.fix: Work in three batches; let the pot recover heat between them.

steps.do: Lower the heat to medium. Add the onion, carrot and the reserved aromatics and cook 4 minutes, scraping up the dark fond.
steps.look: Soft, browned onion; the pot base turning clean as you scrape.
steps.mistake: Burning the fond, which turns bitter.
steps.fix: Add a splash of stock to loosen it if it darkens too fast.

steps.do: Return the oxtail with its juices, add the allspice berries, the whole scotch bonnet and enough hot stock to come almost to the top of the meat. Bring to a simmer, cover and cook on the lowest heat, or in a 300°F (150°C) oven, for 3 to 3 1/2 hours, turning the pieces every hour.
steps.look: A slow, steady bubble and a rich, dark gravy.
steps.mistake: Letting the scotch bonnet burst, which makes the stew fiercely hot.
steps.fix: Handle it gently; lift it out when the heat is right for you.

steps.do: Skim off the fat that rises to the surface with a wide spoon. Check the meat: it should pull from the bone with a fork.
steps.look: Meat that falls away easily; a thick, glossy, dark brown gravy.
steps.mistake: Leaving a thick layer of fat.
steps.fix: Skim thoroughly, or chill overnight and lift off the solid fat.

steps.do: Make the spinners: mix the flour, salt and enough water to make a firm dough. Pinch off small pieces and roll between your palms into thin dumplings 2 inches (5 cm) long.
steps.look: Smooth, firm little cylinders that hold their shape.
steps.mistake: A sticky dough that dissolves in the stew.
steps.fix: Add flour until the dough is firm and no longer sticks to your hands.

steps.do: Add the butter beans and spinners to the pot. Simmer uncovered for 15 to 20 minutes, stirring gently, until the dumplings are firm and cooked through and the gravy has thickened enough to coat a spoon.
steps.look: Glossy, sticky gravy; dumplings plump and cooked inside.
steps.mistake: Butter beans added early, which turn to mush.
steps.fix: They go in at the end only.

steps.do: Remove the thyme stalks and scotch bonnet. Taste and adjust the salt.
steps.look: Rich, deeply savoury and gently hot.
steps.mistake: Over salting after soy sauce and stock.
steps.fix: Taste first; add a splash of water if too salty.

dishes.science: Browning sugar in oil is a caramelisation taken very far: as sugar breaks down, sweetness disappears and colour and bitter roasted notes rise, so the dark caramel colours and deepens the stew without making it sweet. Searing meat in it coats every piece in that colour. Oxtail is made of small cross sections of tail with bone, marrow and lots of collagen; slow, wet heat between about 160 and 200°F (71 and 93°C) over hours converts collagen to gelatine. That gelatine thickens the gravy and gives the sticky, lip coating texture; cold, the gravy sets like jelly. Allspice brings eugenol, the warm clove like compound, and the whole scotch bonnet releases fruity aroma while its heat mostly stays inside the intact skin.
dishes.plating: Serve in a warm, wide bowl over rice and peas: a mound of rice to one side, three or four pieces of oxtail leaning against it, butter beans and spinners around, and plenty of the dark gravy spooned over. Add slices of fried sweet plantain on the side. Bones are meant to be picked up; offer a finger bowl.

pairing.drink: A ripe, spicy Zinfandel or a cold Jamaican lager. Zinfandel's dark fruit and spice match allspice and the rich gravy.
pairing.brennans: Ridge ‘Lytton Springs’ Dry Creek Valley 2022: a Zinfandel based blend on the Brennan's list with the ripeness and spice for a long braised stew.

variations: Pressure cooker: after searing, cook under high pressure for 45 to 50 minutes, then reduce uncovered.
Curry goat technique: use the same browning and braising method with goat and Jamaican curry powder.
Add 1 tbsp (15 ml) ketchup and a little more allspice for a sweeter, rounder gravy.
safety: Hot sugar and oil spatter badly; stand back when the meat goes in, and keep children away.
Handle scotch bonnet gently and wash hands after.
Cool leftovers within 2 hours.

dishes.title: Boeuf Bourguignon
dishes.summary: Beef chuck seared in batches and braised slowly in red Burgundy with lardons, aromatics and stock, then finished with a garnish of mushrooms and small onions cooked separately and folded in, the sauce reduced to a gloss. It is the great French braise and brings together everything this level has drilled: searing, a wine reduction, a long braise and a classical garnish.
skills: garnishing with lardons, mushrooms and glazed onions separately
equipment: Heavy enamelled casserole or Dutch oven, 5 quart (5 litres), with lid
Large frying pan for the garnish

ingredients.note: cut into 2 inch (5 cm) cubes, patted very dry

ingredients.item: Red Burgundy or other Pinot Noir

mise: Dry the beef very well with kitchen paper and season with 2 tsp (12 g) salt and pepper.
Chop the onion and slice the carrot; crush the garlic.
Tie the bouquet garni.
Peel the pearl onions: blanch 1 minute in boiling water, cool, trim the root and slip the skins off.
Clean the mushrooms with a brush or damp cloth.
Heat the oven to 325°F (160°C).

timeline.do: Prep; dry and season beef.
Render lardons; sear beef in batches, 25 minutes.
Aromatics, flour, purée; wine and stock; into the oven 2 1/2 to 3 hours.
Glaze the onions and brown the mushrooms.
Strain and reduce the sauce; fold in the garnish.
Parsley and serve.

steps.do: Put the lardons and 1 tbsp (15 ml) oil in the casserole over medium heat and cook 6 to 8 minutes until the fat runs and they are golden. Lift out with a slotted spoon and keep.
steps.look: Crisp, golden lardons and a pool of clear fat.
steps.mistake: High heat, so the lardons burn before rendering.
steps.fix: Start them gently; raise the heat only when the fat is flowing.

steps.do: Raise the heat to medium high. Sear the beef in batches of about 8 cubes, not touching, for 2 to 3 minutes a side until a dark brown crust forms on at least three sides. Move each batch to a tray.
steps.look: A deep chestnut crust; the meat releases from the pan on its own; a steady sizzle.
steps.mistake: Crowding the pot, so the beef releases water and boils grey.
steps.fix: Fewer pieces each time. Add the remaining oil when the pot looks dry.

steps.do: Lower the heat to medium, add onion and carrot and cook 5 minutes, scraping the fond. Add garlic for 1 minute, then sprinkle in the flour and tomato purée and stir for 2 minutes.
steps.look: Vegetables coated in a brick coloured paste; no raw flour smell.
steps.mistake: A burnt fond, which makes the sauce bitter.
steps.fix: If it is darkening too fast, add a splash of the wine to loosen it.

steps.do: Pour in the wine, scraping the base, and bring to a boil. Boil 5 minutes to reduce by about a third. Return the beef, lardons and juices, add the stock and the bouquet garni. The liquid should just cover the meat.
steps.look: A dark purple sauce that loses its sharp alcohol smell as it reduces.
steps.mistake: Adding the beef before the wine has reduced, leaving a raw, sour wine taste.
steps.fix: Reduce first, then add the meat.

steps.do: Bring back to a simmer, cover and place in the oven at 325°F (160°C) for 2 1/2 to 3 hours, until a cube breaks apart under gentle pressure from a spoon.
steps.look: Very tender meat that yields to a spoon, in a dark, rich sauce.
steps.mistake: Pulling it when the meat is still firm, or overcooking until it shreds into threads.
steps.fix: Check at 2 1/2 hours, then every 20 minutes.

steps.do: For the onions: put them in the small pan with 1 tbsp (14 g) butter, the sugar, a pinch of salt and water to come halfway up. Simmer uncovered 15 to 20 minutes, shaking, until the water evaporates and the onions roll in a golden glaze.
steps.look: Shiny, golden brown onions, tender to a knife.
steps.mistake: Walking away when the water is nearly gone, so the sugar burns.
steps.fix: Stay with them for the last 3 minutes, shaking the pan.

steps.do: For the mushrooms: heat the remaining butter in the frying pan over high heat until it foams. Add the mushrooms in one layer and leave 2 minutes, then toss and cook 3 to 4 minutes more until browned. Season.
steps.look: Golden, browned mushrooms that squeak; no liquid in the pan.
steps.mistake: Crowding the pan, which makes the mushrooms leak and stew.
steps.fix: Cook in two batches.

steps.do: Lift the beef and lardons out of the casserole with a slotted spoon. Pour the sauce through a sieve into a pan, pressing the vegetables, and discard them with the bouquet garni. Skim the fat and boil the sauce until it coats a spoon.
steps.look: A glossy, dark sauce that coats the back of a spoon and holds a line drawn through it.
steps.mistake: A thin, greasy sauce.
steps.fix: Skim thoroughly, then reduce until glossy.

steps.do: Return the beef, lardons, onions and mushrooms to the sauce and simmer 5 minutes to heat through. Taste and season.
steps.look: Every piece of beef coated in a glossy sauce, with the garnish intact.
steps.mistake: Adding the garnish at the start of the braise, so it turns to mush.
steps.fix: Separate cooking keeps each element distinct.

dishes.science: Searing in batches keeps the pot's surface hot enough to evaporate surface moisture so the Maillard reaction can brown the meat, building savoury flavour and a fond that becomes the base of the sauce. Crowding cools the pan and the meat stews. Wine contributes acids, tannins and fruit; reducing it drives off some alcohol and concentrates flavour before the long braise. Chuck is rich in collagen and gently marbled; a low oven keeps the liquid just below a boil so collagen converts to gelatine while the muscle fibres do not dry out. Gelatine gives the sauce body, and the flour helps thicken it. Cooking the garnish separately lets onions caramelise and mushrooms brown, reactions impossible in a wet braise.
dishes.plating: Use a warm, wide, shallow bowl. Arrange four or five cubes of beef in the centre, then place the glazed onions, mushrooms and lardons around and between them so each is visible. Spoon the glossy sauce over and finish with chopped parsley. Serve with buttered mash, buttered tagliatelle or boiled potatoes.

pairing.drink: Red Burgundy, the same style of Pinot Noir used to cook. Its red fruit, earthiness and acidity mirror the sauce and cut the richness.
pairing.brennans: Damien Martin Bourgogne Pinot Noir 2023: a red Burgundy from the Brennan's list; pour the same style you cooked with.

variations: Coq au vin: the same method with a jointed chicken, braised 45 to 60 minutes.
Beef carbonnade: replace the wine with Belgian brown ale and add a spoon of brown sugar and mustard.
Make it a day ahead: the flavour improves overnight, and solidified fat lifts off easily.
safety: Hot fat spatters when beef goes in; lay pieces away from you.
Cool leftovers within 2 hours and refrigerate; reheat until piping hot throughout.

dishes.title: Crème Brûlée
dishes.summary: A cream and egg yolk custard infused with vanilla, baked gently in a water bath until it just sets, chilled, then topped with a thin layer of sugar caramelised with a torch into a crackling glass. It is the custard every pastry section makes, and it teaches tempering yolks, baking in a bain marie and caramelising sugar at the last moment.
equipment: Four shallow ramekins or crème brûlée dishes, about 5 oz (150 ml) each
Deep roasting tin for the water bath, and a folded tea towel to line it

ingredients.note: split, seeds scraped; or 2 tsp (10 ml) vanilla bean paste

ingredients.item: Caster or demerara sugar for the tops

mise: Heat the oven to 300°F (150°C) with a shelf in the middle.
Set the ramekins in the roasting tin on a folded tea towel (it stops them sliding and insulates the base).
Boil the kettle.
Separate the eggs, keeping the whites for meringue or pavlova.
Split the vanilla pod and scrape out the seeds with the back of a knife.
Set the sieve over a jug.

timeline.do: Infuse the cream; temper the yolks; strain.
Bake in the water bath 30 to 40 minutes.
Cool on a rack, then chill at least 4 hours.
Sugar and torch the tops.
Serve within 10 minutes, while the top is crisp.

steps.do: Put the cream, vanilla seeds and pod in the saucepan and heat over medium until steaming with small bubbles at the edge, about 175°F (80°C). Do not boil. Take off the heat, cover and leave 15 minutes to infuse.
steps.look: Black specks of vanilla throughout; a strong vanilla smell.
steps.mistake: Boiling the cream, which can scald and leave a skin.
steps.fix: If it boils, take it off at once; it is still usable.

steps.do: Whisk the yolks, sugar and salt together for 30 seconds until just combined and slightly paler. Do not whip.
steps.look: A smooth, glossy, pale yellow mixture without froth.
steps.mistake: Whisking hard, creating foam that bakes into bubbles on the surface.
steps.fix: Whisk gently. Any bubbles can be skimmed or popped with the torch flame later.

steps.do: Reheat the cream until steaming again. Pour one ladle into the yolks in a thin stream, whisking constantly. Add another ladle, then pour in the rest while whisking gently.
steps.look: A smooth, warm custard with no lumps.
steps.mistake: Pouring all the hot cream in at once, which scrambles the yolks.
steps.fix: Temper slowly. If you see specks of cooked egg, the sieve will catch them.

steps.do: Pour the custard through the sieve into the jug. Skim off any foam with a spoon. Divide among the ramekins.
steps.look: A smooth, glossy liquid with a clean surface, the vanilla seeds spread evenly.
steps.mistake: Not straining, so specks of chalaza and egg end up in the custard.
steps.fix: Always strain.

steps.do: Set the tin on the oven shelf, then pour boiling water from the kettle into the tin, not into the ramekins, until it reaches halfway up their sides. Bake 30 to 40 minutes.
steps.look: The custards are set at the edges and wobble like jelly in the centre, in an area about the size of a coin, when the tin is nudged. The centre reads 170 to 175°F (77 to 79°C).
steps.mistake: Baking until firm all the way through, which makes them grainy and weepy.
steps.fix: Take them out when the centre still trembles; they finish setting as they cool.

steps.do: Lift the ramekins out of the water with tongs and cool on a rack 30 minutes, then cover and chill at least 4 hours or overnight.
steps.look: Fully set and cold, with a smooth, matt surface.
steps.mistake: Covering hot custards, which drips condensation onto the surface.
steps.fix: Cool uncovered first; dab off any water with kitchen paper before sugaring.

steps.do: Just before serving, sprinkle 2 tsp (8 g) of sugar evenly over each custard, tilt and tap to spread it, and pour off the excess. Hold the torch 2 inches (5 cm) away and move the flame steadily over the sugar until it melts and caramelises. Add a second thin layer and torch again.
steps.look: Bubbling sugar that turns from clear to golden to deep amber, forming a smooth, glassy sheet.
steps.mistake: A thick layer of sugar torched once, which burns on top while the bottom stays grainy.
steps.fix: Two thin layers, and keep the flame moving. Stop at amber, not black.

steps.do: Wait 1 to 2 minutes for the caramel to harden, then serve within 10 minutes.
steps.look: A hard, glossy top that cracks cleanly when tapped with a spoon.
steps.mistake: Torching hours ahead; the caramel dissolves into syrup in the fridge.
steps.fix: Always torch at the last minute.

dishes.science: Egg yolk proteins begin to thicken a custard at around 160°F (71°C) and set it by about 180°F (82°C); beyond that, the proteins tighten, squeeze out liquid and turn grainy. The water bath keeps the ramekins at or below the boiling point of water even though the oven is hotter, so the custard heats slowly and evenly and the edges do not overcook before the centre sets. Tempering raises the yolks' temperature gradually so they do not scramble. Infusing in fat matters because vanilla's flavour compounds dissolve well in cream. Under the torch, sucrose melts at about 367°F (186°C) and caramelises into hundreds of flavour compounds; a thin layer melts fully before it burns, and cools into an amorphous glass that shatters.
dishes.plating: Set the ramekin on a small plate lined with a folded napkin or doily so it does not slide. Add two or three fresh raspberries and a small mint leaf beside it, never on the caramel. Serve with a teaspoon, and let the guest break the glass.

pairing.drink: A Sauternes or other sweet botrytised white. Its honeyed, apricot richness echoes the caramel, and its acidity keeps it from cloying.
pairing.brennans: Château Suduiraut Sauternes 2016 (375 ml): a classic Sauternes from the Brennan's list, made for vanilla custard and caramel.

variations: Coffee crème brûlée: infuse 2 tbsp (10 g) crushed coffee beans in the cream instead of vanilla.
Lavender and honey: infuse 1 tsp (1 g) dried culinary lavender and replace a third of the sugar with honey.
Without a torch: chill the custards very cold, sugar them and slide them under a very hot overhead grill (broiler) for 1 to 2 minutes, watching every second.
safety: The custard reaches about 170°F (77°C), cooking the yolks to a safe point; keep it refrigerated and eat within 2 days.
Use the blowtorch away from anything flammable, point it away from you, and turn it off between uses. Hot caramel burns; let it set before serving.
Lift ramekins from hot water with tongs or a gripper.

dishes.title: Irish Apple Cake with Custard Sauce
dishes.summary: A rustic cake made by rubbing butter into flour and sugar, binding it with egg and milk, folding through chunks of cooking apple and baking until golden, served warm with a pouring custard, crème anglaise, cooked just until it coats the spoon. The crème anglaise is the point: it is the stirred custard behind dozens of desserts, and learning to read its thickness is a pastry skill for life.
skills: a rubbed-in cake batter with apples
crème anglaise cooked to coat the spoon
equipment: 8 inch (20 cm) round cake tin, preferably springform, greased and lined with baking paper
Whisk and wooden spoon or silicone spatula
Bowl of iced water large enough to hold the jug

ingredients.note: or plain flour with 2 1/2 tsp (10 g) baking powder
plus 1 tbsp (12 g) for the top

ingredients.item: Bramley or other tart cooking apples
ingredients.note: peeled, cored and cut into 1/2 inch (1 cm) chunks

mise: Heat the oven to 350°F (180°C). Grease and line the tin.
Peel, core and chop the apples; toss them with 1 tsp (5 ml) lemon juice if they will wait.
Dice the cold butter.
Separate the eggs for the anglaise; set the sieve over the jug inside the bowl of iced water.
Beat the egg for the cake with the milk.

timeline.do: Make the rubbed in mixture; fold in apples, egg and milk.
Bake 45 to 55 minutes.
Make the crème anglaise; chill or keep warm.
Cake out; cool 15 minutes in the tin.
Slice warm and pour custard over.

steps.do: Sift the flour, cinnamon and salt into the bowl. Add the cold butter and rub it in with your fingertips, lifting the mixture and letting it fall, until it looks like fine breadcrumbs. Stir in the sugar.
steps.look: Even, sandy crumbs with no large lumps of butter; the mixture stays cool and loose.
steps.mistake: Using warm hands or palms, so the butter melts and the mixture turns pasty.
steps.fix: Use fingertips only. If it gets greasy, chill the bowl for 10 minutes.

steps.do: Stir in the apple chunks. Add the egg and milk and mix with a spatula just until it comes together into a stiff, sticky batter.
steps.look: A thick batter that holds the apple pieces; no dry flour.
steps.mistake: Overmixing, which develops gluten and makes the cake tough.
steps.fix: Stop as soon as no dry flour remains.

steps.do: Spread the batter in the tin, level it roughly and sprinkle the extra sugar over the top. Bake 45 to 55 minutes.
steps.look: A domed, deep golden cake with a crunchy sugar top; a skewer in the centre comes out clean, with perhaps a little apple.
steps.mistake: Pulling it early, so the centre is gummy and raw.
steps.fix: Test with a skewer in several places. If the top browns too fast, lay foil over it.

steps.do: Cool in the tin 15 minutes, then release and slide onto a plate.
steps.look: The cake shrinks slightly from the sides.
steps.mistake: Removing it hot from a non springform tin, so it breaks.
steps.fix: Run a knife round the edge and be patient.

steps.do: Make the anglaise: heat the milk, cream and vanilla in the saucepan until steaming. Whisk the yolks and sugar in a bowl until pale. Pour the hot milk onto the yolks in a thin stream, whisking.
steps.look: A thin, warm, pale yellow liquid.
steps.mistake: Adding the milk too fast, so the yolks scramble.
steps.fix: Pour slowly while whisking constantly.

steps.do: Return the mixture to the pan over low heat. Stir constantly with a spatula in figure of eight movements, covering the whole base, for 4 to 8 minutes until it thickens slightly and reaches 175 to 180°F (79 to 82°C).
steps.look: The custard coats the back of a spoon; draw a finger across it and the line stays clear without the edges running back. Steam rises, but there are no bubbles.
steps.mistake: Letting it boil, which curdles it into sweet scrambled egg.
steps.fix: If it begins to look grainy, plunge the pan base into cold water and whisk hard, then strain. Next time use lower heat.

steps.do: Immediately strain into the jug sitting in iced water and stir for 2 minutes to stop the cooking. Serve warm or chill, covering the surface with clingfilm.
steps.look: A silky, pourable custard the thickness of single cream.
steps.mistake: Leaving it in the hot pan, where it keeps cooking and splits.
steps.fix: Strain and cool at once.

dishes.science: Rubbing cold butter into flour coats the flour particles in fat, which limits how much gluten can form when the liquid goes in, so the cake is tender and slightly crumbly rather than bready. Tart cooking apples like Bramley break down partly into soft, fluffy pockets because their cell walls are weaker and more acidic. Crème anglaise is thickened only by egg yolk: as the proteins warm, they unfold and link loosely into a network that traps liquid, thickening the sauce at about 175°F (79°C). Above about 185°F (85°C) those proteins bond too tightly and clump into curds. The coat the spoon test reads that exact point by eye. Stirring evenly prevents hot spots on the base.
dishes.plating: Cut a generous wedge of warm cake and set it slightly off centre on a warm plate or in a shallow bowl. Pour the crème anglaise around the base, not over the sugar crust, so the top stays crunchy. Serve the remaining custard in a jug at the table.

pairing.drink: An Irish coffee, or a late harvest white wine. Coffee and whiskey warm the apples; a sweet wine echoes the custard.
pairing.brennans: Brennan’s Irish Coffee: the house builds it with brown sugar, chicory coffee and Tullamore Dew under floated cream, a natural partner for an Irish apple cake.

variations: Add 1/3 cup (50 g) sultanas soaked in Irish whiskey with the apples.
Blackberry and apple: replace a quarter of the apples with blackberries in late summer.
Serve with softly whipped cream instead of custard.
safety: The anglaise reaches 175 to 180°F (79 to 82°C), which cooks the yolks safely; chill any left over within 2 hours and use within 2 days.

dishes.title: Clafoutis aux Cerises
dishes.summary: Whole dark cherries baked in a thin, eggy batter, closer to a crêpe batter than a cake, until puffed, golden and just set like a custard, then dusted with icing sugar. The Limousin cherry pudding teaches you to read a bake by its wobble rather than the clock, and shows how one simple batter becomes a custard in the oven.
equipment: Shallow ceramic baking dish or 9 inch (23 cm) round gratin dish
Mixing bowl and whisk, or a blender

ingredients.note: washed and stemmed; traditionally left unpitted
1 tbsp (12 g) for the dish, the rest for the batter

mise: Heat the oven to 375°F (190°C).
Butter the dish generously and sprinkle with 1 tbsp (12 g) sugar, tilting to coat.
Wash, stem and dry the cherries. Decide whether to pit them; pitted cherries are safer for children and guests.
Bring the eggs, milk and cream to room temperature.

timeline.do: Oven on; prepare dish and cherries.
Make the batter and rest it 10 minutes.
Bake 35 to 45 minutes.
Out of the oven; cool 10 to 20 minutes.
Dust with icing sugar and serve warm.

steps.do: Spread the cherries in a single layer in the prepared dish.
steps.look: A snug single layer covering the base.
steps.mistake: Piling the cherries in two layers so the batter cannot set around them.
steps.fix: Use a wider dish or fewer cherries.

steps.do: Whisk the eggs and sugar together for 1 minute until frothy. Whisk in the flour and salt to a smooth paste, then gradually whisk in the milk, cream, vanilla and kirsch. Strain through the sieve if there are lumps. Rest 10 minutes.
steps.look: A smooth, thin batter like single cream, with no lumps.
steps.mistake: Adding the milk all at once to the flour, creating lumps.
steps.fix: Make a paste first, then thin it. A blender also gives a lump free batter in 20 seconds.

steps.do: Pour the batter gently over the cherries. Bake on the middle shelf for 35 to 45 minutes.
steps.look: The clafoutis puffs up around the edges, turns golden brown and the centre is just set: when you nudge the dish, the middle wobbles slightly as one piece, like a set jelly, not as a liquid wave.
steps.mistake: Pulling it when the centre still ripples like liquid, so it is raw in the middle.
steps.fix: Give it 5 more minutes and check again. A small knife in the centre should come out moist but clean.

steps.do: Cool on a rack 10 to 20 minutes.
steps.look: It sinks gently as it cools; that is normal and right.
steps.mistake: Serving straight from the oven, when it is too soft and very hot.
steps.fix: Wait; it is best warm, not hot.

steps.do: Dust with icing sugar through the sieve just before serving.
steps.look: A light snow of sugar over the golden top.
steps.mistake: Dusting too early, so the sugar melts into the surface.
steps.fix: Dust at the last minute.

steps.do: Cut into wedges with a large spoon or knife, and warn guests if the cherries still have their stones.
steps.look: Wedges with dark cherries suspended in a soft, golden custard.
steps.mistake: Forgetting to warn about stones.
steps.fix: Always say so as you serve it.

dishes.science: Clafoutis batter is mostly milk and eggs with a little flour, so it bakes into something between a pancake and a custard. As it heats, egg proteins coagulate and set the liquid, while the flour's starch gelatinises and gives a little body, preventing the liquid from weeping. Steam from the milk lifts the batter at the edges, which is why it puffs and then sinks as it cools and the steam condenses. The wobble test reads the set directly: a liquid centre moves in waves because the proteins have not yet linked, while a set centre moves as one mass. Traditional unpitted cherries keep their juice inside and lend a faint almond note from the stones.
dishes.plating: Bring the dish to the table warm, dusted with icing sugar. Serve wedges on warm plates with a spoon of crème fraîche or a small scoop of vanilla ice cream beside them, and a small dish for stones.

pairing.drink: A fortified sweet red such as Banyuls or a ruby port. Its cherry and cocoa fruit matches the dark cherries.
pairing.brennans: Domaine La Tour Vieille Banyuls Reserva NV: a Roussillon fortified red from the Brennan's list whose dark fruit loves cherries.

variations: Flaugnarde: the same batter with sliced pears, apples or plums.
Apricot and almond: halved apricots and 2 tbsp (15 g) ground almonds in the batter.
Frozen cherries in winter: thaw and drain them well first.
safety: Unpitted cherries are a choking and tooth hazard; warn every guest, and pit them for children.
The custard sets well above the temperature needed to cook eggs; refrigerate leftovers.

dishes.title: Sticky Toffee Pudding
dishes.summary: A dark, moist sponge made with dates softened in boiling water and bicarbonate of soda, baked, stabbed and soaked with a toffee sauce taken to the right colour, then browned under the overhead grill (broiler) until bubbling. It builds on the malva pudding with a richer sponge, and teaches how bicarbonate breaks down fruit and how far to take a sauce for toffee flavour without bitterness.
skills: a toffee sauce taken to the right colour
equipment: 8 inch (20 cm) square baking tin, greased and lined
Small heatproof bowl for the dates
Electric hand mixer or stand mixer
Medium heavy saucepan for the sauce

ingredients.item: Medjool or other soft dates, pitted and chopped
Vanilla ice cream or clotted cream

mise: Heat the oven to 350°F (180°C). Grease and line the tin.
Put the chopped dates in a bowl, pour over the boiling water, stir in the bicarbonate and leave 15 minutes.
Soften the butter; bring eggs to room temperature and beat them.
Weigh out the sauce ingredients.

timeline.do: Soak the dates with bicarbonate.
Cream, add eggs, fold in flour and dates; bake 30 to 35 minutes.
Make the toffee sauce.
Stab the sponge; pour over sauce; rest 10 minutes.
Under the overhead grill until bubbling; serve with ice cream.

steps.do: After soaking, mash the dates roughly with a fork into the liquid.
steps.look: A dark, thick, sludgy purée with some small pieces of date; it foams slightly from the bicarbonate.
steps.mistake: Skipping the bicarbonate, which leaves chewy lumps of date.
steps.fix: It breaks the dates down so they melt into the sponge. Use it.

steps.do: Beat the butter and sugar with the mixer for 3 to 4 minutes until lighter in colour and fluffy. Beat in the eggs a little at a time.
steps.look: A fluffy, caramel coloured mixture that holds soft peaks.
steps.mistake: Adding cold eggs too quickly, which curdles the mixture.
steps.fix: Add a spoonful of the flour and keep beating; it will bind.

steps.do: Fold in the flour with a spatula, then the date mixture and vanilla, until smooth. The batter will be loose.
steps.look: A thin, dark, glossy batter.
steps.mistake: Overmixing after the flour goes in, which makes a tough sponge.
steps.fix: Fold gently and stop once smooth.

steps.do: Pour into the tin and bake 30 to 35 minutes.
steps.look: Well risen and springy; a skewer comes out clean; the edges pull away from the tin.
steps.mistake: An underbaked, sunken centre.
steps.fix: Bake a few minutes longer and test again.

steps.do: Make the sauce: melt the butter and sugar in the saucepan over medium heat, stirring, until the sugar dissolves. Add half the cream and boil 3 to 4 minutes, stirring, until it darkens and thickens. Stir in the rest of the cream and the salt.
steps.look: A glossy, dark brown toffee that coats a spoon thickly and smells of caramel and molasses.
steps.mistake: Boiling hard after the sugar burns on the base, which tastes bitter.
steps.fix: Stir the base constantly, keep the heat at medium, and stop when it smells of toffee.

steps.do: Prick the warm sponge all over with the skewer, right to the bottom. Pour about half the hot sauce over it and leave 10 minutes to soak in.
steps.look: The sauce disappears into the holes, leaving a glossy top.
steps.mistake: Pouring sauce onto a cold sponge, which absorbs it poorly.
steps.fix: Soak it while warm.

steps.do: Slide the tin under a hot overhead grill for 1 to 2 minutes, watching closely, until the top bubbles.
steps.look: A bubbling, glossy, sticky top.
steps.mistake: Leaving it under the grill too long, so the sugar burns.
steps.fix: Watch through the door and pull it as soon as it bubbles.

steps.do: Cut into squares and serve warm with the remaining sauce, reheated, and ice cream or cream.
steps.look: Moist, dark squares sitting in toffee.
steps.mistake: Serving with too little sauce.
steps.fix: Pour generously; the dish is named for it.

dishes.science: Bicarbonate of soda is alkaline, and alkalinity weakens pectin and the cell walls of fruit, so dates soaked with it collapse into a smooth purée that disperses through the batter, making the sponge dark and moist rather than studded. The alkali also speeds up browning, deepening the colour. Creaming butter and sugar beats tiny air bubbles into the fat that expand in the oven with the raising agent. The toffee sauce is a caramel built on brown sugar; muscovado already contains molasses, so it tastes of toffee quickly, and boiling with cream lets milk proteins and sugars react, adding the round, butterscotch flavour of a Maillard reaction. Soaking while warm works because a warm crumb is open and draws in liquid easily.
dishes.plating: Set a warm square of pudding in a warm, shallow bowl, spoon over a pool of hot toffee sauce until it runs down the sides, and set a neat quenelle of vanilla ice cream on top or beside it at the last second. A pinch of flaky salt on the sauce sharpens the toffee.

pairing.drink: A tawny or colheita port. Its nutty, dried fruit and caramel character mirrors the dates and toffee.
pairing.brennans: New Orleans Bread Pudding: the Brennan's warm pudding with whiskey caramel; once you have made this toffee sauce you can describe its caramel to a guest from experience.

variations: Individual puddings: bake in six greased pudding moulds for 20 to 25 minutes and turn out.
Banana toffee pudding: replace a third of the dates with mashed ripe banana.
Add 1 tsp (2 g) ground ginger and a pinch of mixed spice to the batter.
safety: Boiling toffee is very hot and sticks to skin; stir carefully with a long spoon and keep children away.
Contains dairy, egg and wheat.

dishes.title: Bananas Foster
dishes.summary: Bananas cooked briefly in a caramel of butter, brown sugar and cinnamon with banana liqueur, then flamed with dark rum and spooned hot over cold vanilla ice cream. It was created at Brennan's in New Orleans in 1951 and is still flamed tableside there, so it teaches caramel and a safe flambé in the house where you work.
skills: a butter and brown sugar caramel
equipment: Wide, heavy frying pan, 10 to 12 inch (25 to 30 cm), with a long handle
Long reach lighter or long fireplace matches
Measuring jug or glass for the rum (never pour from the bottle)
Pan lid that fits, kept beside you to smother flames

ingredients.note: yellow with a few brown flecks, peeled, halved lengthways then across
very cold, scooped into chilled bowls just before

mise: Clear the area around and above the hob: nothing hanging overhead, no tea towels, paper or open bottles nearby, extractor fan off so it does not draw the flame. Tie back long hair and roll up loose sleeves.
Measure the rum into a glass and put the bottle away.
Put the lid within reach.
Peel and cut the bananas only just before cooking so they do not brown.
Scoop the ice cream into chilled bowls and return them to the freezer.

timeline.do: Clear the hob; measure; chill bowls; scoop ice cream.
Make the caramel.
Bananas in, 1 minute a side.
Off the heat: liqueur, then rum; ignite; spoon until the flames die.
Over ice cream at once.

steps.do: Melt the butter in the pan over medium heat. Stir in the brown sugar and cinnamon and cook, stirring, 2 to 3 minutes until the sugar dissolves and the mixture bubbles into a smooth caramel.
steps.look: A glossy, bubbling, mahogany sauce; it smells of butterscotch.
steps.mistake: High heat, which separates the butter and burns the sugar.
steps.fix: Keep the heat at medium. If the butter separates, add 1 tbsp (15 ml) water and whisk.

steps.do: Add the banana liqueur if using and stir. Lay in the bananas cut side down and cook 1 minute, spooning the caramel over them, then turn carefully and cook 1 minute more.
steps.look: Bananas glazed and just softening at the edges but still holding their shape.
steps.mistake: Cooking the bananas too long so they turn to mush.
steps.fix: One minute a side is enough; they keep cooking in the hot sauce.

steps.do: Turn off the burner and pull the pan off the heat. Pour the measured rum into the pan from the glass. Return the pan to low heat for 10 to 15 seconds to warm the rum.
steps.look: The rum steams gently and starts to give off a strong smell of alcohol.
steps.mistake: Pouring rum from the bottle near a flame, which can carry fire back into the bottle.
steps.fix: Always pour from a measured glass, with the pan away from the flame.

steps.do: Take the pan off the heat again. Holding the long lighter at arm's length, touch the flame to the edge of the pan to ignite the vapours. On a gas hob you can instead tilt the pan's far edge slightly towards the burner flame. Stand back.
steps.look: A soft blue and yellow flame rises across the surface and dances for 15 to 30 seconds.
steps.mistake: Leaning over the pan to light it.
steps.fix: Arm's length, face back, nothing above. If the flames grow too large, slide the lid on to smother them.

steps.do: Gently spoon the flaming sauce over the bananas until the flames die out by themselves, about 30 seconds.
steps.look: The flames shrink and disappear as the alcohol burns off; the sauce turns glossy and slightly thicker.
steps.mistake: Blowing out the flames or adding water.
steps.fix: Let them burn out, or cover with the lid.

steps.do: Immediately spoon the bananas and sauce over the cold ice cream.
steps.look: Hot caramel melting into ice cream, glistening bananas on top.
steps.mistake: Letting the sauce sit, so it thickens and cools.
steps.fix: Serve the second the flames are out.

dishes.science: Flambéing ignites the alcohol vapour above the pan, not the liquid itself. Warming the rum gently increases evaporation, so there is enough vapour to light; cold rum may not catch. The flame burns off some, but far from all, of the alcohol, while caramelising sugars on the surface and adding a slightly toasty note. Brown sugar contains molasses, which gives the sauce its deep toffee colour and flavour quickly. Butter's fat carries the cinnamon flavour, and its milk solids brown in the sugar. Ripe but firm bananas are best: their starch has largely converted to sugars for sweetness, but their cell walls still hold together in the heat. Cold ice cream against hot sauce is a deliberate contrast of temperature.
dishes.plating: Use chilled shallow bowls. Set one scoop of ice cream in the centre, lay four banana pieces against and over it in a star, then spoon the sauce over the top so it pools around. Serve instantly, before the ice cream collapses.

pairing.drink: A coffee with chicory, or a glass of aged rum. Both pick up the caramel and the rum in the sauce.
pairing.brennans: World Famous Bananas Foster: the Brennan's original, flamed tableside; follow the house procedure you are trained on and the tableside safety steps in the service note.

variations: Without flame: add the rum and simmer 1 minute to cook off the raw alcohol; the flavour is nearly the same.
Alcohol free: replace the rum and liqueur with 3 tbsp (45 ml) orange juice and a few drops of vanilla.
Cherries jubilee: the same flambé method with pitted cherries and kirsch over vanilla ice cream.
safety: Flambé only with nothing overhead or nearby that can burn; extractor fan off; long hair tied; keep children and pets well back.
Never pour alcohol from the bottle into a pan near a flame; measure it into a glass first, and add it with the pan off the heat.
Keep a lid beside the pan to smother flames, and never use water on a fire. Hot caramel burns; do not taste from the pan.
Contains alcohol; not everything burns off.

dishes.title: Pastel de Tres Leches
dishes.summary: A light, butter free whisked sponge soaked through with three milks, evaporated, condensed and cream, chilled until it becomes a cold, custardy cake, and crowned with whipped cream and cinnamon. It teaches why whisked sponges are built the way they are: an open, fat free crumb strong enough to drink its own weight in milk without collapsing.
skills: a whisked sponge strong enough to soak
an Italian or whipped cream topping
equipment: 8 inch (20 cm) square baking dish, glass or ceramic, at least 2 inch (5 cm) deep, greased and floured
Stand mixer or electric hand mixer, with two clean bowls
mise: Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C). Grease and flour the dish.
Separate the eggs carefully: not a speck of yolk in the whites. Use a spotless, grease free bowl for the whites.
Sift the flour, baking powder and salt together.
Whisk the evaporated milk, condensed milk and soak cream in a jug and chill.
Chill the topping cream and a bowl.

timeline.do: Make and bake the sponge, 25 to 30 minutes.
Cool 15 minutes; prick all over; pour the milks in stages.
Cover and chill at least 4 hours, ideally overnight.
Whip the cream; spread over the top; dust with cinnamon.
Cut and serve cold.

steps.do: Whisk the yolks with 1/2 cup (100 g) of the sugar on high for 3 to 4 minutes, then beat in the milk and vanilla.
steps.look: Thick, pale yellow, ribbon like mixture that falls from the whisk in a ribbon that rests on the surface for a moment.
steps.mistake: Underwhisking, which leaves the sponge heavy.
steps.fix: Keep whisking until truly pale and thick.

steps.do: In the clean bowl, whisk the whites on medium until foamy, then on high until soft peaks form. Add the remaining sugar a spoonful at a time and whisk to firm, glossy peaks that just bend at the tip.
steps.look: Shiny, smooth whites that hold a peak that curls slightly; the bowl can be tilted without them sliding.
steps.mistake: Overwhisking until dry and grainy, so they will not fold in smoothly.
steps.fix: Stop at glossy, firm peaks. If overwhisked, whisk in one more egg white briefly.

steps.do: Fold a third of the whites into the yolk mixture to loosen it. Sift the flour over in two additions, folding gently each time, then fold in the remaining whites until no streaks remain.
steps.look: A light, airy batter with no white streaks or flour pockets.
steps.mistake: Stirring instead of folding, which knocks out the air and makes a flat, dense cake.
steps.fix: Cut down through the centre with the spatula, sweep along the bottom and up the side, turning the bowl as you go.

steps.do: Pour into the dish, level gently and bake 25 to 30 minutes.
steps.look: Golden, springy, risen; the centre springs back when pressed lightly; a skewer comes out clean.
steps.mistake: Opening the oven early, which makes the sponge sink.
steps.fix: Wait until at least 20 minutes before checking.

steps.do: Cool the sponge in the dish for 15 minutes. Prick it all over, right to the bottom, with the skewer at 1/2 inch (1 cm) intervals.
steps.look: Holes all over the surface, especially near the edges and corners.
steps.mistake: Pricking only the top, so the milk pools there.
steps.fix: Push right through to the base.

steps.do: Pour about a third of the milk mixture slowly over the cake, starting at the edges. Wait 5 minutes for it to soak in, then pour another third, wait, and pour the rest.
steps.look: The cake drinks the milk; by the end a little pools at the edges, and that will soak in as it chills.
steps.mistake: Pouring it all at once, so it floods the top and the cake falls apart.
steps.fix: Pour in stages and let each soak in.

steps.do: Cover and chill at least 4 hours or overnight.
steps.look: Almost all the liquid absorbed; the cake is cold and heavy.
steps.mistake: Serving after an hour, when it is soggy at the bottom and dry on top.
steps.fix: Give it time; overnight is best.

steps.do: Whip the cold cream with the icing sugar to soft, billowy peaks. Spread it over the cake and dust with cinnamon.
steps.look: Soft, smooth cream that holds its shape.
steps.mistake: Overwhipping to grainy butter.
steps.fix: Stop at soft peaks. If grainy, fold in a splash of liquid cream.

dishes.science: A whisked sponge gets its structure from egg foam: whisking unfolds egg proteins, which trap air and set around the bubbles in the oven, giving an open, springy crumb. With no butter, nothing coats the flour or the network in fat, so the crumb stays porous and absorbent rather than water resistant. Sugar stabilises the whites by dissolving into the water around the proteins and slowing their drying out. Folding keeps as much of that air as possible. The three milks bring sugar, milk solids and fat; evaporated milk has had water removed, and condensed milk is evaporated milk with sugar, so the soak is rich and sweet rather than watery. Chilling firms the fats and sets the soaked crumb into something like a custard.
dishes.plating: Cut neat squares with a hot, clean knife, wiping between cuts, and lift out with a fish slice onto chilled plates; a little milk will pool, which is right. Top each square with a small extra swirl of cream, a dusting of cinnamon and a few slices of fresh strawberry or mango.

pairing.drink: A cold glass of pale cream sherry or a café de olla. The sherry's light sweetness and nuttiness flatter the milk and cinnamon.
pairing.brennans: Barbadillo ‘Pale Cream’ Sherry NV: a light, gently sweet sherry from the Brennan's list that suits a milky, cinnamon dusted cake.

variations: Tres leches de coco: replace the cream in the soak with coconut milk and top with toasted coconut.
Cuatro leches: drizzle cajeta or dulce de leche over the cream topping.
Meringue topping: top with Italian meringue and toast it with a torch.
safety: Keep the cake refrigerated; it is a dairy dessert soaked in milk. Eat within 3 days.
Contains dairy, egg and wheat.
