dishes.title: New York Cheesecake
dishes.summary: A dense, creamy, ivory cheesecake on a pre baked biscuit crust, mixed slowly to keep air out, baked low in a water bath and cooled gradually so it stays smooth and flat. It is a custard baked low and slow, the opposite of the Basque method, and each step is insurance against cracks.
skills: cooling in the oven to prevent cracks
equipment: 7 inch (18 cm) springform tin (for a smaller cheesecake that serves 4 with seconds)
Heavy duty foil to wrap the tin, two layers
Roasting tin for the water bath; kettle
Stand mixer with paddle, or a hand mixer
Food processor or a bag and rolling pin for the crumbs
Long sharp knife and a jug of hot water for slicing

ingredients.item: Full fat cream cheese, block style
ingredients.note: at true room temperature, 3 hours out of the fridge

mise: Take the cream cheese, eggs and sour cream out 3 hours ahead.
Heat the oven to 325°F (160°C).
Wrap the outside of the springform tin in two layers of heavy foil, bringing it up the sides, so no water can get in.
Crush the biscuits finely; melt the butter.
Boil the kettle when the cheesecake is nearly ready to go in.

timeline.do: Bake the crust 10 minutes; cool.
Mix the filling slowly; pour; set in the water bath.
Bake 55 to 70 minutes at 325°F (160°C).
Oven off, door ajar, 1 hour; then cool on a rack.
Chill overnight.
Slice with a hot, wet knife.

steps.do: Mix the crumbs, melted butter and sugar until it looks like wet sand. Press firmly and evenly into the base of the tin with the bottom of a glass. Bake 10 minutes, then cool.
steps.look: A compact, even crust that holds together when pressed; lightly golden and smelling toasty.
steps.mistake: A loosely pressed crust that crumbles and lets the filling seep under.
steps.fix: Press hard with a flat bottomed glass, especially at the edges.

steps.do: Beat the cream cheese on low speed for 2 to 3 minutes until completely smooth, scraping the bowl and paddle twice. Add the sugar and flour and beat on low until smooth.
steps.look: A silky, lump free mixture with no visible flecks of cheese.
steps.mistake: Using cold cream cheese, which leaves lumps that you then beat out at high speed, adding air.
steps.fix: Use truly soft cheese. If lumps remain, set the bowl over warm water for a minute and beat again on low.

steps.do: Add the eggs one at a time on low speed, mixing only until each disappears and scraping down after each. Mix in the sour cream, vanilla, zest and salt.
steps.look: A smooth, thick, glossy batter with very few bubbles.
steps.mistake: Beating at high speed, which whips in air that rises, puffs and then cracks the surface.
steps.fix: Low speed only. Tap the bowl on the counter to bring bubbles up and pop them.

steps.do: Pour the filling over the cooled crust and smooth the top. Set the wrapped tin in the roasting tin, put it on the oven shelf, and pour boiling water into the roasting tin to come halfway up the springform.
steps.look: A level, glossy surface, the tin sitting in steaming water.
steps.mistake: A leaky foil wrap, which lets water in and makes the crust soggy.
steps.fix: Wrap with a single wide sheet if possible, or set the springform inside a slightly larger cake tin.

steps.do: Bake at 325°F (160°C) for 55 to 70 minutes.
steps.look: The edges are set and slightly puffed and matt, while a circle in the centre about 2 1/2 inches (6 cm) across wobbles like jelly when the tin is nudged. The centre reads about 150°F (66°C).
steps.mistake: Baking until the centre is firm, which overcooks it, turning it grainy and cracked.
steps.fix: Pull it at the wobble; carryover finishes the set.

steps.do: Turn off the oven, prop the door open a hand's width and leave the cheesecake inside for 1 hour. Then lift it from the water, remove the foil, and run a thin knife round the edge.
steps.look: A smooth, flat, pale top with no cracks.
steps.mistake: Moving it straight into a cold room, where it shrinks fast and cracks.
steps.fix: Cool slowly; then release the edge so it can shrink without tearing.

steps.do: Cool on a rack to room temperature, then chill uncovered for at least 8 hours or overnight.
steps.look: A firm, dense, cold cheesecake.
steps.mistake: Cutting after a few hours, when the texture has not yet set.
steps.fix: Overnight. The texture forms in the fridge.

steps.do: Release the springform. Slice with a long knife dipped in hot water and wiped dry between every cut.
steps.look: Clean, sharp slices with smooth, dense, ivory faces.
steps.mistake: A dry knife, which drags and smears.
steps.fix: Hot, wet, wiped, every cut.

dishes.science: Cheesecake is a custard: egg proteins set the cream cheese and sour cream into a smooth gel. Like any custard, it turns grainy and shrinks when the proteins overheat and tighten. The water bath holds the tin near the boiling point of water, so the edges do not race ahead of the centre. Cracks come from three things: air beaten into the batter expanding and collapsing, overbaking that tightens the proteins, and rapid cooling that shrinks the outside faster than the middle. Low speed mixing, the wobble test and the slow cool address each one. Flour adds starch that helps hold the structure together. The overnight chill firms the fat in the cream cheese, which is what gives the dense, creamy slice.
dishes.plating: Set a slice on a chilled plate with the point towards the guest. Spoon a little fresh berry compote beside it, not over it, so the ivory surface shows, and add two or three whole berries. A small spoon of softly whipped cream to the side is optional.

pairing.drink: A demi sec Chenin Blanc or a late harvest Riesling. Sweetness matches the cake while bright acidity cuts the cream cheese.
pairing.brennans: Domaine Huet ‘Le Mont’ Vouvray Demi-Sec 2023 (375 ml): an off dry Loire Chenin from the Brennan's list with the acidity to lift a rich cheesecake.

variations: Strawberry topping: macerate 2 cups (300 g) sliced strawberries with 2 tbsp (25 g) sugar and a squeeze of lemon for 30 minutes.
Chocolate swirl: drizzle 2 oz (55 g) melted dark chocolate over the filling and swirl with a skewer before baking.
Larger cake: double the filling in a 9 inch (23 cm) tin and bake 75 to 90 minutes.
safety: The filling sets above 150°F (66°C) in the centre with carryover; keep the cheesecake refrigerated and eat within 4 days.
Pour boiling water into the roasting tin while it is already on the oven shelf, so you never carry a tin of boiling water.

dishes.title: Pavlova
dishes.summary: A crisp meringue shell with a soft, marshmallow centre, made with egg whites whisked with sugar added slowly, a little cornflour and vinegar, dried in a low oven and topped at the last moment with whipped cream and sharp fruit. It teaches the rules of meringue: a spotless bowl, sugar added patiently and a long, cool oven.
skills: cornflour and vinegar for a marshmallow centre
equipment: Stand mixer with whisk, or an electric hand mixer, and a spotless glass or metal bowl
Baking tray lined with baking paper, with a 7 inch (18 cm) circle drawn on the underside
Large metal spoon or palette knife

ingredients.note: at room temperature, without a trace of yolk

mise: Heat the oven to 250°F (120°C). Draw the circle on the baking paper and turn it over.
Wipe the bowl and whisk with kitchen paper dipped in vinegar or lemon juice to remove any grease.
Separate the eggs one at a time into a small cup before adding each white to the bowl, so one broken yolk does not spoil the lot.
Weigh the sugar; mix the cornflour, vinegar and vanilla in a small cup.

timeline.do: Make the meringue; shape it.
Bake at 250°F (120°C) for 75 to 90 minutes.
Oven off, door ajar; cool inside at least 1 hour.
Whip the cream; prepare the fruit.
Fill and top just before serving.

steps.do: Whisk the egg whites with the salt on medium speed until foamy and opaque, then on medium high until they form soft peaks, about 2 to 3 minutes.
steps.look: White, fluffy whites whose peaks flop over when the whisk is lifted.
steps.mistake: A trace of yolk or grease in the bowl, so the whites never rise.
steps.fix: Start again with a perfectly clean bowl and fresh whites.

steps.do: With the mixer running at medium high, add the sugar one spoonful at a time, waiting about 15 seconds between spoons. Once all is in, whisk 3 to 5 minutes more on high.
steps.look: A thick, very glossy meringue that stands in stiff peaks; rub a little between finger and thumb and it feels smooth, with no grit of sugar.
steps.mistake: Adding the sugar all at once, so it does not dissolve and the meringue weeps sticky beads of syrup in the oven.
steps.fix: Be patient. Keep whisking until no grains can be felt.

steps.do: Sprinkle the cornflour, vinegar and vanilla mixture over the meringue and fold in gently with a large spoon in a few strokes.
steps.look: The meringue stays thick and glossy.
steps.mistake: Overfolding, which knocks out air.
steps.fix: A few gentle folds are all it needs.

steps.do: Dab a little meringue under each corner of the paper to stick it to the tray. Spoon the meringue into the drawn circle, then shape it with the back of the spoon into a round with a slight hollow in the middle and higher sides, swirling the sides upwards.
steps.look: A round nest about 2 1/2 inches (6 cm) high with a shallow well in the centre.
steps.mistake: Spreading it thin and flat, which bakes to a dry biscuit with no soft middle.
steps.fix: Keep it high; the height protects the marshmallow centre.

steps.do: Put it in the oven and immediately lower to 225°F (110°C). Bake 75 to 90 minutes.
steps.look: A crisp, dry, pale cream shell; it lifts easily from the paper; it should not brown.
steps.mistake: An oven that is too hot, which makes the meringue brown, crack and weep.
steps.fix: Use an oven thermometer. If it colours, lower the heat and prop the door slightly open with a wooden spoon.

steps.do: Turn off the oven, open the door a crack and leave the pavlova inside to cool completely, at least 1 hour.
steps.look: A crisp, dry shell. Some cracking on top is normal and honest.
steps.mistake: Moving it into a cold kitchen at once, so it cracks and collapses.
steps.fix: Cool it slowly in the switched off oven.

steps.do: Just before serving, whip the cream to soft, floppy peaks. Pile it into the hollow, top with berries and kiwi, and spoon passion fruit pulp over the top.
steps.look: Soft cream piled high, glistening fruit and dark passion fruit seeds.
steps.mistake: Assembling an hour ahead, so the cream softens the meringue.
steps.fix: Fill it at the last moment.

dishes.science: Whisking egg whites unfolds their proteins, which then link at the surface of air bubbles to make a foam. Fat, even a trace of yolk, coats the proteins and stops them linking, which is why the bowl must be spotless. Adding sugar slowly lets it dissolve fully into the thin film of water around each bubble, making a thick syrup that stabilises the foam; undissolved sugar draws moisture in the oven and weeps. Vinegar's acid helps proteins hold together, and cornflour absorbs moisture inside the meringue, so the centre stays soft and chewy rather than drying out. A very low oven dries the outside without browning, while the thick centre stays moist, and slow cooling stops the shell shrinking too fast.
dishes.plating: Set the whole pavlova on a flat serving plate or cake stand and fill it at the table if you can. Cut with a large, sharp knife into wedges; it will shatter a little, which is part of the dessert. Serve each wedge with its cream and fruit, and spoon a little extra passion fruit over.

pairing.drink: A demi sec rosé Champagne or a sparkling Moscato. Gentle sweetness and red fruit match the berries, and the bubbles echo the meringue's lightness.
pairing.brennans: Moët & Chandon ‘Nectar Imperial’ Rosé Demi Sec NV: a sweeter rosé Champagne from the Brennan's list, a natural partner for meringue and berries.

variations: Mini pavlovas: shape eight small nests and bake 45 to 50 minutes.
Lemon curd pavlova: spread 1/2 cup (150 g) lemon curd over the base before the cream.
Chocolate pavlova: fold 2 tbsp (12 g) sifted cocoa and 1 oz (30 g) grated dark chocolate into the finished meringue.
safety: Fill and serve within an hour; keep leftover cream topped pavlova in the fridge and eat the same day.
Contains egg and dairy.

dishes.title: Tiramisù
dishes.summary: Layers of savoiardi biscuits dipped briefly in espresso and a cream of mascarpone folded into a zabaglione, egg yolks and sugar whisked over a bain marie until thick and cooked, finished with cocoa. Cooking the yolks makes the tiramisù safe and lighter, and it teaches the bain marie, folding and the one second dip.
skills: a zabaglione cooked over a bain-marie
equipment: Heatproof bowl that sits over a saucepan without touching the water
Balloon whisk or electric hand mixer
Serving dish about 8 by 6 inch (20 by 15 cm), or four glasses
mise: Brew the espresso, pour it into the shallow dish, stir in 1 tbsp (15 ml) of the marsala if you like and cool completely.
Bring a saucepan with 1 inch (2.5 cm) of water to a bare simmer.
Separate the eggs.
Keep the mascarpone and cream cold until needed.
Have the serving dish ready.

timeline.do: Brew and cool the espresso.
Cook the zabaglione to 160°F (71°C); cool it.
Whip cream; fold in mascarpone and zabaglione.
Dip, layer and cover; chill at least 6 hours.
Dust with cocoa; serve.

steps.do: Put the yolks, sugar and remaining marsala in the heatproof bowl and set it over the barely simmering water. Whisk constantly for 5 to 8 minutes until thick and pale and the mixture reaches 160°F (71°C).
steps.look: The yolks triple in volume, turn pale and thick, and leave a trail on the surface that holds for 3 seconds; the thermometer reads 160°F (71°C).
steps.mistake: Water touching the bowl or boiling hard, so the yolks scramble at the edges.
steps.fix: Keep the water at a bare simmer and lift the bowl off for a few seconds if it is getting too hot, whisking all the time.

steps.do: Take the bowl off the heat and keep whisking for 2 to 3 minutes as it cools, then leave it to cool to room temperature.
steps.look: A thick, mousse like zabaglione, warm then cool.
steps.mistake: Folding warm zabaglione into the mascarpone, which melts it and makes the cream runny.
steps.fix: Cool it fully; set the bowl in cold water to speed it up.

steps.do: In the large bowl, whip the cream to soft peaks. Add the mascarpone and fold together with a spatula just until smooth, then fold in the cooled zabaglione in two additions.
steps.look: A smooth, thick, airy cream that holds soft peaks.
steps.mistake: Beating mascarpone hard, which turns it grainy and buttery.
steps.fix: Fold, do not beat. Stop as soon as it is smooth.

steps.do: Dip a savoiardo into the espresso for one second on each side, no longer, and lay it in the dish. Repeat to cover the base in a single layer.
steps.look: Biscuits moist on the outside and still firm in the middle.
steps.mistake: Soaking the biscuits, which collapse into mush and flood the dish with coffee.
steps.fix: One quick dip each side. They soften further in the fridge.

steps.do: Spread half the cream over the biscuits. Add a second layer of dipped biscuits, then the rest of the cream, smoothing the top.
steps.look: Two clean layers with a smooth top.
steps.mistake: Thin cream layers that do not cover the biscuits.
steps.fix: Divide the cream exactly in two before you start.

steps.do: Cover and chill at least 6 hours, preferably overnight.
steps.look: The cream firms and the biscuits soften to a cake like texture.
steps.mistake: Serving straight away, so it is loose and the biscuits are crunchy.
steps.fix: Give it the time.

steps.do: Just before serving, sift cocoa evenly over the top and grate a little chocolate over if using.
steps.look: A velvety brown layer of cocoa.
steps.mistake: Dusting hours ahead, so the cocoa absorbs moisture and turns blotchy.
steps.fix: Dust at the last moment.

dishes.science: Heating egg yolks with sugar while whisking does two things: the proteins unfold and trap air, thickening the mixture into a foam, and the heat to 160°F (71°C) cooks the yolks to a safe point. Sugar raises the temperature at which yolks scramble, which gives a margin of safety, and constant whisking spreads the heat. A bain marie keeps the heat gentle because the bowl never exceeds the temperature of steam. Mascarpone is about three quarters fat; overbeating causes its fat globules to clump together, as when cream turns to butter, so it becomes grainy. Savoiardi are dry and porous and draw liquid in by capillary action; a brief dip is enough, as they keep absorbing moisture from the cream as it chills.
dishes.plating: Cut neat squares with a sharp knife wiped between cuts and lift them out with a fish slice onto chilled plates, showing the layers. A second dusting of cocoa on each plate and a single chocolate coated coffee bean on top finish it. Or set individual portions in glasses so the layers show through.

pairing.drink: An espresso, or a coffee liqueur cocktail. Coffee echoes the soaked biscuits, and the liqueur adds sweetness and depth.
pairing.brennans: Espresso Martini: on the Brennan's dessert menu it is built with chicory, Frangelico and Kahlua, a coffee echo for a coffee dessert; confirm the build with the bar.

variations: Alcohol free: leave out the marsala and add 1/2 tsp (2.5 ml) vanilla to the zabaglione.
Limoncello tiramisù: dip the biscuits in lemon syrup with limoncello and add lemon zest to the cream.
Berry tiramisù: replace the espresso with a sweetened raspberry purée and layer fresh raspberries.
safety: Cooking the yolks to 160°F (71°C) makes this version safe; many traditional recipes use raw eggs, which are not suitable for pregnant guests, young children, the elderly or anyone with a weakened immune system.
Keep refrigerated and eat within 2 days.
Contains egg, dairy, wheat and alcohol if marsala is used.

dishes.title: Alfajores de Maicena
dishes.summary: Pale, crumbly biscuits made mostly with cornflour, which melt on the tongue, sandwiched with thick dulce de leche and rolled in coconut at the edges. The cornflour shortbread teaches tenderness without gluten and the discipline of baking without colour.
skills: dulce de leche cooked or bought
equipment: Stand mixer or electric hand mixer
Rolling pin and two sheets of baking paper
Two baking trays lined with baking paper
mise: Sift the cornflour, flour, baking powder, bicarbonate and salt together twice.
Soften the butter; separate the eggs.
Line two trays.
Put the coconut in a shallow dish.
If your dulce de leche is runny, simmer it in a pan, stirring, until thick enough to hold a peak, then cool.

timeline.do: Make the dough; chill 30 minutes.
Oven to 340°F (170°C). Roll and cut.
Bake 10 to 12 minutes per tray, pale.
Cool completely.
Fill, sandwich, roll in coconut.

steps.do: Beat the butter and sugar on medium speed for 3 minutes until pale and creamy. Beat in the yolks one at a time, then the vanilla, zest and brandy.
steps.look: A smooth, light, pale yellow cream.
steps.mistake: Using melted butter, which makes a greasy, flat biscuit.
steps.fix: Use soft butter that dents under a finger but holds its shape.

steps.do: Add the sifted dry ingredients and mix on low, or with a spatula, just until a soft dough forms.
steps.look: A soft, smooth, slightly crumbly dough that holds together when pressed.
steps.mistake: Overmixing, which warms the butter and makes the dough greasy.
steps.fix: Stop as soon as it comes together; finish by hand.

steps.do: Flatten the dough into a disc, wrap and chill 30 minutes. Heat the oven to 340°F (170°C).
steps.look: Firm but not hard dough.
steps.mistake: Rolling unchilled dough, which sticks and tears.
steps.fix: Chill it; if it gets too hard, leave it out 5 minutes.

steps.do: Roll the dough between the two sheets of baking paper to 1/4 inch (5 mm) thick. Cut rounds with the cutter and lift them onto the trays 1 inch (2.5 cm) apart. Reroll the scraps once.
steps.look: Neat, even rounds with clean edges.
steps.mistake: Rolling too thin, so the biscuits break when filled.
steps.fix: Keep them at 1/4 inch (5 mm) and even.

steps.do: Bake one tray at a time for 10 to 12 minutes.
steps.look: The biscuits are dry and set on top, the bottoms just barely golden, and the tops still pale; they look almost unbaked.
steps.mistake: Baking until golden brown, which makes them hard and loses the melting texture.
steps.fix: Pull them pale. They firm as they cool.

steps.do: Cool 5 minutes on the tray, then move them carefully to the rack and cool completely.
steps.look: Delicate biscuits that crumble easily.
steps.mistake: Moving them hot, so they break.
steps.fix: Wait 5 minutes and use a thin spatula.

steps.do: Spread a thick layer, about 1 heaped tsp (8 g), of dulce de leche on the flat side of half the biscuits. Top with the remaining biscuits and press gently so the filling just reaches the edge.
steps.look: Even sandwiches with a ring of dulce de leche showing at the edges.
steps.mistake: Pressing hard, so the biscuits crack.
steps.fix: Press gently with your fingertips at the centre.

steps.do: Roll the edge of each alfajor in the coconut so it sticks to the dulce de leche. Dust with icing sugar if you like.
steps.look: A neat coconut rim around each one.
steps.mistake: Runny dulce de leche that oozes out.
steps.fix: Thicken it first, or chill the filled alfajores for 15 minutes before rolling.

dishes.science: Cornflour is pure starch with none of wheat's gluten forming proteins, so a dough made mostly of it cannot develop an elastic network; the biscuit is held together only by butter, egg yolk and a little flour, which is why it crumbles and melts on the tongue. Creaming butter and sugar adds tiny air pockets, and baking powder and bicarbonate open the crumb further. Browning would form a firmer, crisper crust and toasted flavours that change the character of the biscuit, so it is baked at a moderate heat and pulled pale. Dulce de leche is milk and sugar cooked slowly until the milk proteins and sugars brown together in Maillard reactions, which gives its caramel flavour and thick texture.
dishes.plating: Stack three or four alfajores on a small plate, slightly offset, with a dusting of icing sugar, or arrange a row on a long board. Serve with coffee or a cortado.

pairing.drink: A Malmsey Madeira or a cortado. Madeira's caramel, nut and acidity meets dulce de leche without cloying.
pairing.brennans: Broadbent ‘Single Cask’ Malvasia Madeira 500 ml 2009: a rich Malvasia Madeira from the Brennan's list, caramel and acid together.

variations: Chocolate alfajores: dip the filled biscuits in tempered dark chocolate and let them set.
Lemon alfajores: add the zest of a whole lemon to the dough and fill with lemon curd.
Homemade dulce de leche: simmer 4 cups (960 ml) whole milk, 1 1/4 cups (250 g) sugar and a pinch of bicarbonate, stirring often, for 1 1/2 to 2 hours until thick and golden.
safety: Contains egg, dairy and wheat; coconut is a common allergen for some guests.

video.search: alfajores de maicena Argentine dulce de leche

dishes.title: Basbousa
dishes.summary: A semolina cake with yoghurt, coconut and ghee, scored into diamonds before baking, each topped with an almond, and soaked the moment it leaves the oven with cold lemon scented syrup. It shows the syrup rule in its purest form, one hot and one cold, and how scoring lets every piece drink evenly.
skills: a cold syrup on a hot cake
equipment: 8 inch (20 cm) square metal baking tin

ingredients.item: Syrup: orange blossom or rose water

mise: Make the syrup first so it has time to cool completely.
Heat the oven to 375°F (190°C).
Grease the tin with the tahini.
Warm the ghee.

timeline.do: Make the syrup; cool it completely.
Mix the batter; rest 30 minutes.
Spread, score, add almonds; bake 30 to 35 minutes.
Pour cold syrup over the hot cake.
After 2 hours of soaking, lift out the diamonds.

steps.do: Put the syrup sugar, water and lemon juice in the saucepan. Stir over medium heat until the sugar dissolves, then stop stirring and boil 6 to 8 minutes until it reaches 220°F (105°C). Stir in the flower water and cool completely.
steps.look: A clear syrup that runs from the spoon in a thin thread, about as thick as maple syrup when cold.
steps.mistake: Pouring warm syrup on the hot cake, which makes the top soggy and the inside dry.
steps.fix: Cool it fully; chill it if needed.

steps.do: Mix the semolina, sugar, coconut and baking powder. Add the yoghurt and warm ghee and mix to a thick, sandy, dropping batter. Leave it 30 minutes.
steps.look: The semolina absorbs the liquid and the batter thickens and swells slightly.
steps.mistake: Baking at once, so the grains stay hard and gritty.
steps.fix: Rest it so the semolina softens.

steps.do: Spread the batter in the tin and smooth it level, about 3/4 inch (2 cm) deep. With the knife, score it into diamonds, cutting right down to the base. Press an almond into the centre of each.
steps.look: Neat, even diamonds with an almond on each.
steps.mistake: Scoring only the surface, so the syrup cannot reach the base.
steps.fix: Cut all the way through; wipe the knife between cuts.

steps.do: Bake 30 to 35 minutes.
steps.look: An even, deep golden brown top, and the cake pulls away slightly from the sides of the tin.
steps.mistake: Pulling it pale, so it is soft and greasy.
steps.fix: Bake until it is properly golden; give it 1 minute under the overhead grill (broiler) if needed to colour the top.

steps.do: As soon as it leaves the oven, pour the cold syrup slowly over the hot cake, aiming into the score lines.
steps.look: A loud hiss and the syrup disappears into the cake within a couple of minutes.
steps.mistake: Pouring more syrup after the cake has stopped absorbing it, leaving a puddle.
steps.fix: Stop when it stops hissing and drinking.

steps.do: Leave the cake to soak and cool for at least 2 hours, then recut along the score lines and lift out the pieces.
steps.look: Moist, golden diamonds that hold their shape and glisten.
steps.mistake: Cutting while hot, so the pieces crumble.
steps.fix: Let it rest fully.

dishes.science: The soak works on a temperature gap. A hot cake is full of steam; as cold syrup meets it, the steam condenses and creates a slight pull that draws syrup deep into the open crumb, while the cold, thick syrup does not dissolve the surface. Hot syrup on a hot cake stays thin and runny and pools at the top, softening it while the centre stays dry. Semolina is coarse durum wheat; resting the batter lets the grains absorb liquid and soften, so the cake is tender but still has a pleasant grainy texture. Lemon juice in the syrup is an acid that breaks some sucrose into glucose and fructose, which helps stop the syrup crystallising as it cools.
dishes.plating: Arrange three diamonds slightly overlapping on a small plate, almonds up, with a spoon of thick yoghurt or clotted cream (ashta) beside them and a few chopped pistachios scattered over. Serve with mint tea or Turkish coffee.

pairing.drink: A sweet Muscat or Moscato d'Asti, or mint tea. The wine's orange blossom notes match the syrup.
pairing.brennans: Castello Banfi ‘Florus’ Moscadello di Montalcino 2011: a late harvest Moscato from the Brennan's list whose orange blossom character suits a syrup soaked cake.

variations: Basbousa with cream filling: bake half the batter, spread with set cream (ashta), cover with the rest and bake.
Orange basbousa: add the zest of an orange to the batter and orange juice to the syrup.
Hazelnut basbousa: replace the almonds with hazelnuts and the coconut with ground hazelnuts.
safety: Hot sugar syrup burns; let it cool before handling.
Contains wheat, dairy, sesame (tahini) and almonds.

video.search: basbousa Egyptian semolina cake syrup

dishes.title: Black Sesame Tang Yuan
dishes.summary: Soft, chewy balls of glutinous rice dough wrapped around a filling of toasted black sesame, sugar and lard chilled firm, boiled until they float and served in a warm ginger syrup. The dough behaves like modelling clay and the filling must be cold to wrap, so it teaches temperature control and quick, smooth hands.
skills: a black sesame and lard filling chilled firm
equipment: Spice grinder or mortar and pestle
Medium saucepan for the ginger syrup

ingredients.note: lard is traditional and sets firmer

ingredients.item: Ginger syrup: rock sugar or brown sugar

mise: Toast the sesame seeds in a dry pan over medium low heat for 3 to 4 minutes, shaking, until fragrant and a few begin to pop. Cool completely.
Grind the sesame with the sugar until it forms a fine, slightly oily powder.
Simmer the ginger syrup ingredients for 15 minutes; keep warm.
Line the tray with baking paper.

timeline.do: Toast and grind the sesame; mix the filling; chill 30 minutes.
Shape the filling into balls; freeze 15 minutes. Ginger syrup on.
Make the dough.
Wrap the balls.
Boil until floating plus 2 minutes; into the ginger syrup.

steps.do: Mix the ground sesame and sugar with the lard into a smooth paste. Chill for 30 minutes until firm enough to roll.
steps.look: A dark, glossy paste that holds its shape when pressed.
steps.mistake: Trying to roll soft filling, which smears.
steps.fix: Chill longer; it must be firm.

steps.do: Roll the filling into 16 small balls about 1/2 inch (1.5 cm) across, set on the tray and freeze 15 minutes.
steps.look: Neat, firm black balls.
steps.mistake: Balls that are too large for the wrapper.
steps.fix: Keep them small; the dough must cover them with room to seal.

steps.do: Put the glutinous rice flour in a bowl and add warm water gradually, stirring, then knead until smooth. Pinch off a small piece of dough the size of a walnut, flatten it, boil it for 1 minute until it floats, then knead it back into the main dough.
steps.look: A soft, smooth dough with the feel of an earlobe that does not crack when pressed.
steps.mistake: A dry dough that cracks at the edges when pressed.
steps.fix: Add water a teaspoon at a time; the cooked piece makes the dough more elastic and crack resistant.

steps.do: Divide the dough into 16 pieces. Keep them covered with a damp cloth. Flatten one into a disc in your palm, thinner at the edges, set a filling ball in the centre and push the dough up and around it, pinching closed. Roll gently between your palms into a smooth ball.
steps.look: A smooth, white ball with no cracks or seams.
steps.mistake: Cracks or thin spots, which burst in the water and leak filling.
steps.fix: Smooth any crack with a damp fingertip; patch thin spots with a pinch of dough.

steps.do: Bring a large pan of water to a boil. Lower the tang yuan in gently and stir once so they do not stick to the bottom. Cook until they float, then 2 minutes more.
steps.look: The balls rise and bob on the surface, swelling slightly and turning glossy.
steps.mistake: Boiling too vigorously, which can split them.
steps.fix: Keep a steady, not violent, boil; add a splash of cold water if it rises.

steps.do: Lift them out with the slotted spoon into bowls of warm ginger syrup. Serve at once.
steps.look: Shiny white balls in amber syrup; bitten, the filling flows out warm and dark.
steps.mistake: Serving straight from the pan, so the filling is scalding.
steps.fix: Warn guests; let them cool a moment in the syrup.

dishes.science: Glutinous rice flour is made from rice whose starch is almost entirely amylopectin, a highly branched starch that forms a sticky, elastic gel when cooked. Raw, the dough has little stretch and cracks easily. Boiling a small piece gelatinises its starch, and kneading it back in spreads that cooked gel through the dough, binding it so it stretches without tearing. The filling uses lard because lard is solid at fridge temperature, so the filling can be rolled and wrapped, but melts in the boiling water into a flowing centre. Toasting sesame seeds develops nutty flavour through browning reactions, and grinding releases their oils, which helps bind the paste.
dishes.plating: Serve four tang yuan in a small warm bowl, half covered with ginger syrup, with a slice of ginger and a few osmanthus flowers or toasted sesame seeds on the surface. Give each guest a spoon.

pairing.drink: A light oolong or jasmine tea. Its floral warmth suits black sesame and ginger.

variations: Peanut tang yuan: replace sesame with finely ground roasted peanuts and sugar.
Fermented rice soup (jiu niang): serve the balls in warm fermented rice wine with an egg ribbon.
Small plain tang yuan: roll dough into pea sized balls without filling and serve in sweet soup.
safety: The filling is molten and very hot; bite carefully and warn guests.
Glutinous rice balls are sticky and chewy; cut them smaller for young children and older guests to avoid choking.
Contains sesame; lard is a pork product.

dishes.title: Ichigo Daifuku
dishes.summary: A whole strawberry wrapped first in sweet red bean paste, then in a thin skin of soft, stretchy mochi made from glutinous rice flour cooked until translucent, dusted with potato starch. Rice cake is wrapped while hot and sticky, so it is a test of quick, light, floured hands.
skills: making gyuhi from glutinous rice flour
equipment: Steamer with a heatproof bowl inside, or a microwave and a microwave safe bowl
mise: Hull the strawberries and pat them completely dry.
Divide the anko into 8 equal portions, about 1 oz (25 g) each.
Wrap each strawberry in anko: flatten a portion in your palm, set the strawberry in it point up and push the paste up the sides, leaving the tip showing. Chill on a plate.
Dust a tray generously with potato starch.
Set up the steamer, or have the microwave ready.

timeline.do: Wrap strawberries in anko; chill.
Mix and cook the gyuhi, stirring between bursts.
Turn out onto starch; divide into 8.
Wrap each strawberry quickly.
Serve the same day, at room temperature.

steps.do: Whisk the rice flour and sugar in the bowl, then whisk in the water a little at a time until completely smooth.
steps.look: A thin, white, milky batter with no lumps.
steps.mistake: Adding the water all at once, which leaves lumps.
steps.fix: Add it gradually, or push the batter through a sieve.

steps.do: Microwave: cover loosely and cook 1 minute on high, stir hard with a wet spatula, cook another minute, stir, then 30 seconds at a time until done. Steamer: steam the covered bowl 15 to 20 minutes, stirring hard every 5 minutes.
steps.look: The dough turns from white and runny to translucent, glossy, thick and very stretchy, pulling from the spatula in elastic sheets.
steps.mistake: Undercooking, so the mochi is pasty and white in parts and tears.
steps.fix: Keep cooking until fully translucent with no opaque white patches.

steps.do: Scrape the hot mochi onto the starch dusted tray and dust the top with more starch. Let it cool 1 to 2 minutes, just until it can be handled.
steps.look: A smooth, glossy mound that holds a soft shape.
steps.mistake: Touching it with bare, unstarched hands, which glues it to your fingers.
steps.fix: Dust your hands and the scraper with starch before every touch.

steps.do: Cut the mochi into 8 equal pieces with the starched scraper. Flatten one piece in your starched palm into a disc about 3 inches (8 cm) across, thinner at the edges.
steps.look: A thin, even disc that stretches without tearing.
steps.mistake: Letting the mochi cool too much, so it stiffens and will not stretch.
steps.fix: Work quickly while it is warm; rewarm stiff mochi for 10 seconds in the microwave.

steps.do: Set an anko wrapped strawberry point down in the centre of the disc. Stretch the mochi up and around it and pinch the edges together firmly at the bottom. Turn it seam side down onto the starch.
steps.look: A smooth, round, white dome with a faint blush of pink through the skin.
steps.mistake: Starch on the edges you are trying to pinch together, which stops them sealing.
steps.fix: Brush starch off the edges before pinching.

steps.do: Brush off excess starch with a dry pastry brush. Serve the same day at room temperature.
steps.look: Soft, pillowy daifuku with a light dusting.
steps.mistake: Refrigerating, which makes mochi hard.
steps.fix: Keep them covered at room temperature and eat within the day.

dishes.science: Glutinous rice flour's starch is almost all amylopectin, which forms a stretchy, sticky gel when cooked with water. Heating gelatinises the starch: the granules absorb water, swell and burst, turning the opaque batter translucent and elastic. Sugar slows the starch from setting back as it cools, so the mochi stays soft longer, though it still firms within a day, and much faster in the fridge, as the starch recrystallises in a process called retrogradation. Potato starch dusts well because it is fine and dry and does not get gluey at room temperature. The anko layer acts as a barrier between strawberry juice and mochi, which would otherwise dissolve the skin.
dishes.plating: Serve two daifuku on a small plate or a dark slate, one whole and one cut in half with a sharp, wet knife to show the cross section: white mochi, dark anko and red strawberry. Serve with green tea.

pairing.drink: A hot green tea, sencha or matcha. Its gentle bitterness balances the sweet bean paste.

variations: Shiro an daifuku: use white bean paste for a paler cross section.
Mango or kiwi daifuku: wrap pieces of ripe mango or kiwi instead of strawberry.
Matcha mochi: add 1 tsp (2 g) matcha to the rice flour.
safety: Mochi is very sticky and is a known choking hazard; cut it into small pieces for children and older guests, and eat slowly.
Hot mochi can burn; let it cool slightly before handling.

video.search: ichigo daifuku strawberry mochi anko

dishes.title: Cendol
dishes.summary: Green jelly noodles made from pandan juice and rice flour, pressed through holes into iced water, served in a glass with shaved ice, salted coconut milk and dark palm sugar syrup. The Malaysian iced dessert teaches how a starch gel sets, how to cook it to the right thickness, and how salt deepens palm sugar.
equipment: A cendol press, a potato ricer, or a colander with large round holes
Ice shaver, or a blender for crushed ice

ingredients.note: fresh or frozen, cut into pieces

ingredients.item: Mung bean starch or tapioca starch

ingredients.note: pinch for the jelly, the rest for the coconut milk

mise: Blend the pandan leaves with the water until fine, then strain through the sieve or muslin, squeezing hard. You need about 1 2/3 cups (400 ml) of bright green juice.
Make the syrup: melt the palm sugar with the water and a knotted pandan leaf over low heat, stirring, then simmer 5 minutes until syrupy; strain and cool.
Stir 1/4 tsp (1.5 g) salt into the coconut milk and chill it.
Fill a large bowl with water and plenty of ice cubes.
Chill the glasses.

timeline.do: Make pandan juice; palm sugar syrup; salt and chill the coconut milk.
Cook the pandan batter until thick and glossy.
Press into iced water; chill the noodles.
Shave the ice; build the glasses.
Pour over syrup and serve with spoons.

steps.do: Whisk the rice flour, starch and a pinch of salt into the pandan juice in the saucepan until completely smooth.
steps.look: A thin, lump free, bright green liquid.
steps.mistake: Heating before whisking out lumps.
steps.fix: Whisk thoroughly cold; strain if needed.

steps.do: Cook over medium heat, stirring constantly with the wooden spoon, for 5 to 8 minutes. It will thicken suddenly. Keep cooking and stirring for another 2 minutes after it thickens.
steps.look: The batter goes from thin to lumpy to a thick, smooth, glossy, translucent green paste, like soft polenta, that pulls away from the pan.
steps.mistake: Stopping when it first thickens, so the noodles are cloudy, soft and fall apart.
steps.fix: Cook until it is glossy and translucent, not chalky.

steps.do: Working quickly while it is hot, put the paste into the cendol press or ricer, or a few spoonfuls at a time onto the colander set over the iced water, and press it through with a spatula so short worms drop into the water.
steps.look: Short, green, tapered noodles that firm up as soon as they hit the iced water.
steps.mistake: Letting the paste cool in the pan, so it becomes too stiff to press.
steps.fix: Press while hot; rewarm briefly with a spoon of water if it stiffens.

steps.do: Leave the noodles in the iced water 10 minutes to firm, then drain.
steps.look: Firm, bouncy, slippery green jelly noodles.
steps.mistake: Leaving them in warm water, so they stay soft.
steps.fix: Keep plenty of ice in the water.

steps.do: To build: put 2 to 3 tbsp (about 40 g) of cendol and a spoon of red beans if using into each glass. Pile shaved ice on top into a mound.
steps.look: A tall mound of white ice over green noodles.
steps.mistake: Coarse ice cubes, which do not blend with the syrup and coconut.
steps.fix: Shave or crush the ice as finely as you can.

steps.do: Pour the salted coconut milk over the ice, then drizzle the dark palm sugar syrup over the top so it runs down the sides. Serve at once with a long spoon.
steps.look: White ice streaked with dark brown syrup, coconut milk pooling below and green noodles at the base.
steps.mistake: Unsalted coconut milk, which tastes flat against the syrup.
steps.fix: The salt matters; taste and add a pinch if needed.

dishes.science: Rice flour and mung bean starch are starches that gelatinise when cooked in water: the granules swell and burst, releasing molecules that form a gel. Mung bean starch is rich in amylose, a straight chained starch that sets into a firm, springy gel when cooled, which gives the noodles their bounce. Cooking until translucent ensures all the granules have burst; undercooked starch stays chalky and weak. Plunging into iced water sets the gel instantly in its shape. Palm sugar is unrefined and contains caramel and smoky compounds formed when the sap is boiled down. Salt suppresses bitterness and enhances the perception of sweetness, which is why salting the coconut milk makes the palm sugar taste deeper.
dishes.plating: Use a tall, clear glass or a wide bowl so the layers show: green cendol and red beans at the base, a high mound of white ice, coconut milk pooling, and dark syrup dripping down the sides. Serve with a long spoon and, in a glass, a wide straw.

pairing.drink: It is a drink and dessert in one; serve on its own, or with a cup of hot jasmine tea for contrast.

variations: Cendol durian: top with a spoon of fresh durian flesh.
Pandan jelly cubes: pour the cooked paste into a tray, chill and cut into cubes instead of pressing.
Use frozen pandan juice or 1/2 tsp (2.5 ml) pandan extract if fresh leaves are unavailable.
safety: Keep the coconut milk chilled and serve immediately; discard leftovers left at room temperature over 2 hours.

video.search: cendol pandan jelly gula melaka Malaysian

dishes.title: Gulab Jamun
dishes.summary: Soft balls of milk powder dough fried slowly in ghee until deep brown and cooked to the centre, then soaked in warm syrup scented with cardamom, saffron and rose water until they swell and turn tender. Frying slowly so the inside cooks before the outside darkens is the lesson, along with a dough mixed as little as possible.
skills: frying at low heat so the centre cooks
equipment: Wide, heavy saucepan or kadai for frying

ingredients.note: added a teaspoon at a time

ingredients.item: Ghee or neutral oil for frying

mise: Make the syrup first: simmer the sugar, water, cardamom and saffron 5 minutes, until slightly sticky but still thin. Add the lemon juice, then the rose water off the heat. Keep warm.
Sift the milk powder, flour and bicarbonate together.
Warm the milk.
Set up the frying pan with the thermometer, the slotted spoon and the rack.

timeline.do: Make the syrup and keep it warm.
Mix the dough barely; rest 10 minutes.
Roll 16 crack free balls.
Fry slowly at 275 to 300°F (135 to 150°C), 7 to 10 minutes.
Into the warm syrup; soak at least 2 hours.
Serve warm with pistachios.

steps.do: Rub the ghee into the dry ingredients with your fingertips. Add the yoghurt, then the warm milk a teaspoon at a time, mixing gently with your fingers just until a soft, slightly sticky dough comes together. Do not knead. Cover and rest 10 minutes.
steps.look: A soft, smooth, slightly tacky dough that holds together when pressed.
steps.mistake: Kneading the dough, which makes the jamun dense and rubbery.
steps.fix: Mix only until combined; a few seconds of gentle pressing, no more.

steps.do: Grease your palms with a little ghee. Divide the dough into 16 equal pieces and roll each between your palms into a perfectly smooth ball, with no cracks, about 3/4 inch (2 cm) across.
steps.look: Smooth, crack free balls with a soft sheen.
steps.mistake: Cracked balls, which split open in the oil.
steps.fix: Press and roll again with greased palms until smooth; if the dough is dry, add a drop of milk.

steps.do: Heat the frying ghee to 275°F (135°C). Add a test ball: it should sink, then slowly rise to the top after a few seconds with small bubbles around it.
steps.look: Gentle, small bubbles; the ball rises slowly.
steps.mistake: Oil too hot, so the ball rises instantly and browns in seconds with a raw middle.
steps.fix: Lower the heat and wait for the thermometer to fall.

steps.do: Fry the balls in two batches at 275 to 300°F (135 to 150°C), stirring the oil gently around them, not touching them at first, so they roll and colour evenly. Fry 7 to 10 minutes until a deep, even brown.
steps.look: The balls swell slightly and turn evenly from pale gold to a deep reddish brown.
steps.mistake: Pushing them with the spoon early, which dents them.
steps.fix: Swirl the oil instead; turn them gently only once they have firmed.

steps.do: Lift them out with the slotted spoon, drain for 30 seconds on the rack, then drop them straight into the warm syrup.
steps.look: They sizzle slightly and float in the syrup.
steps.mistake: Hot jamun into hot syrup, or cold syrup, which stops them soaking properly or makes them shrivel.
steps.fix: Syrup should be warm, about 140°F (60°C), not boiling and not cold.

steps.do: Soak at least 2 hours, turning them occasionally. Warm gently before serving and garnish with pistachios.
steps.look: The jamun swell to nearly twice their size, soft and syrup filled; a spoon cuts through with no resistance and no dry core.
steps.mistake: Serving after 15 minutes, when they are still dry inside.
steps.fix: Give them the full soak.

dishes.science: Milk powder stands in for khoya, milk reduced to solids: its proteins and milk sugar (lactose) brown readily, which is why the jamun turn so dark. Because lactose browns at relatively low temperatures, frying must be slow and gentle so the centre cooks through before the outside burns. Bicarbonate releases gas in the heat, lightening the dough so it can soak up syrup. Kneading builds gluten from the flour and compacts the dough, making it dense. Warm syrup soaks in best: a warm, porous ball draws in syrup as it cools, while a syrup that is too concentrated or too hot pulls water out by osmosis and makes the surface shrivel. Rose water and cardamom are added late because their aromas are volatile.
dishes.plating: Serve two or three warm jamun in a small bowl with a spoonful of syrup, scattered with slivered pistachios and a few dried rose petals. For a modern plate, set them beside a scoop of vanilla ice cream or a spoon of thick, cold rabri.

pairing.drink: A cup of masala chai, or a late harvest Gewürztraminer. Chai's spice matches cardamom; Gewürztraminer's lychee and rose notes echo the syrup.

variations: Kala jamun: add a spoon of sugar to the dough and fry until almost black.
Stuffed gulab jamun: press a little chopped pistachio and cardamom into each ball before rolling.
Khoya jamun: use 7 oz (200 g) fresh khoya instead of milk powder for the traditional version.
safety: Deep frying: fill the pan no more than a third full, use a thermometer, never leave it, keep a lid nearby and never use water on an oil fire.
Hot syrup burns; handle with care.
Contains dairy, wheat and pistachios.

video.search: gulab jamun milk powder recipe slow frying

dishes.title: Puff-Puff
dishes.summary: A loose, sweet yeasted batter with a hint of nutmeg, left to rise until bubbly, then squeezed through the fist into hot oil where it puffs into round, golden balls, soft and airy inside. It teaches proofing a wet dough and the hand drop that makes round puffs, as well as reading oil temperature.
skills: dropping by hand into oil for round puffs
equipment: Large mixing bowl and a wooden spoon or your hand
Clingfilm or a damp tea towel
Heavy, deep saucepan, at least 4 quart (4 litres)
Tray lined with kitchen paper, and a bowl of water for your hand
mise: Check the water temperature: warm like a baby's bath, not hot; above 130°F (55°C) kills yeast.
Mix the dry ingredients in the bowl.
Find a warm, draught free spot for the batter to rise.
Set up the pan, thermometer, slotted spoon, paper lined tray and a small bowl of water.

timeline.do: Mix the batter; beat 3 minutes.
Rise 1 hour until doubled and bubbly.
Heat the oil to 340°F (170°C).
Drop and fry in batches, 3 to 4 minutes each.
Roll in sugar and serve warm.

steps.do: Pour the warm water into the dry ingredients and beat with a wooden spoon or your hand for 3 minutes into a smooth, thick, stretchy batter.
steps.look: A sticky batter, thicker than pancake batter, that stretches in strands when lifted.
steps.mistake: A runny batter, which spreads into flat shapes in the oil, or a stiff dough, which makes heavy balls.
steps.fix: Add flour or water a tablespoon at a time to adjust.

steps.do: Cover and leave in a warm place for 1 hour, until doubled in size and full of bubbles.
steps.look: A domed, airy batter with large bubbles on the surface; it smells yeasty and slightly sweet.
steps.mistake: Leaving it far longer, so it over proofs, smells sour and collapses.
steps.fix: One rise is enough. If it has gone too far, beat it down and use it after a short 15 minute rest.

steps.do: Heat the oil to 340°F (170°C) in the pan, no more than half full.
steps.look: A small drop of batter rises at once with steady bubbles around it.
steps.mistake: Oil too hot, so the outside browns before the inside cooks.
steps.fix: Use the thermometer and adjust the heat between batches.

steps.do: Wet your hand, scoop up a handful of batter and close your fist. Squeeze so a ball of batter rises between your thumb and index finger, then scrape it off with your thumb or a wet spoon and drop it gently into the oil, close to the surface. Fry 6 to 8 at a time.
steps.look: Round balls that sink briefly, rise and begin to puff.
steps.mistake: Dropping from a height, which splashes oil.
steps.fix: Release the batter just above the oil surface. If hand dropping is awkward at first, use two wet spoons.

steps.do: Fry 3 to 4 minutes, turning with the slotted spoon so they colour evenly; many turn themselves.
steps.look: An even, deep golden brown all over; they feel light when lifted.
steps.mistake: Crowding the pan, which drops the temperature and makes greasy puffs.
steps.fix: Fry in small batches and let the oil recover.

steps.do: Lift onto the paper lined tray and test one: break it open to check the inside is cooked and airy. Roll in sugar while warm if you like.
steps.look: Golden outside, soft and honeycombed inside, with no raw batter.
steps.mistake: Raw centres from oil too hot or puffs too big.
steps.fix: Lower the heat slightly and make smaller balls.

dishes.science: Yeast feeds on the sugar and flour and produces carbon dioxide and alcohol; in a wet batter the gas is trapped by the stretchy gluten formed during beating, so the batter rises and fills with bubbles. Warmth speeds the yeast, but heat above about 130°F (55°C) kills it. Over proofed batter has used up its food, and the gluten weakens, so it collapses and tastes sour. In hot oil, the gas bubbles expand and water turns to steam, puffing the ball rapidly, while the outside sets and browns. A round shape cooks evenly, which is why the fist squeeze matters; flat or irregular pieces cook unevenly. Nutmeg's aroma is fat soluble and carries well in fried dough.
dishes.plating: Pile the puff-puff high in a bowl or paper cone, dusted with sugar, or serve on a small plate with a dish of warm chocolate or a fruit sauce for dipping. They are best within 30 minutes.

pairing.drink: A cold Chapman, or a hot spiced tea. Both pair with sweet, fried dough.

variations: Spiced puff-puff: add 1/2 tsp (1 g) cinnamon and a pinch of ground cloves.
Pepper puff-puff: add 1 finely chopped scotch bonnet and a chopped onion for a savoury version.
Coconut puff-puff: replace half the water with coconut milk.
safety: Hot oil: fill no more than half, use a thermometer, never leave it unattended, keep a lid nearby and never put water on burning oil.
Keep your wet hand well above the oil; never let water drip into the pan.
Let the oil cool completely before moving or straining it.

dishes.title: Churros con Chocolate
dishes.summary: A paste of flour cooked into boiling water and butter, piped through a large star nozzle into hot oil, fried crisp and golden, rolled in sugar and dunked in a thick, spoon coating hot chocolate. Churro dough is cooked before it is fried, a first step towards choux pastry, and the star nozzle is the physics that makes it crisp.
skills: a cooked flour and water paste
equipment: Strong piping bag, or a churrera, with a large open star nozzle, about 1/2 inch (1.2 cm)
Small saucepan and whisk for the chocolate

ingredients.note: mixed with 2 tbsp (30 ml) of the cold milk

mise: Fit the star nozzle into the piping bag and fold the top back over a jug.
Mix the rolling sugar and cinnamon in a wide dish.
Chop the chocolate; mix the cornflour slurry.
Set up the frying pan with the thermometer, a paper lined tray and oiled scissors.
Beat the egg if using.

timeline.do: Make the chocolate; keep it warm.
Make the dough; cool 5 minutes; fill the bag. Heat oil to 375°F (190°C).
Pipe and fry in batches, 3 to 4 minutes each.
Roll in sugar and serve with the chocolate.

steps.do: Make the chocolate: heat the milk until steaming. Add the chocolate and whisk until melted. Whisk in the cornflour slurry and sugar and simmer gently, whisking, 3 to 5 minutes until thick. Keep warm over the lowest heat.
steps.look: A glossy, thick chocolate that coats a spoon heavily, like a loose pudding.
steps.mistake: Boiling hard, so it catches and scorches on the base.
steps.fix: Whisk constantly over low heat; if lumpy, whisk hard or strain.

steps.do: Put the water, butter, sugar and salt in the saucepan and bring to a full boil. Take off the heat, add all the flour at once and beat hard with the wooden spoon until smooth. Return to low heat and beat 1 minute more.
steps.look: A smooth, thick paste that pulls away from the pan sides into a ball, leaving a thin film on the base.
steps.mistake: Adding the flour slowly, which makes lumps.
steps.fix: All at once, and beat vigorously; lumps beat out in the next minute.

steps.do: Tip the dough into a bowl and cool 5 minutes. Beat in the egg if using until smooth and glossy. Spoon the dough into the piping bag, pushing out any air pockets.
steps.look: A smooth, stiff, glossy dough that holds a ridged shape when piped.
steps.mistake: Air pockets in the bag, which can make the dough burst or spit in the oil.
steps.fix: Pack it down firmly and twist the bag tight.

steps.do: Heat the oil to 375°F (190°C). Pipe a 4 to 5 inch (10 to 12 cm) length directly over the oil, close to the surface, and snip it off with the oiled scissors. Fry 4 or 5 at a time.
steps.look: The ridged ropes sizzle immediately and float.
steps.mistake: Piping with a small or smooth nozzle, so the churros are dense or burst.
steps.fix: Use a large star nozzle; the ridges give more surface to crisp and let steam escape.

steps.do: Fry 3 to 4 minutes, turning once, until deep golden and crisp. Lift out onto the paper and roll in cinnamon sugar while still hot.
steps.look: Deep golden churros with sharp, crisp ridges; sugar clings to them.
steps.mistake: Pulling them pale, so they are soft and raw inside.
steps.fix: Fry to a deep gold. Break one open to check the inside is cooked.

steps.do: Serve at once with cups of the hot chocolate for dunking.
steps.look: Crisp outside, tender inside; the chocolate coats them thickly when dipped.
steps.mistake: Letting them sit, so they soften.
steps.fix: Serve straight from the oil.

dishes.science: Churro dough is a panade: flour cooked into boiling water and butter so its starch gelatinises and forms a thick, smooth paste before it ever meets the oil. That pre cooking lets the paste hold its piped shape and hold water, which turns to steam in the fryer and puffs the inside while the outside crisps. The star nozzle's ridges increase surface area, so more of the churro dries and browns quickly, and they let steam escape evenly; a smooth, thick rope can trap steam and burst. Adding egg introduces proteins and fat that make the inside softer and richer. Cornflour thickens the chocolate because its starch swells in the hot milk, giving the spoon coating Spanish texture.
dishes.plating: Lay four or five sugared churros on a small plate or a paper cone in a fan, beside a cup or small bowl of thick chocolate. Dust a little extra cinnamon over the chocolate.

pairing.drink: The thick chocolate itself, or a sweet Pedro Ximénez sherry. PX's raisin and coffee notes meet chocolate and cinnamon.

variations: Churros rellenos: pipe thick, straight churros, fry, cool slightly and fill with dulce de leche using a small nozzle.
Porras: use a thicker, smooth nozzle and a dough with a little bicarbonate for fluffy Madrid porras.
Mexican style: roll in sugar with plenty of cinnamon and serve with a cinnamon spiced chocolate.
safety: Hot oil: no more than half full, thermometer, never unattended, lid nearby, never water on burning oil.
Pipe close to the oil surface and keep your hand above, not over, the hottest part; oil can spit.
Hot chocolate and dough can burn; let them cool slightly before eating.

dishes.title: Beignets
dishes.summary: Squares of an enriched yeast dough made with milk, egg, sugar and butter, rolled, cut and fried until they puff hollow, then buried under a drift of icing sugar and eaten hot with coffee. The New Orleans café beignet teaches frying an enriched dough so it puffs into a pillow, and how a slow, cold rise improves both flavour and handling.
equipment: Stand mixer with dough hook, or a large bowl and your hands
Large lightly oiled bowl and clingfilm
Large sharp knife or pizza wheel

ingredients.item: Plain flour (or bread flour for chewier beignets)

mise: Warm the milk and water to body temperature.
Soften the butter; bring the egg to room temperature.
Oil a large bowl.
The next day, take the dough out 30 minutes before rolling; set up the fryer, paper lined tray and sieve of icing sugar.

timeline.do: Make and knead the dough; cold rise overnight in the fridge.
Dough out; heat oil to 360°F (180°C).
Roll 1/4 inch (6 mm), cut squares.
Fry at once in batches, 1 to 2 minutes a side.
Bury in icing sugar and serve hot.

steps.do: Mix the flour, yeast, sugar and salt in the mixer bowl. Add the milk, water and egg and mix on low with the dough hook until a shaggy dough forms. Add the butter a little at a time and knead on medium for 6 to 8 minutes.
steps.look: A soft, smooth, slightly sticky dough that pulls away from the bowl and stretches thin without tearing (the windowpane test).
steps.mistake: Adding lots of extra flour to stop the stickiness, which makes the beignets dense.
steps.fix: A soft, slightly tacky dough is right; use oiled hands rather than more flour.

steps.do: Shape into a ball, put in the oiled bowl, turn to coat, cover and refrigerate overnight, 8 to 18 hours.
steps.look: The dough rises slowly to about one and a half times its size and smells pleasantly yeasty.
steps.mistake: Rushing it with a short warm rise when you have time for cold.
steps.fix: If you must do it the same day, rise 1 to 2 hours at warm room temperature until doubled.

steps.do: Heat the oil to 360°F (180°C), no more than half full. Roll the cold dough on a floured surface to an even 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick. Cut into 2 1/2 inch (6 cm) squares with the knife or wheel.
steps.look: Even squares with clean, sharp edges.
steps.mistake: Rolling thick, so the beignets stay doughy inside.
steps.fix: Keep to 1/4 inch (6 mm); they will triple in height.

steps.do: Fry at once, without a second proof, 3 or 4 at a time. Lower each square gently into the oil away from you. It should sink, then float and puff within seconds. Spoon oil over the top to help it puff, and fry 1 to 2 minutes a side.
steps.look: The square balloons into a puffy pillow and turns golden brown on each side.
steps.mistake: Flat beignets from oil that is too cool, or dark ones with raw middles from oil that is too hot.
steps.fix: Hold 350 to 365°F (175 to 185°C), adjusting the heat between batches.

steps.do: Lift onto the paper lined tray for 30 seconds, then onto a plate, and sift icing sugar over them in a thick drift while still hot.
steps.look: Golden pillows half buried in white sugar.
steps.mistake: Letting them cool before sugaring, so the sugar will not stick.
steps.fix: Sugar them hot, and lots of it.

steps.do: Serve immediately, three to a plate.
steps.look: Crisp outside, hollow and tender inside, steaming when torn.
steps.mistake: Making them ahead; they go leathery within the hour.
steps.fix: Fry to order.

dishes.science: An enriched dough contains fat, sugar, milk and egg, all of which tenderise it by coating gluten strands and limiting how tightly they bond, so the beignet is soft rather than chewy. Kneading still builds enough gluten to hold gas. A cold, slow rise gives the yeast time to make flavour compounds and lets the dough firm up, so it rolls cleanly. When the thin, cold square hits hot oil, water inside turns to steam and the gas cells expand rapidly; the outside sets almost immediately, and the trapped steam inflates the centre into a hollow pocket. Frying straight after cutting, without a second rise, keeps the structure tight enough to puff dramatically rather than spread.
dishes.plating: Serve three beignets on a small plate, piled slightly on top of each other, with so much icing sugar that it falls onto the plate around them. Serve with a cup of café au lait made with chicory coffee and hot milk.

pairing.drink: Café au lait made with chicory coffee. Its roasted bitterness balances the sugar and fried dough.
pairing.brennans: New Orleans-Style Coffee with Chicory: the Brennan's coffee and chicory, the classic New Orleans partner for beignets.

variations: Filled beignets: pipe chocolate hazelnut spread or crème pâtissière into the side of each beignet.
Savoury crab beignets: fold crab meat and spring onion into a choux style batter and drop by spoonfuls into oil.
Calas: the old Creole rice fritter, made with cooked rice, egg and flour.
safety: Hot oil: no more than half full, thermometer, never unattended, lid nearby, never water on burning oil.
Lower dough away from you; puffing beignets can spit oil.
Contains wheat, dairy and egg.

dishes.title: Hotteok
dishes.summary: A soft yeast dough, chewy with glutinous rice flour, wrapped around a filling of brown sugar, cinnamon and chopped nuts, then fried and pressed flat in an oiled pan so the sugar melts into a molten syrup. The filled Korean pancake teaches sealing a sticky dough cleanly and pressing it as it browns.
skills: a brown sugar, cinnamon and nut filling
equipment: Heavy frying pan or flat griddle
A hotteok press, or a flat bottomed metal cup or spatula, oiled
Small bowl of oil for your hands

ingredients.note: for the dough, plus more for frying

ingredients.item: Filling: walnuts and peanuts, finely chopped

mise: Warm the milk.
Mix the filling ingredients in a small bowl.
Oil the press or cup.
Have a small bowl of oil ready to coat your hands.

timeline.do: Mix the dough; rise 1 hour until doubled.
Mix the filling; knock back the dough; divide into 8.
Fill and seal each ball.
Fry, press and flip in batches.
Cool 1 minute; serve warm.

steps.do: Mix the flours, yeast, sugar and salt. Add the warm milk and oil and stir with the spatula, then beat for 2 minutes into a very soft, sticky dough. Cover and leave in a warm place 1 hour until doubled.
steps.look: A soft, bubbly, sticky dough that has doubled and jiggles when the bowl is shaken.
steps.mistake: Adding flour to make it handleable, which makes tough hotteok.
steps.fix: It should be sticky; you will handle it with oiled hands.

steps.do: Oil your hands and punch down the dough. Divide into 8 pieces.
steps.look: Soft, smooth pieces that stretch easily.
steps.mistake: Dry hands, which stick to the dough.
steps.fix: Re oil your hands before every piece.

steps.do: Flatten a piece in your oiled palm into a disc about 3 1/2 inches (9 cm) across. Put 1 heaped tbsp (15 g) of filling in the centre. Pull the edges up over it and pinch tightly to seal, like a dumpling. Set seam side down on an oiled plate.
steps.look: A sealed ball with no filling showing.
steps.mistake: A weak seal, so the sugar leaks out, burns in the pan and splatters.
steps.fix: Pinch firmly and twist off any excess dough at the top.

steps.do: Heat 2 tbsp (30 ml) oil in the pan over medium heat. Put 2 or 3 balls in, seam side down, and cook 30 to 60 seconds until the bottom is golden.
steps.look: A light golden base and a gentle sizzle.
steps.mistake: High heat, which burns the outside before the sugar melts.
steps.fix: Medium heat; they need time for the filling to melt.

steps.do: Flip each ball and immediately press it down firmly with the oiled press into a flat round about 4 inches (10 cm) across. Hold for a few seconds. Cook 1 to 2 minutes until golden.
steps.look: A flat, round pancake; the sugar starts to melt and you may see it bubble at the edges.
steps.mistake: Pressing before flipping, so the raw top sticks to the press.
steps.fix: Flip first, then press the cooked side.

steps.do: Flip again, lower the heat slightly and cover the pan for 1 minute so the filling melts fully. Cook until both sides are deep golden and crisp.
steps.look: Golden brown, crisp edges and a slightly puffed centre.
steps.mistake: Serving with unmelted, grainy sugar inside.
steps.fix: Cover the pan for a minute to trap heat and melt the filling.

steps.do: Cool for 1 minute before serving, folded in half in a paper cup or on a plate.
steps.look: When bitten, molten brown syrup with nuts runs out.
steps.mistake: Eating immediately; the filling is like hot caramel and burns.
steps.fix: Wait a full minute, and warn guests.

dishes.science: Glutinous rice flour's amylopectin starch gelatinises into a sticky, elastic gel, adding chew and a slight stretch that plain wheat dough lacks. The yeast creates gas that keeps the dough light even after pressing. Pressing flattens the dough thin so heat reaches the sugar filling quickly; brown sugar melts and dissolves in the moisture from the dough and nuts into a syrup. Covering the pan traps steam and heat, which finishes the melting without burning the outside. The molten filling is extremely hot because sugar syrup holds heat well and can be far above the boiling point of water, which is why it scalds more than a jam filling.
dishes.plating: Fold each hotteok in half, sugar side in, and stand it in a small paper cup, street style, or lay two overlapping on a plate with a scoop of vanilla ice cream and a drizzle of honey.

pairing.drink: Korean barley tea or a sweet cinnamon punch (sujeonggwa). Both echo the cinnamon.

variations: Seed hotteok: fill with toasted sunflower and pumpkin seeds with the sugar, as sold in Busan.
Savoury japchae hotteok: fill with seasoned glass noodles and vegetables.
Green tea hotteok: add 2 tsp (4 g) matcha to the dough.
safety: The melted sugar filling is extremely hot; let them cool a minute and warn guests.
Contains wheat, dairy and nuts (walnuts and peanuts).

video.search: hotteok Korean sweet pancake brown sugar filling

dishes.title: Kanelbullar (Swedish Cardamom Cinnamon Buns)
dishes.summary: A soft, enriched dough perfumed with freshly ground cardamom, rolled with a butter, sugar and cinnamon filling, folded, cut into strips and twisted into knots, then glazed with egg and topped with pearl sugar. Swedish buns teach a different shaping from the rolled spiral, and show what fresh ground cardamom brings to a dough.
skills: a butter, sugar and cinnamon filling
equipment: Stand mixer with dough hook, or a large bowl
Mortar and pestle for the cardamom
Two baking trays lined with baking paper

ingredients.note: beaten with 1 tbsp (15 ml) milk for glazing

mise: Split the cardamom pods, tip out the black seeds and grind them finely in the mortar.
Warm the milk; soften the butter for the dough and the filling.
Beat the filling butter with the brown sugar, cinnamon and cardamom to a spreadable paste.
Line two trays.

timeline.do: Grind cardamom; make and knead the dough; rise 1 hour.
Roll, fill, fold, cut and knot.
Second proof 45 minutes; oven to 425°F (220°C).
Glaze, pearl sugar; bake 10 to 12 minutes.
Cool on a rack; serve warm.

steps.do: Mix the flour, yeast, sugar, salt and cardamom. Add the warm milk and mix on low until a shaggy dough forms. Add the soft butter in pieces and knead on medium for 8 to 10 minutes.
steps.look: A smooth, soft, elastic dough that springs back slowly when poked and smells strongly of cardamom.
steps.mistake: Underkneading, so the buns are dense and do not hold their twists.
steps.fix: Knead until it passes the windowpane test: a small piece stretches thin enough to see light through.

steps.do: Cover and leave in a warm place about 1 hour until doubled.
steps.look: Doubled, domed dough; a floured finger poked in leaves a dent that springs back slowly.
steps.mistake: Under proofing, giving tight, heavy buns.
steps.fix: Wait until doubled; a cool kitchen can take 90 minutes.

steps.do: Roll the dough on a lightly floured surface into a rectangle about 16 by 12 inches (40 by 30 cm). Spread the filling evenly over it right to the edges.
steps.look: An even rectangle with a thin, even layer of filling.
steps.mistake: Cold, hard filling that tears the dough.
steps.fix: Make sure the filling is very soft and spreadable.

steps.do: Fold the dough in three like a letter, along the long side, to make a strip about 16 by 4 inches (40 by 10 cm). Roll lightly to press. Cut across into 12 strips about 1 1/4 inch (3 cm) wide.
steps.look: Neat strips with visible layers of filling.
steps.mistake: Pressing too hard, squeezing the filling out.
steps.fix: Roll gently, just to seal the layers.

steps.do: To knot: hold a strip at both ends and twist it in opposite directions several times. Wind it twice around two fingers, then bring the end over the top and tuck it underneath into the centre. Set on the tray, tucked end down.
steps.look: A compact, twisted knot with the filling showing in the twists.
steps.mistake: Loose knots that unravel in the oven.
steps.fix: Tuck the end firmly under the bun.

steps.do: Cover loosely and proof 45 minutes until puffy. Heat the oven to 425°F (220°C).
steps.look: The buns swell by about half and look soft and airy.
steps.mistake: Over proofing, so the buns collapse and lose their shape.
steps.fix: Press one gently: if the dent springs back slowly, they are ready.

steps.do: Brush gently with the egg glaze and sprinkle generously with pearl sugar. Bake 10 to 12 minutes, one tray at a time.
steps.look: Deep golden brown, glossy buns with white sugar on top; the filling bubbles slightly.
steps.mistake: Overbaking, which dries them out.
steps.fix: Pull them when deep golden; they bake fast at this heat.

steps.do: Cool on the rack for 10 minutes and eat warm, ideally within a few hours.
steps.look: Soft, fragrant buns with sticky, caramelised edges.
steps.mistake: Storing them uncovered, so they stale.
steps.fix: Freeze extras once cool and reheat 5 minutes at 350°F (180°C).

dishes.science: Cardamom's aroma comes from volatile oils, mainly cineole and terpinyl acetate, held inside the seeds; grinding them fresh releases the oils, and pre ground cardamom loses them quickly. Kneading develops gluten so the dough is elastic enough to stretch, twist and hold its knot. The butter, sugar and milk enrich the dough, tenderising it and helping it brown. Folding the filled dough creates layers, and twisting exposes them, so the filling caramelises in the ridges during the short, hot bake. The high oven sets the outside quickly and browns it before the inside dries. Pearl sugar is made of dense, compressed sugar that does not melt at baking temperatures, so it stays as crunchy white nuggets.
dishes.plating: Serve two or three buns on a small plate or a wooden board with a cup of strong black coffee, in the Swedish manner of fika. A pat of soft butter on the side is optional.

pairing.drink: Strong, freshly brewed black coffee. Its roast and acidity balance the sweet, spiced bun.
pairing.brennans: Congregation Single-Origin Coffee: the house single origin coffee on the Brennan's list, a fitting fika cup; read the origin from the coffee card on shift.

variations: Kardemummabullar: leave out the cinnamon and use a cardamom and sugar filling.
Classic spirals: roll the filled rectangle into a log, cut slices 1 inch (2.5 cm) thick and bake in paper cases.
Semla: shape plain buns, bake, and fill with almond paste and whipped cream.
safety: Contains wheat, dairy and egg.
