dishes.title: Kolaches
dishes.summary: Soft, rich yeast buns with a deep well pressed into each, filled with fruit or poppy seed filling and sprinkled with posipka, a buttery crumb, then baked golden. The Czech filled bun builds on enriched dough with a new challenge: fillings that must stay in their well as the dough rises around them.
equipment: Stand mixer with dough hook, or a large bowl
Two baking trays lined with baking paper
A small glass or spice jar with a flat 1 1/2 inch (4 cm) base, floured, for pressing wells

ingredients.note: plus 1 tbsp (14 g) melted for brushing
simmered with 1/2 cup (120 ml) water and 2 tbsp (25 g) sugar, then puréed thick

mise: Make the fillings so they can cool and thicken: simmer the apricots 15 minutes and purée; simmer the poppy seeds with the milk, sugar and butter for 8 to 10 minutes until thick, then cool.
Rub the posipka ingredients together into coarse crumbs and chill.
Warm the milk; soften the butter; separate the yolks.
Line the trays.

timeline.do: Make fillings and posipka; make the dough; rise 1 hour.
Divide into 12 balls; rise 30 minutes.
Press deep wells; fill; posipka; rest 20 minutes. Oven to 375°F (190°C).
Glaze edges; bake 15 to 18 minutes.
Brush with butter; cool.

steps.do: Mix the flour, yeast, sugar, salt and zest. Add the milk and yolks and mix to a shaggy dough. Add the soft butter in pieces and knead 8 minutes until smooth and soft. Cover and rise 1 hour until doubled.
steps.look: A soft, silky, slightly sticky dough that doubles.
steps.mistake: Too much flour, making dense buns.
steps.fix: Keep it soft; flour your hands, not the dough.

steps.do: Divide into 12 equal pieces of about 2 oz (55 g) and roll each into a smooth ball. Set 2 inches (5 cm) apart on the trays, flatten slightly, cover and rise 30 minutes.
steps.look: Smooth, puffy balls.
steps.mistake: Balls too close together, so they merge in the oven.
steps.fix: Space them well; use both trays.

steps.do: Dip the flat glass base in flour and press it firmly into the centre of each bun, down almost to the tray, to make a wide, deep well with a raised rim.
steps.look: A deep well about 1 1/2 inches (4 cm) across with a thick rim of dough.
steps.mistake: A shallow well, which the dough closes up as it rises, pushing the filling out.
steps.fix: Press deep. Press again just before filling if the wells have risen back.

steps.do: Fill each well with 1 heaped tbsp (20 g) of apricot or poppy seed filling. Sprinkle posipka over the filling and rim. Rest 20 minutes while the oven heats to 375°F (190°C).
steps.look: Neat wells of filling under a sandy crumb.
steps.mistake: Loose, runny filling that boils over in the oven.
steps.fix: Cook fillings until thick enough to hold a mound.

steps.do: Brush the dough rims with beaten egg, avoiding the filling. Bake 15 to 18 minutes until golden.
steps.look: Golden brown buns; filling set and glossy; posipka lightly coloured.
steps.mistake: Pale, underbaked buns that are doughy underneath.
steps.fix: Check the base: it should be golden. Bake a few minutes more if pale.

steps.do: Brush the rims with melted butter as soon as they come out, then cool on a rack.
steps.look: Soft, shiny rims.
steps.mistake: Skipping the butter, so the crust is drier.
steps.fix: Brush while hot for a soft crust.

dishes.science: Enriching a dough with milk, egg yolk, sugar and butter shortens the gluten strands and adds tenderness and colour; yolk lecithin also keeps the crumb soft and fine. The well must be pressed deep because the dough keeps rising in the oven as the yeast's gas expands with heat, an effect called oven spring, which pushes the base up and the walls in. Fillings are cooked thick because sugar and fruit pectin or poppy seeds hold water once reduced; a thin filling boils in the oven heat and overflows. Posipka is a rubbed in crumb: cold butter coats flour and sugar so the topping bakes into sandy, crisp clusters rather than melting.
dishes.plating: Arrange the kolaches on a board or a plate in a mix of fillings so the colours alternate, apricot orange and poppy seed black, and dust the rims lightly with icing sugar. Serve with coffee.

pairing.drink: A cup of coffee, or a glass of Tokaji or sweet Riesling. Coffee balances the sweet dough; a sweet wine echoes the apricot.

variations: Cream cheese kolaches: fill with cream cheese beaten with sugar, egg yolk and lemon zest.
Prune (povidla) kolaches: fill with a thick plum butter.
Klobasnek: wrap the same dough around a small sausage for the savoury Texan style bun.
safety: Contains wheat, dairy, egg and poppy seeds.

video.search: Czech kolaches poppy seed apricot posipka

dishes.title: Linzer Torte
dishes.summary: A short, spiced pastry made with ground toasted hazelnuts, filled with redcurrant jam and topped with a lattice, baked until dark biscuit brown and left a day to mature. The Austrian tart teaches a nut pastry too fragile to handle warm, and the patience to chill, patch and wait.
equipment: 8 inch (20 cm) loose bottomed tart tin, about 1 inch (2.5 cm) deep
Rolling pin and two sheets of baking paper
Sharp knife or fluted pastry wheel
mise: Toast the ground hazelnuts on a tray at 350°F (180°C) for 6 to 8 minutes, stirring once, until fragrant and light golden; cool completely.
Cube the butter and keep it cold.
Separate the eggs; zest the lemon.
Grease the tart tin lightly.

timeline.do: Toast nuts; make the dough; chill 2 hours.
Line tin, jam, lattice; chill 20 minutes.
Bake 40 to 50 minutes at 350°F (180°C).
Cool completely in the tin; wrap and keep a day.
Dust with icing sugar; cut and serve.

steps.do: Pulse or rub the flour, hazelnuts, sugar, spices, salt and zest with the cold butter until it looks like coarse damp sand.
steps.look: Even, cool crumbs with no visible butter lumps larger than a pea.
steps.mistake: Overworking until it is a warm paste.
steps.fix: Work quickly and stop at crumbs; chill the bowl if it warms.

steps.do: Add the yolks and rum and pulse or press just until the dough clumps together. Gather into a disc, wrap and chill 2 hours.
steps.look: A soft, crumbly dough that holds when pressed.
steps.mistake: Kneading the dough, which makes it oily and tough.
steps.fix: Bring it together in as few movements as possible.

steps.do: Take two thirds of the dough and press it into the tin with your fingers, covering the base about 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick and pushing it 3/4 inch (2 cm) up the sides.
steps.look: An even layer with no thin spots or gaps.
steps.mistake: Trying to roll and lift this soft dough, which tears.
steps.fix: Press it in by hand; it is meant to be patched.

steps.do: Spread the jam evenly over the base, leaving the sides clear.
steps.look: A smooth layer of jam about 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick.
steps.mistake: A loose jam that floods the pastry as it warms.
steps.fix: Use a firmly set jam, or simmer it 5 minutes to thicken and cool it.

steps.do: Roll the remaining dough between two sheets of baking paper to 1/8 inch (3 mm) thick. Chill it flat 10 minutes, then cut into strips 1/2 inch (1.2 cm) wide. Lay half the strips across the tart in one direction and the rest diagonally across them to make a diamond lattice. Patch any breaks with your fingers and press the ends onto the edge.
steps.look: A neat lattice of strips over the red jam, pressed to the rim.
steps.mistake: Strips that are too warm, which break and stick.
steps.fix: Chill the sheet again whenever it softens; breaks are simply pressed back together.

steps.do: Brush the lattice and rim with beaten egg, press flaked almonds around the edge and chill 20 minutes. Bake at 350°F (180°C) for 40 to 50 minutes.
steps.look: Deep biscuit brown pastry and jam bubbling slowly between the strips.
steps.mistake: Underbaked, pale pastry that is soft and greasy.
steps.fix: Bake until it is a deep golden brown; cover the edge with foil if it darkens too fast.

steps.do: Cool completely in the tin on a rack. Wrap and keep at room temperature for a day before cutting.
steps.look: The pastry firms and the spices mellow and deepen.
steps.mistake: Cutting it warm, so it crumbles and the jam runs.
steps.fix: Wait a full day; the crumb softens slightly as it absorbs moisture from the jam.

steps.do: Dust lightly with icing sugar and cut into wedges with a sharp knife.
steps.look: Clean wedges showing the jam layer and lattice.
steps.mistake: Dusting heavily so it hides the lattice.
steps.fix: A light dusting at the edges only.

dishes.science: Nearly half the dry weight of this pastry is ground nut, which contains fat and protein but none of the gluten forming proteins in wheat, so the dough has very little elasticity. That is why it tears easily and must be pressed and patched rather than stretched, and why the texture is short and crumbly. Toasting the hazelnuts develops nutty flavour through browning reactions and dries them slightly. Chilling solidifies the butter, which is the only thing holding the dough together, so cold dough can be handled. The day of rest lets moisture move from the jam into the pastry, softening it slightly, while the spices' aromatic compounds spread through the fat and mellow.
dishes.plating: Set a wedge on a plate so the lattice faces the guest, with a spoon of softly whipped cream or crème fraîche beside it. A few fresh redcurrants on the side echo the jam.

pairing.drink: A sweet German Riesling Auslese. Its apricot and honey sweetness and high acidity cut through the rich nut pastry and match the redcurrant.
pairing.brennans: Dr. Hermann ‘Erdener Prälat’ Riesling Auslese 2014 (375 ml): a sweet Mosel Riesling from the Brennan's list with the acidity for a buttery nut tart.

variations: Linzer biscuits: roll the dough, cut rounds, cut small windows from half, bake 10 to 12 minutes and sandwich with jam.
Almond Linzer: replace the hazelnuts with ground almonds.
Apricot Linzer: use apricot jam and a little orange zest.
safety: Contains wheat, dairy, egg, hazelnuts and almonds.

dishes.title: Baklava
dishes.summary: Many layers of paper thin phyllo brushed with clarified butter, filled with finely ground pistachios, cut into diamonds before baking and soaked with cold lemon syrup the moment it leaves the oven. Baklava unites three skills: handling phyllo, clarifying butter and the syrup rule of one hot and one cold.
equipment: 8 by 8 inch (20 by 20 cm) metal baking tin
Small saucepan for clarifying butter, and a fine sieve lined with muslin
Two clean, damp tea towels and clingfilm

ingredients.note: about 24 sheets, trimmed to fit the tin; thaw overnight in the fridge

mise: Make the syrup first: boil the sugar and water 8 to 10 minutes until slightly syrupy, add the lemon juice, then cool completely.
Clarify the butter: melt it slowly, let it bubble gently 5 minutes until the foam separates, skim the foam, then pour the clear butter off through the muslin, leaving the milky solids behind.
Grind the pistachios with the sugar to fine crumbs.
Unroll the phyllo, trim it to the tin size and cover it with clingfilm and a damp towel so it does not dry out.
Heat the oven to 340°F (170°C).

timeline.do: Make and cool the syrup; clarify the butter; grind nuts.
Layer the phyllo and nuts; cut into diamonds.
Bake 45 to 50 minutes until deep golden.
Cold syrup over hot baklava; rest 4 hours.
Serve at room temperature.

steps.do: Brush the tin with clarified butter. Lay a sheet of phyllo in it, brush it lightly all over with butter, and repeat until you have 10 buttered sheets. Keep the waiting sheets covered.
steps.look: Flat, evenly buttered sheets lying smooth in the tin.
steps.mistake: Leaving the phyllo uncovered, so it dries and cracks within minutes.
steps.fix: Keep it under clingfilm and a damp towel; a cracked sheet is simply laid in and buttered, and it disappears in the stack.

steps.do: Spread half the ground pistachios evenly over the stack. Add 4 more buttered sheets, then the remaining pistachios.
steps.look: An even layer of bright green nuts.
steps.mistake: Clumped nuts, which make uneven layers.
steps.fix: Spread with your fingers or a spoon to the edges.

steps.do: Top with the remaining 10 sheets, buttering each, and brush the top sheet generously.
steps.look: A level stack with a glossy buttered top.
steps.mistake: Pressing the layers down hard, which makes the baklava dense.
steps.fix: Lay each sheet gently; let the butter do the joining.

steps.do: With the sharp knife, cut all the way through to the base into diamonds: first parallel lines 1 1/4 inches (3 cm) apart, then diagonal lines across them. Hold the top layers steady with your other hand as you cut.
steps.look: Clean diamonds cut right through to the tin.
steps.mistake: Cutting only the top, or trying to cut after baking, which shatters the layers.
steps.fix: Cut fully before baking; recut along the lines after baking if needed.

steps.do: Bake 45 to 50 minutes until deep golden brown and crisp all the way through.
steps.look: A deep, even golden top; the sides are golden too when you peer down the edge.
steps.mistake: Pulling it pale, so the inner layers are soggy and white.
steps.fix: Bake until truly golden; lift a corner to check the bottom.

steps.do: As soon as it leaves the oven, pour the cold syrup slowly and evenly over the hot baklava, into the cuts.
steps.look: A loud crackle as the syrup hits, and it sinks into the layers.
steps.mistake: Pouring hot syrup on hot baklava, which makes it soggy.
steps.fix: One hot, one cold, always.

steps.do: Sprinkle with the chopped pistachios and leave uncovered at room temperature for at least 4 hours to absorb the syrup. Recut along the lines and serve.
steps.look: Glossy, crisp diamonds, moist inside but still flaky.
steps.mistake: Covering or refrigerating, which softens the top layers.
steps.fix: Keep it uncovered at room temperature, loosely covered with paper after a day.

dishes.science: Phyllo is dough rolled so thin that each sheet is almost all surface. Brushed with fat, each sheet bakes separately: water in the dough turns to steam, the butter fries the sheets crisp, and the layers stay distinct. Clarified butter is used because it has had its water and milk solids removed; water would make the layers soggy and milk solids would burn in a long bake. Cutting before baking matters because baked phyllo shatters under a knife. The soak follows the same temperature rule as basbousa: hot pastry full of steam pulls in cold, thick syrup through the cuts, while the crisp layers stay intact. Lemon juice partly inverts the sugar, which stops the syrup crystallising.
dishes.plating: Serve three diamonds on a small plate, slightly overlapping, with a scattering of chopped pistachio and, in the Turkish manner, a small spoon of kaymak or clotted cream beside them. Serve with Turkish coffee or black tea.

pairing.drink: A sweet Austrian Auslese or Tokaji, or Turkish coffee. Sweet wine needs to be at least as sweet as the dessert, with enough acidity to cut the butter.
pairing.brennans: Kracher ‘Cuvée’ Auslese Burgenland 2017: a rich Austrian sweet wine on the Brennan's list, sweet enough for syrup soaked pastry.

variations: Walnut baklava: replace the pistachios with walnuts and add 1 tsp (2 g) cinnamon.
Greek style: use a syrup with honey, cinnamon and orange peel, and a walnut and almond filling.
Baklava rolls: roll buttered sheets round a thin stick with nuts, push to crinkle, slide off and bake.
safety: Hot sugar syrup burns; make it first and let it cool.
Contains wheat, dairy and pistachios (a tree nut).

dishes.title: Pecan Pie
dishes.summary: An all butter pastry case, crimped and part baked, filled with toasted pecans in a dark sugar, syrup and egg custard with bourbon and vanilla, baked until just set with a slight wobble at the centre. The Southern pie trains the crust and a sweet custard that sets as it cools.
skills: a sugar custard set just to a wobble
equipment: 9 inch (23 cm) glass or metal pie dish
Large mixing bowl and pastry blender or fingertips
Baking paper and baking beans or rice
Baking tray for toasting nuts and to hold the pie

ingredients.item: Dark corn syrup or cane syrup

mise: Cube the butter and chill it; put ice in the water.
Toast the pecans at 350°F (175°C) for 8 minutes until fragrant; cool.
Melt the butter for the filling and let it cool slightly.
Have baking paper and baking beans ready.

timeline.do: Make pastry; chill 1 hour.
Roll, line, crimp; chill 30 minutes.
Part blind bake 20 minutes.
Fill and bake 50 to 60 minutes at 350°F (175°C).
Cool at least 4 hours.
Slice and serve.

steps.do: Mix the flour, salt and sugar. Rub or cut in the cold butter until most is the size of peas with a few larger, flatter pieces. Sprinkle over 3 tbsp (45 ml) iced water and toss with a fork until it holds when squeezed, adding more water a teaspoon at a time if needed. Press into a disc, wrap and chill 1 hour.
steps.look: A shaggy dough that holds together when pressed, with visible streaks of butter.
steps.mistake: Overworking or adding too much water, which makes a tough, shrinking crust.
steps.fix: Stop as soon as it holds; visible butter is what makes it flaky.

steps.do: Roll the dough on a floured surface to a 12 inch (30 cm) circle about 1/8 inch (3 mm) thick, turning it often. Lift it into the dish, ease it into the corners without stretching, and trim to 1 inch (2.5 cm) overhang. Fold the overhang under and crimp: push the edge between the thumb and finger of one hand with the knuckle of the other, all the way round. Chill 30 minutes. Heat the oven to 375°F (190°C).
steps.look: An even crust with a high, fluted edge.
steps.mistake: Stretching the pastry into the dish, so it shrinks down the sides in the oven.
steps.fix: Lift and lower the pastry into place; chill before baking.

steps.do: Line the chilled case with baking paper, fill with beans and bake 15 minutes. Remove the paper and beans and bake 5 minutes more. Lower the oven to 350°F (175°C).
steps.look: Set, pale golden pastry with no shiny raw patches.
steps.mistake: Skipping the blind bake, so the base is soggy under the wet filling.
steps.fix: Part bake the case; patch any cracks with a little raw dough.

steps.do: Whisk the eggs, brown sugar, syrup, melted butter, bourbon, vanilla and salt until smooth, without whisking in air. Scatter the toasted pecans in the case and pour the filling over.
steps.look: The pecans float up to form a top layer.
steps.mistake: Beating the filling hard, which makes a foamy top that cracks.
steps.fix: Whisk gently just to combine.

steps.do: Set the pie on a tray and bake at 350°F (175°C) for 50 to 60 minutes. Cover the edge with foil after 25 minutes if it browns quickly.
steps.look: The filling is puffed and set at the edges, with the centre trembling slightly as one mass, like set jelly, when nudged. A thermometer in the centre reads about 200°F (93°C).
steps.mistake: Baking until the centre is firm, which makes the filling grainy and cracked.
steps.fix: Pull it at a slight wobble; it sets as it cools.

steps.do: Cool on a rack for at least 4 hours before slicing.
steps.look: A set, glossy filling that holds a clean cut.
steps.mistake: Cutting warm, so the filling runs.
steps.fix: Patience; it sets fully only when cool.

steps.do: Slice with a sharp knife, wiping between cuts.
steps.look: Clean slices showing a crisp crust, a set amber custard and a crown of pecans.
steps.mistake: A dull knife that drags the pecans.
steps.fix: Use a sharp knife, cut firmly, wipe between cuts.

dishes.science: Flaky pastry depends on pieces of cold butter staying separate in the dough. In the oven, the water in those pieces turns to steam and pushes the layers apart, while the fat keeps them from fusing. Too much water or handling develops gluten, which makes the crust tough and shrink. Blind baking sets the base before a wet filling arrives. The filling is a custard of eggs and a lot of sugar. Sugar raises the temperature at which egg proteins set, so pecan filling sets near 200°F (93°C), much higher than a plain custard, and it firms further as it cools. Toasting pecans develops their flavour through browning and makes them crisper; their oils carry the toasted aroma.
dishes.plating: Set a slice on a plate with the point towards the guest. Add a spoon of softly whipped cream lightly sweetened and flavoured with a few drops of bourbon, or a small scoop of vanilla ice cream, beside it. A few pecan halves on the plate echo the filling.

pairing.drink: A late bottled vintage or tawny port, or a bourbon served neat. Rich fruit and caramel stand up to the very sweet filling.
pairing.brennans: Feist Late Bottled Vintage Port 2006: a port from the Brennan's list with the dark fruit and sweetness for a caramel nut pie.

variations: Chocolate pecan pie: scatter 3 oz (85 g) chopped dark chocolate with the pecans.
Maple pecan pie: replace the corn syrup with dark maple syrup.
Pecan tartlets: bake in a muffin tin with small pastry rounds for 20 to 25 minutes.
safety: The filling contains raw egg and must bake until set; the centre reaches about 200°F (93°C), well past the 160°F (71°C) that cooks eggs.
Refrigerate leftovers after a few hours and eat within 3 days.
Contains wheat, dairy, egg and pecans (a tree nut).

dishes.title: Tarte Tatin
dishes.summary: Halved apples packed tightly into a pan of amber caramel and butter, cooked on the hob until they drink the caramel, covered with a disc of pastry, baked and turned out hot so the glossy caramelised apples sit on top of the crisp pastry. The upside down tart joins caramel, fruit and pastry, and ends with a confident flip.
equipment: 9 to 10 inch (23 to 25 cm) heavy ovenproof frying pan, cast iron or a tatin mould
Small sharp knife and a melon baller or teaspoon for coring
Serving plate larger than the pan
Oven gloves and long sleeves for the flip

ingredients.item: Firm apples (Braeburn, Cox, Pink Lady or Golden Delicious)

mise: Peel, halve and core the apples. If you have time, leave them uncovered in the fridge overnight to dry out a little, so they release less juice.
Roll the pastry into a circle 1 inch (2.5 cm) larger than the pan, prick it all over with a fork, and keep it cold on a tray in the fridge.
Cube the butter.
Heat the oven to 400°F (200°C).
Have the serving plate, oven gloves and a clear path to the counter ready for the flip.

timeline.do: Peel, halve and core the apples; leave uncovered in the fridge.
Roll and chill the pastry; oven on.
Make the caramel; pack in the apples.
Cook on the hob 15 to 20 minutes.
Cover with pastry; bake 25 to 30 minutes.
Rest 5 minutes; flip; serve warm.

steps.do: Sprinkle the sugar evenly over the base of the dry pan and set it over medium heat. Leave it, swirling the pan gently once it begins to melt, until all the sugar has melted and turned a deep amber, 6 to 10 minutes.
steps.look: The sugar melts from the edges, turns clear, then golden, then a deep amber like dark honey, and smells of caramel.
steps.mistake: Stirring early, which can make the sugar clump and crystallise.
steps.fix: Swirl rather than stir. If lumps form, keep heating gently; they will melt.

steps.do: Take the pan off the heat and stir in the cold butter and salt. It will bubble up fiercely. Stir until smooth.
steps.look: A thick, glossy, bubbling butterscotch.
steps.mistake: Caramel taken too dark, almost black, which turns bitter.
steps.fix: If it smells burnt, start again; bitterness does not cook out.

steps.do: Off the heat, pack the apple halves into the pan standing on their sides, rounded side down against the base, in tight concentric circles. Squeeze them in; fill the centre with a halved half. Sprinkle the lemon juice over.
steps.look: Apples packed so tightly they lean against each other with no gaps.
steps.mistake: Loose packing; the apples shrink as they cook and leave holes in the finished tart.
steps.fix: Overcrowd them; add extra pieces into any gaps.

steps.do: Return the pan to medium low heat and cook 15 to 20 minutes, without stirring, spooning the caramel juices over the apples now and then.
steps.look: The caramel bubbles up around the apples, turning darker, and the apples soften at the base and turn golden; the juices reduce to a thick syrup.
steps.mistake: Lots of thin juice remaining, which floods the plate when turned out.
steps.fix: Cook longer to reduce the juice; tilt the pan and spoon off excess if needed.

steps.do: Take the pan off the heat. Lay the cold pastry over the apples and tuck the edges down inside the pan around them with a spoon, like tucking in a blanket.
steps.look: The pastry covers the apples snugly with the edges tucked in.
steps.mistake: Tucking with your fingers, which burns.
steps.fix: Use a spoon handle; the caramel is extremely hot.

steps.do: Bake at 400°F (200°C) for 25 to 30 minutes.
steps.look: The pastry is puffed, crisp and deep golden brown, and caramel bubbles up at the edges.
steps.mistake: Pale, soft pastry that collapses when turned out.
steps.fix: Bake until deep golden; the pastry becomes the base.

steps.do: Rest for 5 minutes only. Run a knife round the edge. Put on oven gloves, place the serving plate upside down over the pan, hold both firmly together and, in one confident movement, turn them over away from your body. Lift the pan off.
steps.look: Glossy, deep amber apples on a crisp pastry base, with caramel running down the sides.
steps.mistake: Waiting too long, so the caramel sets and welds the apples to the pan; or hesitating mid flip.
steps.fix: Flip at 5 minutes. Any apple that sticks can be lifted out and replaced on the tart with a knife.

steps.do: Spoon any caramel left in the pan over the apples. Serve warm with cold crème fraîche.
steps.look: Shiny caramel glaze over every apple.
steps.mistake: Serving straight from the oven, when caramel is dangerously hot.
steps.fix: Let it cool for 10 minutes before cutting.

dishes.science: Caramelisation breaks sugar molecules apart under heat into hundreds of new compounds that give colour and a rich, slightly bitter flavour; deep amber is the point where flavour is greatest before burning. Adding cold butter stops the cooking and creates an emulsion of fat and caramel. Apples release juice as their cell walls soften in the heat; cooking on the hob before baking reduces that juice into the caramel, so the finished tart is glossy rather than wet. Drying the apples overnight reduces the water they carry. Firm apples hold their shape because their pectin is more stable. The pastry, baked on top, stays crisp because it is above the steam; flipping makes it the base.
dishes.plating: Bring the whole tart to the table on its plate, then cut into wedges with a sharp knife. Set each wedge on a warm plate with a quenelle of cold crème fraîche beside it, never on top, so the guest gets hot and cold, sweet and sharp in each forkful.

pairing.drink: A late harvest Chenin Blanc or a Calvados. Apple and honey notes match the caramelised fruit, and acidity balances the sweetness.
pairing.brennans: Pineapple Tarte Tatin: the Brennan's dessert menu serves a tatin built on charred pineapple and puff pastry, the same caramel and flip technique with a different fruit.

variations: Pear tatin: use firm pears, quartered, and add a little star anise to the caramel.
Savoury shallot tatin: caramelise whole shallots in butter, sugar and balsamic vinegar, top with pastry and bake.
Shortcrust tatin: use a sweet shortcrust instead of puff pastry for a crumblier base.
safety: Caramel is far hotter than boiling water and sticks to skin. Wear long sleeves and oven gloves for the flip, turn away from your body, and keep children well away.
Never taste caramel from the pan.
Contains wheat and dairy.
